beginner.content:
What is Algorithm Complexity?

  • Time complexity describes how an algorithm's running time grows as the input size (n) grows. Space complexity describes how memory usage grows.
  • Big-O notation expresses the WORST-CASE growth rate, ignoring constant factors - it answers "how does this scale?" not "how many milliseconds does it take?"

Common Complexities (fastest to slowest)

1. O(1) - Constant: array index access.
2. O(log n) - Logarithmic: binary search.
3. O(n) - Linear: a single loop over n elements.
4. O(n log n) - Linearithmic: efficient sorting (merge sort, quicksort average case).
5. O(n²) - Quadratic: nested loops over n elements (bubble sort).
6. O(2ⁿ) - Exponential: naive recursive Fibonacci.

What is a 1D Array?

A 1D array is a fixed-size, contiguous block of memory holding elements of the same type, accessed by an integer index starting at 0.
  • Contiguous memory is what makes arr[i] an O(1) operation - the address is computed directly as base + i * elementSize.
  • Fixed size - once created, a Java array cannot grow or shrink; use ArrayList when the size is unknown up front.
  • Default values: 0 for numeric types, false for boolean, null for objects.

Common Pitfalls

  • ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException - accessing arr[arr.length] or a negative index throws at runtime; Java never silently clamps or wraps.
  • length is a field, not a method - no parentheses, unlike String.length() or List.size().
  • Arrays of objects hold references: int[][] grid = new int[3][] creates 3 null rows, not usable 2D storage, until each row is assigned.

expert.content:
Arrays in Memory - Stack, Heap and Reference Semantics

The array reference lives on the stack (or inside an enclosing object); the array's actual elements live on the heap as one contiguous block. Assigning b = a copies the reference, not the data - both variables then point at the same backing array.

Passing an array to a method passes that reference by value: the method cannot reassign the caller's variable, but it CAN mutate the elements the reference points to.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why is array access O(1) but insertion at the front O(n)?Access computes a direct memory offset; inserting at the front must shift every following element one slot over
Can a Java array change size after creation?No - the length is fixed at allocation. "Growing" an array (as ArrayList does internally) means allocating a new, bigger array and copying elements over
Is passing an array to a method pass-by-value or pass-by-reference?Pass-by-value of the reference itself - the method gets its own copy of the pointer, so it can mutate elements but cannot make the caller's variable point elsewhere
What's the default value of an uninitialized int[] element?0 - Java always zero-initializes primitive array slots, unlike C which leaves them as garbage

beginner.content:
What is a 2D Array?

A 2D array is "an array of arrays" - grid[i] is itself an array (a row), so grid[i][j] means "column j of row i".
  • Rectangular (rows all the same length) is the common case, but Java allows jagged arrays where each row has a different length.
  • grid.length = number of rows; grid[0].length = number of columns in row 0.
  • Traversal is almost always a nested loop: outer loop over rows, inner loop over columns.

Jagged Arrays

Each row can be a different length because grid[i] is an independent array object - only allocating new int[3][] creates the rows as null until you assign each one.

expert.content:
Common Matrix Techniques

  • Transpose: swap grid[i][j] with grid[j][i] - only meaningful for square matrices in-place.
  • Rotate 90° clockwise: transpose, then reverse each row.
  • Spiral traversal: shrink four boundaries (top, bottom, left, right) inward after each pass.
  • Row-major vs column-major: Java stores arrays row-major, so iterating row-by-row is cache-friendlier than column-by-column for large matrices.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How do you rotate a matrix 90 degrees without extra space?Transpose the matrix, then reverse each row - both are in-place O(1) extra space operations
What is a jagged array?A 2D array whose rows are independently-sized 1D arrays, so different rows can have different lengths
Why is row-major traversal faster than column-major for a large matrix?Java stores each row contiguously in memory; iterating row-by-row hits sequential memory addresses (cache-friendly), while column-by-column jumps across rows (cache misses)

beginner.content:
What is a Prefix Sum?

A prefix sum array pre stores running totals: pre[i] = arr[0] + arr[1] + ... + arr[i]. Once built (O(n) once), the sum of ANY range [l, r] can be answered in O(1) instead of O(n):
  • sum(0, r) = pre[r]
  • sum(l, r) = pre[r] - pre[l - 1] (for l > 0)
This is the single biggest win of prefix sums: many range-sum queries, each O(1), after one O(n) precomputation.

expert.content:
Prefix Sum for Subarray-Sum Problems

The classic trick: to find a subarray whose sum equals k, note that sum(i+1, j) = pre[j] - pre[i] = k means pre[i] = pre[j] - k. Store every prefix sum seen so far in a HashMap, and for each new prefix check whether pre[j] - k already occurred - this turns an O(n²) brute force into O(n).

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why use a prefix sum array instead of recomputing each range sum?Recomputing is O(n) per query; a prefix array answers each range-sum query in O(1) after one O(n) build
What's the 2D generalization of prefix sums?A 2D prefix sum matrix, letting any rectangular sub-rectangle's sum be computed in O(1) using inclusion-exclusion
When does prefix sum stop being the right tool?When the underlying array is updated frequently between queries - a Fenwick Tree or Segment Tree supports O(log n) updates that a plain prefix array cannot

beginner.content:
What is a Suffix Sum?

The mirror image of a prefix sum: suf[i] = arr[i] + arr[i+1] + ... + arr[n-1], the total from index i to the end. Built by scanning right to left.

Useful whenever a problem needs "everything to the right of index i" alongside "everything to the left" - a classic pairing is Product of Array Except Self, where result[i] = prefixProduct(0..i-1) * suffixProduct(i+1..n-1).

expert.content:
Product of Array Except Self - Prefix + Suffix Together

Compute, for every index i, the product of all elements except arr[i] - without using division and in O(n) time. Combine a left-to-right prefix product pass with a right-to-left suffix product pass.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why avoid division in Product of Array Except Self?Division breaks if any element is zero, and the problem is often explicitly asked without division as a constraint
Can suffix sum be computed with only O(1) extra space (excluding the output)?Yes - fold the suffix pass into the output array itself using a single running variable, as shown in the product-except-self example

beginner.content:
What is a Difference Array?

A difference array is the inverse trick of a prefix sum: it makes range updates O(1) instead of O(range length). Given diff[i] = arr[i] - arr[i-1], to add val to every element in [l, r]:
  • diff[l] += val
  • diff[r + 1] -= val (if r + 1 is within bounds)
After all updates are applied, take the prefix sum of diff to recover the final array - each range update was O(1), and the one final reconstruction pass is O(n).

expert.content:
Why Difference Array Beats Naive Range Updates

Naively adding val to every element in [l, r] is O(r - l + 1) per update - with Q updates over a range of size n, worst case O(Q·n). A difference array makes EVERY update O(1), and reconstructs the final array with a single O(n) prefix-sum pass at the end - total O(Q + n) instead of O(Q·n).

The trade-off: difference array only helps when you apply ALL updates first and THEN read the final array. If you need to read intermediate states between updates, you need a Segment Tree with lazy propagation instead.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What problem does a difference array solve that a plain array doesn't?Applying many range-add updates efficiently - each update becomes O(1) instead of O(range size)
How do you get the final array back from a difference array?Take its prefix sum - diff[i] accumulated left to right reconstructs the actual values
What if you need to query the array's state BETWEEN updates?A plain difference array can't do that - use a Segment Tree with lazy propagation for range updates plus arbitrary-time range queries

beginner.content:
Maximum Subarray Sum in O(n)

Kadane's Algorithm finds the maximum-sum contiguous subarray in a single pass. The insight: at each index, a running sum either extends the previous subarray or restarts from the current element - whichever gives a bigger sum.
  • currentSum = Math.max(arr[i], currentSum + arr[i])
  • maxSum = Math.max(maxSum, currentSum)
If currentSum ever drops below arr[i] itself, it's better to abandon the old subarray and start fresh at i.

expert.content:
Tracking the Actual Subarray, and the All-Negative Edge Case

Interviewers often ask for the subarray's START and END indices, not just the sum - track them whenever a "restart" happens. Also watch the all-negative-numbers case: the algorithm still works correctly and returns the least-negative single element, as long as you seed maxSum with arr[0] rather than 0.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is Kadane's Algorithm's time and space complexity?O(n) time, O(1) extra space - a single pass with two running variables
How does it handle an array of all negative numbers?Correctly returns the maximum (least negative) single element, as long as maxSum is seeded with arr[0], not 0
How would you adapt Kadane's for maximum PRODUCT subarray?Track both a running max AND running min product at each step, since multiplying by a negative number can flip the smallest product into the largest

beginner.content:
What is the Sliding Window Pattern?

Sliding window solves problems about a contiguous range (subarray/substring) by maintaining a window with two pointers, left and right, and sliding it across the array instead of recomputing from scratch for every position.
  • Fixed-size window: the window size k never changes - slide it one step at a time, subtracting the element leaving and adding the element entering.
  • Variable-size window: grow the window by moving right; shrink it by moving left whenever a condition is violated.
Both turn an O(n·k) or O(n²) brute force into O(n).

expert.content:
Variable-Size Window - Smallest Subarray with Sum ≥ Target

Grow the window by moving right forward, adding each new element. As soon as the window's sum meets the target, shrink from left as much as possible while it still meets the target, recording the smallest length seen.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why is sliding window O(n) instead of O(n*k)?Each element enters and leaves the window at most once, so total pointer movement across the whole run is bounded by 2n, not n*k
When would you reach for sliding window vs two pointers generally?Sliding window is specifically for CONTIGUOUS ranges (subarrays/substrings); two pointers is the broader technique that also covers non-contiguous scans, like on a sorted array
How do you handle "longest substring with at most K distinct characters"?Variable-size window with a frequency map: grow right and add to the map; shrink from left whenever distinct count exceeds K, tracking the max window length seen

beginner.content:
What is the Two Pointers Technique?

Two pointers walk through data using two indices instead of one, usually moving toward each other (from both ends) or in the same direction at different speeds - turning an O(n²) nested-loop scan into O(n).
  • Opposite ends: left = 0, right = n-1, move them toward the middle based on a condition. Requires the array to be sorted for most classic uses (like Two Sum on a sorted array, or reversing an array).
  • Same direction: both pointers start at 0 and move forward at different rates (e.g. fast/slow pointer, or a read/write pointer for in-place removal).

expert.content:
Removing Duplicates In-Place - Same-Direction Two Pointers

A "read pointer" (i) scans every element while a "write pointer" (writeIndex) only advances when a genuinely new value is found - this compacts a sorted array to its unique elements in O(n) time and O(1) extra space, no auxiliary array needed.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why does the opposite-ends two-pointer Two Sum require a sorted array?The decision to move left up or right down relies on knowing whether the current sum is too small or too large relative to sorted order - it breaks on unsorted data
What's the time complexity of the opposite-ends technique?O(n) - each pointer moves at most n times total, combined, before they meet
How is this different from sliding window?Sliding window pointers move in the SAME direction over a contiguous range; two pointers can move toward each other from opposite ends, which sliding window never does

beginner.content:
The Fast & Slow (Tortoise and Hare) Pattern

Two pointers start at the same place but move at different SPEEDS - typically slow moves 1 step and fast moves 2 steps per iteration. It's most famous for cycle detection in a linked list, but the same idea applies to arrays where values act as "next pointers" (each value tells you the next index to jump to).

The key insight: if there's a cycle, the fast pointer will eventually lap the slow pointer and they will meet INSIDE the cycle - if there's no cycle, fast simply reaches the end first.

expert.content:
Why the Meeting Point Reveals the Cycle's Start

Let the distance from the start to the cycle entrance be a, and the cycle length be c. By the time slow and fast meet, slow has traveled a + b steps and fast has traveled a + b + k·c for some integer k, while covering exactly twice slow's distance. Solving that equation shows the distance from the START back to the cycle entrance equals the distance from the MEETING POINT forward to the cycle entrance - which is exactly why resetting one pointer to the start and advancing both at speed 1 makes them meet at the entrance.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What are the two phases of Floyd's cycle-finding algorithm?Phase 1 finds ANY meeting point inside the cycle by running slow/fast until they collide; Phase 2 resets one pointer to the start and advances both at speed 1 until they meet again, which happens exactly at the cycle's entrance
What's the time and space complexity?O(n) time, O(1) space - no hash set needed, unlike the naive "seen before" approach
Where else does this exact pattern appear?Linked list cycle detection (LeetCode "Linked List Cycle II"), and detecting a repeated number in a bounded array by treating values as implicit next-pointers, as shown above

beginner.content:
Rotating an Array by K Positions

Rotating right by k moves every element k positions forward, wrapping around at the end. The naive approach shifts one element at a time, k times - O(n·k). A much better approach uses O(n) extra space with a temp array, or O(1) extra space with the reversal trick.

expert.content:
The Reversal Trick - O(1) Extra Space

Rotating right by k is equivalent to: reverse the WHOLE array, then reverse the first k elements, then reverse the remaining n-k elements. Three reversals, each O(n), still O(n) total time but with NO extra array.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why take k % n before rotating?Rotating by exactly n positions returns the array to its original order, so any k larger than n has redundant full rotations that can be stripped off
What's the time/space trade-off between the extra-array and reversal approaches?Both are O(n) time; the extra-array approach uses O(n) space, the reversal trick uses O(1) extra space at the cost of three passes instead of one
How is left rotation different from right rotation?Left rotation by k is the same as right rotation by (n - k); with the reversal trick, just reverse the first k elements, then the rest, then the whole array (order of the three reversals flips)

beginner.content:
What is Cyclic Sort?

Cyclic Sort is a specialized O(n) sorting technique for arrays containing numbers in a known, bounded range like [1, n] or [0, n-1] - each number's VALUE tells you its correct index. Instead of comparing elements, swap each value directly to the index it belongs at.
  • At index i, the correct value is i + 1 (for a 1..n range).
  • If arr[i] isn't already correct, swap it to its rightful home and check again - don't advance i until the current slot is correct.
This "swap into place" idea is also the base for a whole family of "find the missing/duplicate number" problems.

expert.content:
Finding the Missing Number - The Real Power of Cyclic Sort

After a cyclic sort pass, ANY index i where arr[i] != i + 1 immediately points at a missing or duplicate number - no second pass or hash set needed.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why is cyclic sort O(n) when it has a swapping loop nested inside a while loop?Each swap places at least one value into its FINAL correct position - across the whole run, at most n swaps total happen, giving O(n) amortized despite the nested-looking structure
What class of problems is cyclic sort the classic solution for?"Find the missing number", "find all duplicates", "find the first missing positive" - any problem with values in a known, small range tied to array indices
Why doesn't cyclic sort work for arbitrary unbounded integers?It relies on the value directly telling you the target index (value - 1); with unbounded or negative values there's no valid index to map to

beginner.content:
The Dutch National Flag Problem

Named by Edsger Dijkstra after the three horizontal stripes of the Dutch flag: given an array of only three distinct values (classically 0, 1, 2), sort it in a single pass with O(1) extra space - no counting sort, no comparison sort needed.

Three pointers partition the array into three zones as they scan:
  • low - boundary of the "all 0s" zone (everything before it is 0)
  • mid - the current element being examined
  • high - boundary of the "all 2s" zone (everything after it is 2)

expert.content:
Why mid Doesn't Advance After Swapping with high

When arr[mid] == 2, swapping brings an UNKNOWN value from index high into mid - it could be 0, 1, or another 2, and hasn't been classified yet. Advancing mid anyway would skip examining it. Contrast with the low swap: the value that lands at mid from low is guaranteed to be either 0 or 1 (since everything before low was already 0), so it's always safe to move past it.

This three-way partitioning is also the core of 3-way Quicksort, which handles arrays with many duplicate keys far better than standard 2-way partitioning.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is the time and space complexity of the Dutch flag algorithm?O(n) time, single pass, O(1) extra space - it's an in-place partition, not a comparison sort
Why can't a simple counting sort be used instead?Counting sort works fine here too and is also O(n), but Dutch flag is the go-to answer when the interviewer specifically wants a SINGLE-PASS in-place partition, as with 3-way quicksort partitioning
Where else does this exact 3-pointer partition pattern show up?3-way (Dutch-flag) Quicksort partitioning, which is much faster than standard quicksort on arrays with many duplicate keys

beginner.content:
Merging Overlapping Intervals

Given a list of intervals like [start, end], merge all that overlap into the minimum set of non-overlapping intervals.
  • Step 1: sort intervals by START time - O(n log n). Without sorting, overlaps can't be detected in one pass.
  • Step 2: scan left to right; if the current interval's start is ≤ the last merged interval's end, merge them (extend the end); otherwise, start a new interval.

expert.content:
Inserting a New Interval Without Re-Sorting

If the intervals are ALREADY sorted and non-overlapping (a common follow-up), a new interval can be inserted and merged in a single O(n) pass, without re-sorting: collect intervals ending before the new one starts, merge all overlapping ones together, then collect the rest.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why must intervals be sorted by start time before merging?Merging relies on scanning left to right and only ever comparing against the last merged interval - without sorting, a later interval could overlap an earlier one already passed
What's the overall time complexity of merge intervals?O(n log n), dominated by the initial sort; the merge scan itself is O(n)
How do you check if two intervals overlap at all?a and b overlap when a.start <= b.end AND b.start <= a.end - equivalently, they do NOT overlap when one ends strictly before the other begins

beginner.content:
What is a Monotonic Array?

An array is monotonic if it is entirely non-increasing or entirely non-decreasing - values only move in one direction (or stay flat), never both.
  • Monotonically increasing: arr[i] ≤ arr[i+1] for every i.
  • Monotonically decreasing: arr[i] ≥ arr[i+1] for every i.
Checking is a single O(n) pass: track whether any "increasing" violation and any "decreasing" violation occurs - the array is monotonic if at least one of the two never happens.

expert.content:
Why "Monotonic" Matters: It Unlocks Binary Search and Monotonic Stacks

A monotonic array/sequence is the precondition that makes several techniques valid:
  • Binary search only works correctly on a monotonic (sorted) sequence - the "discard half" logic depends on knowing which half the target could possibly be in.
  • Monotonic stack/queue problems (Next Greater Element, Sliding Window Maximum) work by MAINTAINING a monotonic invariant inside the stack/deque as elements are processed, popping anything that would break monotonicity.
  • "Binary search on the answer" problems require proving the answer space itself is monotonic (e.g. "if capacity X works, every capacity > X also works") before binary search can be applied to it.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is the time complexity of checking if an array is monotonic?O(n) - a single pass tracking two booleans is enough, no need to check increasing and decreasing separately in two passes
Why does binary search require a sorted (monotonic) array?Discarding half the search space on each step is only valid if you can guarantee the target cannot be in the discarded half - that guarantee comes directly from monotonic order
What does it mean for a monotonic STACK to be increasing?The elements from bottom to top of the stack are in increasing order - maintained by popping any element that is smaller than the one about to be pushed

beginner.content:
What is a Range Query?

A range query asks a question about a sub-range [l, r] of an array - "what's the sum?", "what's the minimum?", "how many elements are ≥ x?" - and it usually needs to be answered MANY times over the same array. The right data structure depends on whether the array changes between queries:
  • Static array, many sum queries: Prefix Sum - O(n) build, O(1) per query.
  • Array updated between queries, sum/min/max queries: Segment Tree or Fenwick Tree - O(log n) per update AND per query.
  • Static array, many min/max queries (no updates): Sparse Table - O(n log n) build, O(1) per query.

expert.content:
Choosing the Right Structure - the Decision Table

SituationStructureBuildQueryUpdate
No updates, sum queriesPrefix SumO(n)O(1)-
No updates, min/max queriesSparse TableO(n log n)O(1)-
Point updates, sum queriesFenwick Tree (BIT)O(n log n)O(log n)O(log n)
Point/range updates, min/max/sumSegment TreeO(n)O(log n)O(log n) point, O(log n) range with lazy propagation
Many range updates, one final readDifference ArrayO(n)O(n) at the endO(1) per update
Interviewers care most about WHY you'd pick one over another - a Sparse Table beats a Segment Tree for static min/max queries because it never needs to support updates, trading that flexibility for O(1) query time instead of O(log n).

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why can't prefix sum handle updates efficiently?A single update at index i invalidates every prefix sum from i onward, requiring an O(n) rebuild - a Fenwick or Segment Tree localizes the update cost to O(log n)
Why does a Sparse Table achieve O(1) min/max queries but not O(1) updates?It precomputes the answer for every power-of-two-length range; a range query is answered by combining two overlapping precomputed ranges (min/max tolerate overlap, unlike sum), but any update would invalidate many precomputed ranges
What does "lazy propagation" add to a Segment Tree?The ability to apply an update to an entire RANGE in O(log n) instead of O(n) - by marking a "pending update" at a node and only pushing it down to children when that subtree is actually visited

beginner.content:
Java Strings Are Immutable

Every "modification" of a String - concatenation, substring, replace - creates a new String object; the original is never changed. This is why building a string inside a loop with += is O(n²): each concatenation allocates a whole new copy.
  • Use StringBuilder for repeated modifications - it's mutable and appends in amortized O(1).
  • charAt(i), substring(l, r), toCharArray() are the core building blocks for most string algorithms.

expert.content:
String Pool and == vs equals()

String literals are interned into a shared string pool - two literals with the same text point at the SAME object, so == can appear to "work" by accident. Strings built with new String(...) or by concatenation at runtime are NOT pooled, so == silently breaks. Always use .equals() for content comparison.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why is repeated String concatenation in a loop O(n²)?Each += creates a brand new String, copying all previous characters plus the new one - across n iterations the total copying is 1+2+...+n = O(n^2)
When should you use StringBuilder over String?Whenever building a string incrementally, especially in a loop - StringBuilder appends into a resizable internal char array in amortized O(1)
Why should you never use == to compare string content?== compares object references, not characters - it only "works" for pooled literals, and silently breaks for strings built with new String(...) or produced by concatenation

beginner.content:
Counting Character Occurrences

A huge fraction of string problems (anagrams, first-unique-character, valid-anagram-window) start with a frequency count. For ASCII/lowercase-letter input, a fixed-size int[26] array is faster than a HashMap - no hashing/boxing overhead, direct index access via c - 'a'.

expert.content:
int[26] vs HashMap<Character, Integer>

For the common case of lowercase English letters, int[26] beats a HashMap on every axis: O(1) guaranteed array access (no hash collisions), no autoboxing of Character/Integer, and a tiny fixed memory footprint. Reach for a HashMap only when the character set is unknown or large (full Unicode, arbitrary bytes) where a fixed array would waste memory or not cover the range.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why prefer int[26] over a HashMap for lowercase-letter problems?Direct array indexing is faster than hashing and avoids Integer autoboxing overhead, and the fixed 26-slot size is a perfect match for the known alphabet
How do you check if two strings are permutations of each other using frequency counts?Build a frequency array for each and compare them for equality - or increment for one string and decrement for the other, then check all counts are zero
What's the time and space complexity of a frequency-count solution?O(n) time to build the count, O(k) space where k is the alphabet size (constant, e.g. 26) - so effectively O(1) space for a fixed alphabet

beginner.content:
What is an Anagram?

Two strings are anagrams if one can be rearranged into the other - same characters, same counts, different order. Two classic checks:
  • Sort both strings and compare - O(n log n).
  • Compare frequency counts - O(n), faster since it avoids sorting entirely.

expert.content:
Grouping Anagrams Together

A common follow-up: given a list of strings, group all anagrams together. The trick is finding a canonical key shared by every anagram of the same word - the sorted string is the simplest such key, since all anagrams sort to the identical character sequence.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why is the frequency-count anagram check faster than sorting?Sorting is O(n log n); counting each character once and comparing counts is O(n), with no comparison-based sort overhead
What key would you use to group anagrams without sorting each word?A fixed-length count signature, e.g. a 26-length frequency array converted to a string like "2#0#0#1#...", avoiding the O(n log n) sort per word entirely and doing O(n) counting instead
Does the anagram check work for Unicode strings?Not with a fixed int[26] array - use a HashMap instead, since Unicode has far more than 26 possible characters

beginner.content:
Checking a Palindrome

A palindrome reads the same forward and backward. The classic O(n) check uses two pointers starting at both ends, moving toward the middle - no need to build a reversed copy of the string.

expert.content:
Longest Palindromic Substring - Expand Around Center

A palindrome is symmetric around its center. For each possible center (n centers for odd-length palindromes, n-1 "between characters" centers for even-length ones), expand outward while both sides match - O(n²) total, much simpler to reason about than DP, and the standard interview answer before jumping to Manacher's Algorithm for the O(n) solution.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why does "expand around center" need 2n-1 centers, not n?Odd-length palindromes are centered ON a character (n such centers); even-length palindromes are centered BETWEEN two characters (n-1 such centers) - together 2n-1
What's the time complexity of expand-around-center, and what beats it?O(n^2) worst case (n centers, each expansion up to O(n)); Manacher's Algorithm solves the same problem in O(n) using previously computed palindrome radii to skip redundant comparisons
How would you check if a string can be REARRANGED into a palindrome?Count character frequencies - a rearrangement is possible only if at most one character has an odd count (that one becomes the middle character for odd-length strings)

beginner.content:
Substring vs Subsequence

These two terms get confused constantly, and interviewers test the distinction directly:
  • Substring - a CONTIGUOUS block of characters. "abc" has substrings "a", "ab", "abc", "b", "bc", "c" (n(n+1)/2 total).
  • Subsequence - characters in the SAME relative order, but NOT necessarily contiguous (can skip characters). "abc" has subsequences "a", "b", "c", "ab", "ac", "bc", "abc", "" (2ⁿ total).
"ac" is a subsequence of "abc" (skip the b) but NOT a substring (not contiguous).

expert.content:
Why Subsequence Problems Reach for Dynamic Programming

There are 2ⁿ possible subsequences of a length-n string - far too many to enumerate for problems like Longest Common Subsequence or Longest Increasing Subsequence. DP works by defining dp[i][j] as "the answer using only the first i characters of string A and first j of string B", building up from smaller subproblems instead of generating every subsequence explicitly.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How many substrings and how many subsequences does a length-n string have?n(n+1)/2 substrings (contiguous), 2^n subsequences (each character independently included or not)
Is every substring also a subsequence?Yes - contiguous is a special case of "order preserved, gaps allowed"; the reverse is not true
How do you check if one string is a subsequence of another in O(n)?Two pointers: walk through the longer string once, advancing the shorter string's pointer only when characters match; if the shorter pointer reaches the end, it's a valid subsequence

beginner.content:
Prefixes and Suffixes of a String

A prefix is a substring starting at index 0; a suffix is a substring ending at the last index. A length-n string has exactly n non-empty prefixes and n non-empty suffixes.
  • s.startsWith(p) checks if p is a prefix.
  • s.endsWith(suf) checks if suf is a suffix.
These are the building blocks of pattern-matching algorithms like KMP, which precomputes "the longest prefix that is also a suffix" for every position of the pattern.

expert.content:
The Longest Prefix-Suffix (LPS) Array - the Engine Behind KMP

For each prefix of a pattern, lps[i] stores the length of the longest proper prefix of pattern[0..i] that is ALSO a suffix of it. This precomputed array is exactly what lets KMP pattern matching skip re-examining characters after a mismatch, achieving O(n + m) instead of the naive O(n·m).

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is the Longest Common Prefix of a list of strings, and how do you find it in O(n*m)?The longest string that is a prefix of every string in the list; compare characters column by column across all strings, stopping at the first mismatch or shortest string
Why must a prefix-suffix in the LPS array be "proper"?A proper prefix/suffix excludes the whole string itself - otherwise every string trivially has itself as both its own prefix and suffix, making the array useless for skipping comparisons
What real algorithm is built directly on top of the LPS array?The KMP (Knuth-Morris-Pratt) pattern matching algorithm, which uses it to avoid re-scanning characters already known to match after a mismatch

beginner.content:
What is String Hashing?

String hashing converts a string into a single number (a "hash") so two strings can be compared in O(1) instead of O(length) - useful for detecting duplicates, comparing substrings quickly, or as the key in a HashMap.

A simple polynomial hash treats the string as a number in some base p: hash(s) = s[0]·p⁰ + s[1]·p¹ + ... + s[n-1]·pⁿ⁻&sup9; (mod M)

expert.content:
Hash Collisions and Why We Need Two Moduli

Hashing is PROBABILISTIC: two different strings CAN map to the same hash (a collision), especially against an adversarial test case crafted to break a known base/modulus combo (common on competitive judges). The standard defenses:
  • Use a large prime modulus (e.g. 10⁹ + 7) to keep collision probability low.
  • For competitive programming, compute two independent hashes (different base/modulus pairs) and combine them - the chance both collide simultaneously is astronomically small.
  • In an interview, ALWAYS mention that hashing is probabilistic and a false positive is possible, then verify with a direct character comparison as a safety net if correctness matters more than speed.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why can string hashing give a false positive?Different strings can map to the same hash value (a collision) - the hash function compresses a large string space into a smaller number space, so collisions are mathematically unavoidable
Why use a prime base and a large prime modulus?Primes reduce systematic patterns/cycles in the hash distribution, spreading values more uniformly and lowering the practical collision rate
What problem does Rolling Hash solve on top of basic string hashing?Recomputing a hash for every substring window from scratch is O(n) per window; rolling hash updates the hash in O(1) as the window slides, by removing the outgoing character's contribution and adding the incoming one

beginner.content:
What is a Rolling Hash?

A rolling hash updates a window's hash in O(1) as the window slides by one position, instead of recomputing from scratch (which would be O(k) per slide, O(n·k) overall). It's the "sliding window" idea applied to string hashing, and it's the engine behind Rabin-Karp pattern matching.

To slide a window of size k forward by one character: remove the outgoing character's contribution, shift everything, then add the incoming character.

expert.content:
Rabin-Karp: Rolling Hash Applied to Pattern Matching

Rabin-Karp finds all occurrences of a pattern in a text by comparing HASHES of each window instead of characters directly - O(n) average time using a rolling hash to slide the window in O(1), only falling back to an O(m) direct character comparison on a hash MATCH (to rule out a false-positive collision).

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time complexity of Rabin-Karp with rolling hash?O(n + m) average case; worst case O(n*m) if many hash collisions force repeated character-by-character verification (rare with a good modulus)
Why must you verify a hash match with a direct string comparison?A hash match doesn't guarantee content equality due to possible collisions - skipping verification risks false positives
What other problems use the exact same rolling-hash technique?Longest duplicate substring (binary search on length + rolling hash to check for duplicates of that length), and checking if one string is a rotation of another

beginner.content:
The Naive Pattern Matching Approach

Given a text of length n and a pattern of length m, find every position where the pattern occurs. The naive approach tries every starting position and compares character by character - O(n·m) worst case (e.g. text "aaaa...a", pattern "aaa...b").

expert.content:
Why Naive Matching is O(n·m) and What Beats It

The naive approach's worst case comes from repeatedly re-examining characters it already matched, right before a mismatch forces it to restart from the very next position - throwing away all that earlier work. Three algorithms fix this in different ways:
AlgorithmIdeaTime
KMPPrecomputes a prefix-suffix table so a mismatch skips ahead without re-checking known-matching charactersO(n + m)
Rabin-KarpRolling hash compares window hashes in O(1), only verifying character-by-character on a hash matchO(n + m) average
Z AlgorithmBuilds a Z-array of "longest match with the prefix" for every position of pattern+text combinedO(n + m)

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What input causes naive pattern matching's worst-case O(n*m)?Highly repetitive text where many characters match before a late mismatch, e.g. text = "aaaa...a", pattern = "aaa...b" - every starting position does nearly a full comparison
How does KMP avoid re-examining already-matched characters?It never moves the text pointer backward; on a mismatch, it uses the precomputed LPS array to jump the pattern pointer forward to the next possible match position, skipping known-good comparisons
When would you pick Rabin-Karp over KMP?When searching for MULTIPLE patterns at once (hash each pattern, then check every window's hash against the set) - Rabin-Karp generalizes to this naturally, while KMP is built for a single pattern

beginner.content:
Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) Pattern Matching

KMP finds all occurrences of a pattern in a text in O(n + m) time - guaranteed, no bad worst case like the naive O(n·m) approach. The key idea: precompute an LPS array (Longest Proper Prefix which is also a Suffix) for the pattern, so that on a mismatch, the algorithm knows exactly how far it can safely skip WITHOUT re-checking characters it already knows match.

expert.content:
Why the Text Pointer i Never Moves Backward

This is what guarantees KMP's O(n + m) bound: i only ever increases, so the text is scanned at most once. All the "backtracking" happens on the PATTERN pointer j, which jumps using the LPS table instead of restarting from 0. Total work across the whole run is bounded by 2n comparisons (each advance of i does at most one comparison; each LPS fallback of j is amortized against earlier progress) plus the O(m) LPS precomputation.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is the time complexity of KMP, and why is it guaranteed (not just average-case)?O(n + m) - the text pointer only ever moves forward, and the LPS fallback on the pattern pointer is bounded by amortized analysis, unlike Rabin-Karp's average-case bound which assumes few hash collisions
What does lps[i] represent exactly?The length of the longest PROPER prefix of pattern[0..i] that is also a suffix of pattern[0..i] - "proper" meaning it excludes the whole substring itself
How do you find OVERLAPPING matches with KMP?After recording a full match, don't reset j to 0 - set j = lps[j-1] instead, which continues the search from the longest known-matching suffix, allowing overlapping occurrences to be found

beginner.content:
What is the Z Array?

For a string s, the Z array's entry z[i] is the length of the longest substring starting at i that matches a PREFIX of s. By definition z[0] is usually left undefined/0 (comparing the whole string to itself is trivial and unused).

For pattern matching, build the Z array of pattern + '#' + text (a separator character not in either string) - any position in the "text" section where z[i] == pattern.length() marks a match.

expert.content:
Pattern Matching with the Z Array - and Why the [left, right) Window Matters

The [left, right) window tracks the rightmost Z-box found so far (a substring known to match the prefix). When computing z[i] for an i INSIDE that window, the answer is already partly known from z[i - left] (the mirrored position) - this reuse is what makes the whole algorithm O(n) instead of O(n²), exactly the same idea as KMP's LPS fallback but framed differently.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How does the Z Algorithm compare to KMP for pattern matching?Both are O(n + m); Z is often considered more intuitive to derive (the array has a direct meaning: "match length with the prefix"), while KMP's LPS array requires more careful reasoning about what it represents
Why is a separator character needed between pattern and text?Without it, a match that spans across the pattern/text boundary could produce a Z value larger than the pattern length, causing false positives
What is z[i - left] reused for when i falls inside the current Z-box?Since s[left..right) is known to match s[0..right-left), position i inside it mirrors position i-left relative to the start - so z[i] can start from min(right-i, z[i-left]) instead of comparing from scratch

beginner.content:
Rabin-Karp: Hashing for Pattern Matching

Rabin-Karp finds a pattern in a text by comparing hashes of each candidate window instead of characters, sliding the window with a rolling hash in O(1) per step. Average case O(n + m); relies on verifying real matches with a direct comparison to rule out hash collisions.

expert.content:
Searching for Multiple Patterns Simultaneously

Rabin-Karp's real advantage over KMP shows up when searching for MANY patterns of the same length at once: hash every pattern into a HashSet, then slide one rolling-hash window across the text and check set membership - O(n + total pattern length) instead of running KMP once per pattern.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why is Rabin-Karp's worst case O(n*m) despite being O(n+m) on average?An adversarial input causing many hash collisions forces the O(m) direct-comparison fallback on nearly every window - rare in practice with a good modulus, but possible
When is Rabin-Karp preferred over KMP?Searching for multiple fixed-length patterns at once (hash them into a set, scan text once), or when a simple probabilistic solution is acceptable and easier to implement correctly under time pressure
What's the role of the modulus, and what happens if it's too small?It bounds the hash value's range; too small a modulus (or a predictable one, as in the demo above) increases collision frequency and can be deliberately exploited by adversarial test data

beginner.content:
Finding the Longest Palindromic Substring in O(n)

Expand-around-center finds the longest palindromic substring in O(n²). Manacher's Algorithm does the same job in O(n) by REUSING previously computed palindrome radii, the same "don't redo known work" idea behind KMP and the Z Algorithm.

The trick that avoids handling odd/even length palindromes separately: insert a separator character (like #) between every character (and at both ends), so every palindrome in the transformed string has ODD length.

expert.content:
The Full Manacher's Algorithm

Maintains a "rightmost palindrome boundary" (center C, right edge R), exactly mirroring the Z Algorithm's window reuse: for a position i inside the current rightmost palindrome, its radius can be seeded from its mirror position 2C - i before expanding further, avoiding redundant character comparisons.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why insert separator characters before running Manacher's?It normalizes every palindrome to odd length, so the algorithm handles even-length and odd-length palindromes with one uniform code path instead of two
What guarantees Manacher's O(n) time despite the nested while loop?The right boundary R only ever moves forward across the whole run - each expansion of the while loop advances R, so total expansion work is bounded by O(n), same amortized argument as the Z Algorithm
When would you use Manacher's over expand-around-center?When n is large enough that O(n^2) is too slow (competitive programming constraints, or n in the hundreds of thousands+) - for typical interview-sized inputs, expand-around-center is usually accepted and much simpler to write correctly

beginner.content:
Why a Trie for String Problems?

A Trie (prefix tree) stores strings character by character down a tree, so all words sharing a prefix share the same path from the root. This makes prefix-based operations - "does any word start with X?", "insert", "search" - O(word length) instead of scanning every word in the dictionary.

expert.content:
Word Search II - Trie + DFS Backtracking on a Grid

A classic hard interview problem: given a grid of letters and a dictionary of words, find every dictionary word that can be formed by a path of adjacent cells. Building a Trie of all dictionary words FIRST lets the DFS prune a search branch the moment no word shares that prefix - dramatically faster than checking each word independently against the whole grid.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time complexity of insert/search in a Trie?O(L) where L is the word's length - independent of how many other words are stored, unlike scanning a list of words
Why build a Trie for Word Search II instead of checking each word separately against the grid?The Trie lets the DFS share work across words with a common prefix and prune branches early the moment no dictionary word continues down that path - checking words independently repeats the same grid exploration for every word
What's the space trade-off of a Trie vs a HashSet of words?A Trie can use MORE memory when words share few prefixes (each node has overhead), but a HashSet can't answer "does any word start with X?" in better than O(number of words) - the Trie trades some memory for fast prefix queries

beginner.content:
What is a Singly Linked List?

A chain of nodes, each holding a value and a reference to the NEXT node - unlike an array, the elements are NOT contiguous in memory.
  • head points to the first node; the last node's next is null.
  • Insertion/deletion at the FRONT is O(1) - no shifting needed, unlike an array.
  • Random access (get(i)) is O(n) - there's no direct index, you must walk from the head.

expert.content:
Insertion at a Given Position and Deletion

Both require walking to the node just BEFORE the target position, then relinking pointers - O(n) to reach the position, O(1) for the relink itself. This is the opposite trade-off from an array: linked lists are cheap to modify once you're AT the right spot, expensive to get there; arrays are the reverse.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why is insertion at the front O(1) for a linked list but O(n) for an array?A linked list just repoints head to a new node; an array must shift every existing element one slot to the right to make room at index 0
Why is random access O(n) for a linked list?There's no formula to jump directly to index i like arr[i] - the only way to reach node i is by following next pointers from the head, one node at a time
When would you choose a LinkedList over an ArrayList in Java?Rarely in practice - ArrayList's cache locality usually wins even for front-insertion-heavy workloads; a genuine linked-list win is when you already hold a reference to the node and need O(1) insertion/deletion AT that exact node without re-searching

beginner.content:
What is a Doubly Linked List?

Each node holds a reference to BOTH the next node and the previous node, allowing traversal in either direction and O(1) deletion of a KNOWN node without needing to walk from the head to find its predecessor.

expert.content:
O(1) Deletion of a Known Node - Why This Matters

Given a REFERENCE to a node in a singly linked list, deleting it still requires an O(n) walk from the head to find its predecessor (to relink prev.next). A doubly linked list skips that walk entirely - the node already knows its own predecessor via prev. This is exactly why an LRU Cache is implemented with a doubly linked list: eviction and promotion both need O(1) removal of an arbitrary node.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the memory trade-off of a doubly linked list vs singly linked?Each node stores an extra pointer (prev), roughly doubling per-node pointer overhead, in exchange for backward traversal and O(1) deletion of a known node
Why does LRU Cache use a doubly linked list specifically?Moving a recently-used node to the front (or evicting the least-recently-used node at the back) both need O(1) removal-from-current-position plus O(1) insertion-elsewhere - only possible without an O(n) predecessor search because of the prev pointer
What is Java's built-in doubly linked list class?java.util.LinkedList implements both List and Deque using a doubly linked internal structure

beginner.content:
What is a Circular Linked List?

Instead of ending at null, the LAST node's next points back to the FIRST node, forming a loop. Useful for anything that naturally cycles: round-robin CPU scheduling, a circular playlist, or the Josephus problem.

expert.content:
Josephus Problem - The Classic Circular List Application

n people stand in a circle; starting from person 1, every kth person is eliminated until one remains. A circular linked list models this directly - no modulo-arithmetic index juggling needed, just remove the current node and advance k-1 steps around the ring.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How do you traverse a circular linked list without an infinite loop?Track the starting node and stop when the traversal returns to it, or track a known count of nodes and iterate exactly that many times
Why point at 'last' instead of 'head' in a circular singly linked implementation?last.next directly gives the head (O(1)), while also keeping O(1) access to the tail for appends - pointing at head alone would make appends O(n) to find the tail
What real systems use a circular linked list?Round-robin CPU/process scheduling, circular buffers for streaming data, and multiplayer turn rotation are classic examples

beginner.content:
Reversing a Linked List Iteratively

Reversing means flipping every node's next pointer to point BACKWARD instead of forward. Three pointers do it in one O(n) pass with O(1) extra space: prev, current, and a temporary to hold current.next before it gets overwritten.

expert.content:
Recursive Reversal, and Reversing Only a Sub-Range

The recursive version reverses the REST of the list first, then fixes up the current node's link - O(n) time like the iterative version, but O(n) space for the call stack instead of O(1). A common hard follow-up: reverse only nodes between positions left and right, leaving the rest untouched.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why is the temp variable for current.next needed before reversing the link?Once current.next is overwritten to point at prev, the original "next node" reference is lost forever unless it was saved first - the temp preserves the path forward
What's the space complexity trade-off between iterative and recursive reversal?Iterative: O(1) extra space. Recursive: O(n) space for the call stack - each recursive call stays on the stack until the base case returns
How would you reverse only nodes between position left and right?Walk to the node just before 'left', then run the standard iterative reversal for (right - left + 1) nodes, and finally reconnect the reversed segment's new head/tail back into the rest of the original list

beginner.content:
Detecting a Cycle with Two Pointers

Floyd's Cycle Detection (the "tortoise and hare") uses a slow pointer moving 1 step and a fast pointer moving 2 steps at a time. If there's a cycle, fast will eventually lap slow and they'll land on the SAME node; if there's no cycle, fast reaches null first.

expert.content:
Why Fast is Guaranteed to Catch Slow (Not Just Skip Past It)

Once BOTH pointers are inside the cycle, fast gains exactly 1 net position on slow every iteration (fast moves 2, slow moves 1). Since the cycle has finite length, the GAP between them shrinks by 1 each step until it hits 0 - fast cannot "jump over" slow, because a gap of 1 becomes a gap of 0 (a meeting), never a gap of -1.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time and space complexity of Floyd's algorithm?O(n) time, O(1) space - a huge improvement over the O(n) space naive approach of storing every visited node in a HashSet
Why check fast != null AND fast.next != null in the loop condition?fast.next.next would throw a NullPointerException if fast.next were null - both checks together guarantee it's safe to jump two steps ahead
Could fast ever skip over slow and miss the meeting?No - once both are in the cycle, the gap between them shrinks by exactly 1 each iteration (2-step minus 1-step), so it passes through every integer value down to 0, guaranteeing a meeting

beginner.content:
Finding WHERE the Cycle Begins

Detecting a cycle exists is phase 1 of Floyd's algorithm. Phase 2 finds exactly which node the cycle starts at: reset one pointer to the head, keep the other at the meeting point, then advance BOTH one step at a time - they meet exactly at the cycle's entrance.

expert.content:
The Math Behind Why Phase 2 Works

Let a = distance from head to the cycle's start, b = distance from the cycle's start to the meeting point, and c = the remaining cycle length back to the start. When they meet: slow traveled a + b, fast traveled a + b + n·(b + c) for some integer n, and fast's distance is exactly double slow's. Substituting and simplifying shows a = (n-1)·(b+c) + c - meaning "distance from head to cycle start" equals "distance from meeting point to cycle start" (mod cycle length). That's precisely why resetting one pointer to head and stepping both by 1 makes them converge at the entrance.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why reset a pointer to HEAD instead of just continuing from the meeting point?The meeting point is some arbitrary position inside the cycle, not necessarily near the start - the head-reset + equal-speed trick uses the distance relationship proven by Floyd's math to land exactly on the entrance
What's the overall time and space complexity of finding the cycle start?O(n) time (two O(n) phases), O(1) space - same complexity class as just detecting a cycle exists
What LeetCode problem is this exactly, and what's the naive alternative?"Linked List Cycle II" - the naive alternative is a HashSet tracking visited nodes, O(n) time but O(n) space; Floyd's approach keeps O(n) time while dropping to O(1) space

beginner.content:
Merging Two Sorted Linked Lists

Given two already-sorted linked lists, merge them into one sorted list in O(n + m) time and O(1) extra space (reusing existing nodes) - the same core comparison step as the merge phase of Merge Sort, just applied to linked nodes instead of array slots.

expert.content:
Merging K Sorted Lists with a Min-Heap

Merging just two lists is O(n + m). Merging K lists naively (repeatedly merging two at a time) is O(K·N) where N is the total node count. A min-heap holding the current HEAD of each list gives O(N log K): always extract the smallest head, advance that list, repeat.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why use a dummy head node in the merge function?It eliminates a special-case check for "is this the very first node" - tail always has something valid to attach to, and the real result is simply dummy.next
Why is the min-heap approach O(N log K) instead of O(N log N)?The heap never holds more than K elements at once (one per list) - every poll/offer is O(log K), and there are N total nodes processed, giving O(N log K)
What's the alternative to a min-heap for merging K lists, and its complexity?Pairwise merge (merge lists 2 at a time, repeat) gives O(N log K) too, via divide-and-conquer pairing - asymptotically the same as the heap approach, sometimes preferred to avoid heap overhead for small K

beginner.content:
Finding Where Two Lists Merge

Two singly linked lists that eventually MERGE into a shared tail (like a Y shape) - find the exact node where they intersect. The naive approach: HashSet all nodes of one list, then check each node of the other list for membership - O(n + m) time, O(n) space.

expert.content:
The Two-Pointer O(1)-Space Trick

Run a pointer down each list; when a pointer reaches the end, redirect it to the OTHER list's head. Both pointers then travel exactly lenA + lenB total steps before either reaching the intersection node or both becoming null together - the length difference between the two lists is automatically cancelled out by the redirect.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why does redirecting a pointer to the other list's head equalize the distances?Pointer A travels lenA + lenB total steps before reaching the intersection (or end); pointer B travels lenB + lenA - the SAME total, so they arrive at the intersection point simultaneously regardless of each list's individual length
What if the two lists don't intersect at all?Both pointers eventually become null at the same "step" (after traveling lenA + lenB each), and pA == pB == null exits the loop correctly, returning null
Why compare node REFERENCES, not values, to detect the intersection?Two different nodes could coincidentally hold the same value; only reference equality (pA == pB) guarantees it's the actual shared node, not a value collision

beginner.content:
Removing the Nth Node From the End - One Pass

Removing the Nth node from the END is awkward because a singly linked list only knows its length by walking it fully first (two passes), OR by using a gap of N between two pointers to solve it in ONE pass.

expert.content:
Why the Dummy Node and the n+1 Head Start Matter

The dummy node handles the edge case of removing the HEAD itself (when n equals the list's full length) without a special-cased branch - slow can safely start "before" the real head. Advancing fast exactly n+1 steps (not n) is what leaves slow pointing at the node just BEFORE the target, ready to relink in one step, rather than landing ON the target itself.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time/space complexity of the two-pointer one-pass solution?O(L) time (L = list length), O(1) extra space - a single traversal, versus a two-pass approach that also achieves O(L) time but conceptually walks the list twice
Why is a dummy head node used here specifically?It uniformly handles removing the actual head node (when n == list length) without an if-branch, since slow always ends up at a real "previous" node, even when that's the dummy itself
What happens if n is larger than the list's length?The loop advancing fast would run off the end (fast becomes null) before completing n+1 steps, causing a NullPointerException - a robust implementation should validate n against the list length first

beginner.content:
Finding the Middle Node

Beyond cycle detection, fast/slow pointers solve "find the middle in one pass" cleanly: when fast (2 steps) reaches the end, slow (1 step) is exactly at the middle - no need to count the length first and walk again.

expert.content:
Palindrome Linked List - Combining Three Techniques

Checking if a linked list reads the same forward and backward, in O(n) time and O(1) extra space, combines THREE fast/slow-pointer-family techniques in sequence: find the middle, reverse the second half, then compare both halves node by node.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why does the "find middle" trick give the SECOND middle on an even-length list?When fast reaches exactly the end (fast == null) after an even number of nodes, slow has advanced n/2 times, landing on the second of the two middle nodes - a deliberate, useful convention for the palindrome check
Is the palindrome check's O(1) space claim really true if it reverses half the list?Yes - the reversal happens IN PLACE by rewiring existing next pointers, no new nodes or auxiliary array are allocated
What's a courtesy step a careful implementation would add after the palindrome check?Re-reverse the second half back to restore the original list structure, if the caller shouldn't observe the list being mutated

beginner.content:
What is an LRU Cache?

A Least-Recently-Used cache holds a fixed number of items; when full, adding a new item EVICTS the item that hasn't been accessed in the longest time. Both get and put must run in O(1) - which needs a HashMap (O(1) lookup) PLUS a doubly linked list (O(1) reordering) working together:
  • HashMap maps key → node, for instant lookup.
  • Doubly linked list keeps items ordered by recency - most-recently-used at the front, least-recently-used at the back, ready for O(1) eviction.

expert.content:
Building LRU Cache From Scratch - HashMap + Doubly Linked List

The from-scratch version (what interviews actually want) makes the O(1) behavior explicit: every get or put moves the touched node to the FRONT of the list; when over capacity, the node at the BACK (tail) is evicted - both are O(1) because it's a doubly linked list with direct node references from the HashMap.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why does LRU Cache need BOTH a HashMap and a doubly linked list?The HashMap alone can't maintain recency order; the linked list alone can't do O(1) lookup by key - together, the map gives instant node access and the list gives O(1) reordering/eviction
Why specifically a DOUBLY linked list, not singly linked?Moving a node to the front requires removing it from its CURRENT position first, which needs its predecessor - only O(1) reachable via a prev pointer, avoiding an O(n) search
Why use dummy head/tail nodes instead of tracking real head/tail references?They eliminate null-checking edge cases (empty list, removing the only node) - every real node always has a valid prev and next to work with, even at the boundaries

beginner.content:
What is a Stack?

A stack is a LIFO (Last In, First Out) structure - the last element pushed is the first one popped, like a stack of plates. Three core operations, all O(1):
  • push(x) - add to the top
  • pop() - remove and return the top
  • peek() - look at the top without removing it
Java's Deque (via ArrayDeque) is the recommended stack implementation - java.util.Stack is legacy and synchronized (slower, unneeded overhead for single-threaded use).

expert.content:
Array-Backed vs Linked-List-Backed Stack

ArrayDeque is backed by a resizable circular array - amortized O(1) push/pop with excellent cache locality, no per-node pointer overhead. A hand-rolled linked-list-backed stack is simpler to reason about (push/pop just manipulate the head) but pays for a Node allocation and pointer chasing on every operation. This is exactly why the JDK recommends ArrayDeque over building your own linked stack, and over the legacy Stack class.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why does the JDK recommend ArrayDeque over java.util.Stack?Stack extends the legacy synchronized Vector, adding unnecessary locking overhead for single-threaded use; ArrayDeque is unsynchronized and faster, explicitly documented as the preferred stack implementation
What's the amortized time complexity of push on a resizable-array-backed stack?O(1) amortized - most pushes are O(1), and the occasional resize (doubling capacity, copying all elements) is O(n) but happens rarely enough that it averages out to O(1) per operation
How would you implement a stack using two queues, or vice versa?Classic exercise: a queue-based stack makes push O(n) (rotate the queue after adding) or pop O(n), depending which operation you optimize - it's a good way to test understanding of the FIFO vs LIFO distinction

beginner.content:
Checking Balanced Brackets

The textbook stack application: scan left to right, PUSH every opening bracket, and on a closing bracket POP and check it matches the most recent unmatched opener. Any mismatch, or leftover brackets at the end, means unbalanced.

expert.content:
Minimum Insertions to Make Parentheses Valid

A harder follow-up: given an unbalanced string, find the MINIMUM number of insertions needed to make it valid (each ) must be part of a pair, and here specifically )) closes one (). This uses the stack idea without literally pushing/popping - tracking counts is enough.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why must you check stack.isEmpty() at the very end, not just during the scan?A string like "(((" never triggers a mismatch during the scan (no closing brackets appear), but leaves unmatched openers on the stack - only the final emptiness check catches this
What's the time and space complexity of the balanced-brackets check?O(n) time (one pass), O(n) space worst case (a string of all openers pushes every character)
How would you find the LONGEST valid parentheses substring (only round brackets)?Push indices instead of characters, seeding the stack with -1; on a valid match, the current length is index - stack.peek() after popping - a stack-based variant that tracks positions, not just characters

beginner.content:
What is a Monotonic Stack?

A stack maintained so its elements stay in strictly increasing (or decreasing) order from bottom to top - enforced by POPPING any element that would break that order before pushing a new one. It's the go-to tool whenever a problem asks "what's the next/previous element that's bigger/smaller than me?" across a whole array, in O(n) total instead of O(n²).
  • Increasing stack (bottom→top gets bigger): pop while the top is ≥ the incoming element - used for "next SMALLER element".
  • Decreasing stack (bottom→top gets smaller): pop while the top is ≤ the incoming element - used for "next GREATER element".

expert.content:
Why Every Element is Pushed and Popped At Most Once - O(n) Total

It's easy to worry the nested while-loop makes this O(n²). It doesn't: across the ENTIRE run, every element is pushed exactly once and popped AT MOST once - so total pop operations across all iterations is bounded by n, giving amortized O(1) per element and O(n) overall. This is the same amortized argument used for dynamic array resizing and KMP's LPS fallback.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How do you decide increasing vs decreasing stack for a given problem?Ask what you're popping FOR: popping smaller elements when a bigger one arrives (decreasing stack) resolves "next greater"; popping bigger elements when a smaller one arrives (increasing stack) resolves "next smaller"
What class of problems is monotonic stack the standard tool for?Next/previous greater or smaller element, largest rectangle in histogram, stock span, trapping rain water, and daily temperatures - anywhere the answer depends on the nearest larger/smaller neighbor
Why store INDICES on the stack instead of values in most implementations?Indices let you compute distances/widths (e.g. "how many days until a warmer temperature") once a match is found - the value alone doesn't tell you position

beginner.content:
Next Greater Element - Standard Version

For every element, find the first element to its RIGHT that is strictly greater (or -1 if none exists). A DECREASING monotonic stack of indices solves this in O(n): scan left to right, and whenever the current element beats the stack's top, that's the top's "next greater".

expert.content:
Next Greater Element in a CIRCULAR Array

When the array wraps around (element n-1's "next" can be element 0), simulate circularity by iterating the index range TWICE (using i % n), without actually duplicating the array in memory.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why does the circular version loop 2n times instead of n?It gives every index one full "lap" of potential right-neighbors to compare against, simulating the wraparound without physically duplicating the array
Why only push indices during the FIRST lap (i < n)?Pushing again during the second lap would create duplicate index entries on the stack, corrupting future pop/compare logic - each real index should only ever be pushed once
What's the time and space complexity?O(n) time (amortized, same monotonic-stack argument as the linear version, just over 2n iterations), O(n) space for the stack and result array

beginner.content:
Next Smaller Element - the Mirror of Next Greater

For every element, find the first element to its RIGHT that is strictly smaller (or -1 if none exists). Same monotonic-stack shape as Next Greater Element, just with the comparison flipped: use an INCREASING stack instead of decreasing.

expert.content:
Application: Largest Rectangle in Histogram Setup

Next Smaller Element (on both sides) is exactly the precomputation the Largest Rectangle in Histogram problem needs: for each bar, knowing the nearest shorter bar to its left and right tells you the WIDEST rectangle that bar can be the height of, without scanning outward from every bar individually.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How do Next Greater and Next Smaller differ in implementation?Only the comparison direction changes - Next Greater pops while stack top < current (decreasing stack), Next Smaller pops while stack top > current (increasing stack); everything else is identical
Why use >= (not just >) when popping for the "left boundary" in the histogram setup?Using >= treats equal-height bars correctly as boundaries too, avoiding double-counting width when there are duplicate heights in the array
What's the time complexity of computing next-smaller on BOTH sides?Still O(n) total - two separate O(n) monotonic stack passes (one left-to-right, one right-to-left), not O(n^2)

beginner.content:
Looking LEFT Instead of Right

"Previous Greater/Smaller Element" asks the mirror question of Next Greater/Smaller: for each element, find the nearest one to its LEFT that is bigger (or smaller). Same monotonic stack technique, just scanned left to right while comparing against elements that came BEFORE - so a match is recorded immediately (no deferred pop-and-record needed).

expert.content:
Why "Previous" Problems Resolve in ONE Pass, "Next" Problems Sometimes Don't

Previous-element problems always know the answer the moment they visit a position (everything relevant is already on the stack, to the left). Next-element problems must WAIT until a qualifying element appears later, which is why Next Greater/Smaller stores indices and fills in the result array as a side effect of popping, while Previous Greater/Smaller can fill in the result array directly, inline, as it goes.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Can you push values directly instead of indices for Previous Greater/Smaller?Yes when only the VALUE is needed - unlike Next Greater/Smaller, there's no deferred lookup requiring you to track WHERE the answer came from, since the answer is resolved immediately at each position
How would Largest Rectangle in Histogram use previous-smaller specifically?The nearest strictly-shorter bar to the LEFT gives the left boundary of the widest rectangle that bar's height can span - computed with exactly this previous-smaller-element pattern
What happens with duplicate values - does >= or > matter for correctness?It determines tie-breaking: using >= treats equal elements as "not previous greater" (they get popped), which matters for problems needing a STRICT previous greater rather than greater-or-equal

beginner.content:
The Problem

Given bar heights of a histogram, find the area of the LARGEST rectangle that fits entirely within the bars. The brute force tries every pair of left/right boundaries - O(n²) or worse. A monotonic stack solves it in a single O(n) pass.

expert.content:
O(n) Monotonic Stack Solution

Keep an increasing stack of bar indices. When a shorter bar arrives, pop the taller bars - each popped bar's MAXIMUM possible rectangle is now fully determined: its height times the width between the new shorter bar and whatever's now below it on the stack. This resolves every bar's best rectangle in one pass.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why is a height-0 sentinel added at the end of the loop?It forces the stack to flush every remaining bar, since a 0-height "bar" is guaranteed to be shorter than anything real - without it, bars still on the stack at the end would never have their rectangle computed
How is the width calculated when a bar is popped?It spans from the CURRENT new stack top (exclusive, since that bar is shorter and bounds the rectangle) to the current index i (exclusive, the new shorter bar that triggered the pop)
What's the relationship between this problem and Maximal Rectangle in a binary matrix?Maximal Rectangle reduces to running Largest Rectangle in Histogram once per row, treating each row as a histogram of consecutive 1s stacked from previous rows - O(rows × cols) overall

beginner.content:
The Stock Span Problem

For each day's stock price, the "span" is how many CONSECUTIVE days (ending today, going backward) had a price ≤ today's price. This is Previous Greater Element in disguise: the span is the distance back to the nearest previous day with a STRICTLY GREATER price (or back to the start, if none).

expert.content:
Streaming Version - a StockSpanner Class

The interview follow-up wraps this into a class that processes prices ONE AT A TIME as they arrive (like a live feed), rather than given the whole array up front - the same monotonic stack idea, just maintained as persistent state across calls instead of computed in one function.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why absorb a popped day's span into the new day's span in the streaming version?Once a day is popped, its own days-back count is already known to be entirely covered by the new higher price - adding it in avoids re-scanning those days individually
What's the amortized time complexity per call to next()?O(1) amortized - same monotonic stack argument: across all calls combined, total pushes and pops are each bounded by the number of calls made
How does stock span relate to Next/Previous Greater Element?It's literally Previous Greater Element with the answer expressed as a DISTANCE (days back) instead of a value - the exact same decreasing-stack mechanics apply

beginner.content:
Evaluating an Expression with a Stack

A stack naturally handles operator precedence and parentheses: numbers get pushed, and operators trigger a "resolve now" step based on precedence rules. The canonical simple case is evaluating a Reverse Polish Notation (postfix) expression - no precedence ambiguity at all, since the operator always applies to the two most recently pushed operands.

expert.content:
Evaluating a Standard Infix Expression with Precedence and Parentheses

A full calculator (e.g. "3 + 5 * ( 2 - 8 )") needs TWO stacks: one for numbers, one for operators. An operator is only applied once a higher-or-equal-precedence operator or a closing parenthesis forces it to resolve.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why is postfix so much easier to evaluate than infix?Postfix has no ambiguity about operator order or precedence - every operator immediately applies to the two most recently seen operands, in the exact order written
Note the popped operand order: applyOp(nums.pop(), nums.pop(), op) - why does order matter?For non-commutative operators (- and /), popping gives the SECOND operand first and the first operand second, so it must be applyOp(secondPop, firstPop, op) to get a - b, not b - a; the code above pops b then a for exactly this reason
How would you convert infix to postfix directly (the Shunting Yard algorithm)?Same operator-stack idea, but instead of applying operators immediately, output operands directly and push popped operators to an output list instead of computing - producing the postfix token sequence

beginner.content:
The Three Notations

  • Infix - operator BETWEEN operands: a + b. Natural for humans, ambiguous for computers without precedence rules and parentheses.
  • Prefix (Polish Notation) - operator BEFORE operands: + a b. No parentheses or precedence ever needed - the structure is unambiguous just from token order.
  • Postfix (Reverse Polish Notation) - operator AFTER operands: a b +. Same unambiguous property as prefix; this is what calculators and stack machines actually evaluate internally.

expert.content:
Infix to Prefix - Reverse, Convert, Reverse Again

A clever trick avoids writing a separate prefix converter from scratch: reverse the infix string (swapping ( and )), run the SAME infix-to-postfix logic, then reverse the result. This works because prefix is postfix read backward, with mirrored parentheses.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why don't prefix and postfix need parentheses or precedence rules?The position of each operator relative to its operands fully determines the structure - there's exactly one way to parse a valid prefix/postfix expression, unlike infix where "a+b*c" is ambiguous without a precedence convention
Why must equal-precedence operators NOT be popped when converting infix to PREFIX (only to postfix)?Because the conversion works on the reversed string, popping on equal precedence would flip the evaluation order of same-precedence operators (e.g. a-b-c), producing an incorrect prefix expression once re-reversed
Which notation do CPUs / stack-based virtual machines (like the JVM) actually use internally?Postfix (RPN) - bytecode instructions push operands and apply operators to the top of an operand stack, exactly matching postfix evaluation order

beginner.content:
A Stack That Also Tracks Its Minimum, in O(1)

Design a stack supporting push, pop, top, AND getMin - all O(1). The obvious idea (scan the stack for the minimum) is O(n) per query. The trick: maintain a SECOND stack that tracks the minimum-so-far at each point in time, growing and shrinking in lockstep with the main stack.

expert.content:
The O(1) Extra Space Version - One Stack Only

Instead of a full second stack, store the running minimum in a SINGLE variable, and when a new minimum is pushed, push a specially-encoded value that lets popping restore the previous minimum. This trades a second full stack for pure arithmetic (works well when values fit safely in a wider type like long).

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why must the auxiliary min-stack push a value on EVERY push, not just new minimums?Keeping it the exact same size as the main stack means pop() can always pop both together, staying in sync - if it only pushed on new minimums, popping would need extra logic to know whether to also pop the min-stack
What's the space trade-off of the two-stack approach vs the one-stack encoding trick?Two stacks: O(n) extra space, simple to reason about. One-stack encoding: O(1) extra space (just one long variable), but trickier logic and risk of overflow if not using a wider type
