Finding ALL Root-to-Leaf Paths That Match - Backtracking

The follow-up asks to RETURN every matching path, not just say yes/no - this needs backtracking: add the current node to a running path before recursing, and REMOVE it after recursing (regardless of the outcome), so the same list can be reused across all branches without leaking state between them.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why must path.remove() happen even when a match WAS found?The path list is shared and mutated across the entire traversal - forgetting to remove would leave stale entries when the recursion returns to try a sibling branch, corrupting every subsequent path
Why copy the path (new ArrayList<>(path)) when adding it to the result?The same 'path' list object keeps being mutated as the search continues; storing a reference to it directly would mean every result entry ends up pointing at the SAME final (wrong) state once backtracking finishes
How would "Path Sum III" (paths that don't need to start at the root) differ?It needs prefix-sum + HashMap at every node (similar to Subarray Sum Equals K), tracking running sums along the root-to-current path and checking if (currentSum - target) was seen earlier ANYWHERE on that path

beginner.content:
Left View - the First Node Visible at Each Level

Standing to the LEFT of the tree, which nodes can you see? Exactly the FIRST node encountered at each depth during a level-order (BFS) traversal. Group by level, take the first element of each group.

expert.content:
DFS Alternative - First Visit Wins

Left view can also be computed with DFS (preorder, visiting LEFT before right), tracking the maximum depth seen so far - a node is added to the result only the FIRST time its depth is reached, which happens to always be its leftmost representative since left is explored first.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why does DFS need to visit left before right for this trick to work?The "first time reaching a depth" logic only picks the LEFTMOST node at that depth if left is explored first - visiting right first would incorrectly capture the rightmost node instead
What's the time and space complexity of either approach?O(n) time (every node visited once), O(w) space for BFS (queue holds one level, up to the tree's max width) or O(h) space for DFS (call stack, up to the tree's height)
How is Right View different in the BFS version?Just take the LAST node of each level's group instead of the first - one condition flip (i == levelSize - 1 instead of i == 0)

beginner.content:
Right View - the Last Node Visible at Each Level

The mirror of Left View: standing to the RIGHT of the tree, you see the LAST node at each depth during level-order traversal. Same BFS grouping, just take the last element of each level instead of the first.

expert.content:
DFS Alternative - Right First This Time

The DFS version of Right View flips the exploration order: visit RIGHT before LEFT, so the "first time reaching a depth" trick now captures the rightmost node instead of the leftmost.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the single-line difference between Left View and Right View's DFS code?Swapping the recursive call order: dfs(left) then dfs(right) for Left View, dfs(right) then dfs(left) for Right View - everything else is identical
Could a tree's Left View and Right View ever be identical?Yes - for a tree with only one node per level (a "staircase" or fully skewed shape), or a tree with exactly one node at each depth, left and right views coincide
How does Right View relate to a heap's array representation or a complete binary tree's rightmost path?They're unrelated concepts that are sometimes confused - Right View is about VISUAL visibility from one side across ALL levels, not a single root-to-node path

beginner.content:
Top View - What's Visible Looking Down

Assign each node a HORIZONTAL DISTANCE (HD) from the root: root = 0, left child = parent's HD - 1, right child = parent's HD + 1. The top view shows the FIRST node encountered at each distinct horizontal distance during a level-order (BFS) scan - "first" matters because BFS processes shallower nodes before deeper ones at the same HD.

expert.content:
Why BFS (Not DFS) is Required for Correctness

Top view specifically needs the SHALLOWEST node at each horizontal distance to win ties - DFS visits nodes in a depth-first order, so a DEEPER node at some HD could be recorded before a SHALLOWER one at that same HD arrives later, giving the wrong answer. BFS processes level by level, guaranteeing the first node encountered at any HD is always the shallowest one - this is why putIfAbsent combined with BFS order is correct, but the same trick with DFS order is NOT.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is "horizontal distance" and why is it the key to this problem?It's each node's horizontal offset from the root (left = -1, right = +1 relative to parent) - nodes with the SAME horizontal distance appear in the same vertical column when the tree is drawn, which is exactly what "view from above" needs to group
Why use TreeMap instead of a plain HashMap for hdToValue?TreeMap keeps keys sorted, so iterating its values directly gives the horizontal distances in left-to-right order - a HashMap would need an extra sort step
How does Bottom View differ from Top View in implementation?Use put() (unconditional overwrite) instead of putIfAbsent() - since later-arriving (deeper) nodes at the same HD should WIN for bottom view, the opposite priority from top view

beginner.content:
Bottom View - What's Visible Looking Up

Same horizontal-distance idea as Top View, but the LAST (deepest) node at each horizontal distance wins instead of the first. Use unconditional overwrite (put) rather than putIfAbsent - since BFS processes in increasing depth order, each new node at a given HD replaces the previous one, so whatever remains after the full scan is the deepest.

expert.content:
Handling Ties at the SAME (Horizontal Distance, Depth)

When two nodes share BOTH the same horizontal distance AND the same depth (e.g. one is a left-child's right-child, the other is a right-child's left-child, both landing at HD 0 at the same level), the convention is that whichever was processed LATER in the BFS traversal order wins - typically the one reached via the RIGHT branch, since BFS processes a node's left child before its right child at each step, but siblings across different parents follow queue insertion order.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why does bottom view need BFS specifically, just like top view?Both rely on processing nodes in strictly increasing DEPTH order so that "overwrite" (bottom view) or "first write wins" (top view) correctly reflect which node is shallower vs deeper - DFS gives no such depth ordering guarantee across different horizontal distances
Can top view and bottom view ever be identical for the same tree?Yes - for any tree where each horizontal distance is occupied by exactly one node total (e.g. a tree with no HD collisions at all)
What's the time and space complexity of computing bottom view?O(n log n) - O(n) for the BFS traversal, plus O(log n) per TreeMap insertion; a HashMap plus separate min/max HD tracking and a final sort could also achieve this, with similar overall complexity

beginner.content:
Tracing the Tree's Outline

Boundary traversal prints the tree's OUTER EDGE, counter-clockwise: the left boundary (top to bottom), then all LEAVES (left to right), then the right boundary (bottom to top). Each of the three parts needs its own careful traversal, with rules to avoid duplicating corner nodes.

expert.content:
Why Corner Nodes Need Careful Handling to Avoid Duplicates

The three passes (left boundary, leaves, right boundary) can EASILY double-count nodes at the corners: if the root itself is a leaf, or if the leftmost/rightmost boundary node IS also a leaf, naive concatenation would print it twice. The pattern above explicitly EXCLUDES leaves from the boundary-walk functions (if (!isLeaf(cur))) since the separate addLeaves pass already covers every leaf exactly once.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why is the right boundary collected then REVERSED, but the left boundary isn't?The overall traversal order is counter-clockwise: left boundary goes top-to-bottom naturally, but the right boundary is walked top-to-bottom for convenience (easier to code) then reversed to appear bottom-to-top in the final output
What's the time complexity of boundary traversal?O(n) - each of the three passes visits a subset of nodes, and leaves are visited exactly once total across the whole traversal, giving linear overall work
Why exclude leaves from the left/right boundary walking functions?To avoid printing corner leaf nodes twice - once from the boundary walk and again from the dedicated leaves pass; excluding them from the boundary walk and relying solely on the leaves pass for those nodes keeps each node counted exactly once

beginner.content:
Grouping Nodes by Vertical Column

Extends the Top/Bottom View's "horizontal distance" idea: instead of keeping only ONE node per column, vertical traversal returns EVERY node in each column, top to bottom. Nodes sharing both the same column AND the same row are typically sorted by VALUE as a tiebreak.

expert.content:
Why Vertical Traversal Needs a Full Sort, Unlike Top/Bottom View

Top/Bottom View only ever keep ONE winner per column (first or last by depth), so BFS ordering alone determines correctness. Vertical Traversal keeps EVERY node per column, so ties (same row AND column, from different parents) need an explicit tiebreak - by value, per the standard problem definition - which requires collecting everything first and sorting, rather than resolving winners on the fly during a single pass.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time complexity of vertical traversal, and why?O(n log n) - dominated by the sort over all n nodes; the collection pass itself is O(n)
How does vertical traversal relate to Top View and Bottom View?All three use the same "horizontal distance / column" concept; Top View keeps the first (shallowest) node per column, Bottom View keeps the last (deepest), and Vertical Traversal keeps ALL nodes per column in sorted order
Could you solve this with BFS instead of collecting all nodes and sorting?BFS naturally gives correct ROW order for free (shallower rows processed first), but same-row same-column ties still need value-based sorting within that group - a hybrid approach (BFS + per-level sort) is possible but the collect-and-sort approach is simpler to get correct

beginner.content:
Level Order, Alternating Direction Each Level

Also called "spiral traversal": level 0 goes left-to-right, level 1 goes right-to-left, level 2 left-to-right again, and so on. Built directly on top of standard level-order BFS - just reverse every OTHER level's collected list before adding it to the result.

expert.content:
A Deque-Based Alternative That Avoids Reversing

Instead of collecting each level normally then reversing it after the fact, a Deque can insert at the FRONT or BACK depending on the current direction - producing the zigzag order directly, without a separate reverse step.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Does the QUEUE ever process nodes out of normal left-to-right order?No - children are always enqueued in the same left-then-right order regardless of the current level's display direction; only the COLLECTED result for that level gets reversed (or built in reverse via the deque), not the underlying BFS traversal itself
What's the time complexity of the reverse-after-collect vs deque approach?Both are O(n) overall - reversing each level costs O(level size), summing to O(n) across all levels; the deque approach does the same total work, just distributed differently
How would you adapt this for a "boustrophedon" (ox-plowing) traversal across MULTIPLE trees or a graph?The same level-alternating-direction principle applies to any BFS-based level structure - the key requirement is a well-defined notion of "level" to alternate on

beginner.content:
Converting a Tree to a String and Back

Serialization turns a tree into a string (for storage/network transfer); deserialization rebuilds the exact same tree from that string. Preorder traversal, with an explicit marker for null children, makes this straightforward - the null markers preserve the tree's exact shape, not just its values.

expert.content:
Why Preorder + Null Markers Preserve the EXACT Shape

Preorder ALONE (without null markers) is ambiguous - multiple different tree shapes can share the same preorder sequence. Adding explicit null tokens removes that ambiguity: deserialization always knows exactly when a subtree ends, since a null token is an unambiguous "stop" signal, letting the recursive rebuild consume tokens in lockstep with how they were written.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why is plain preorder (without null markers) ambiguous for reconstruction?Without explicit "no child here" markers, the same value sequence can correspond to multiple different tree shapes - there's no way to tell where one subtree ends and another begins
Could level-order (BFS) be used instead of preorder for serialization?Yes - BFS with null markers works equally well (this is what LeetCode's "Codec" problem commonly uses), as long as nulls are still explicitly recorded to preserve shape
What's the time and space complexity of serialize/deserialize?O(n) time for both directions (every node/null visited once), O(n) space for the resulting string and the token queue during deserialization

beginner.content:
The Full Set: Insert, Search, Delete, Min, Max

Every core BST operation follows the same shape - use the ordering property to decide left or right, and recurse: O(h) time, where h is the tree's height (O(log n) balanced, O(n) worst case skewed).

expert.content:
Converting a Sorted Array into a BALANCED BST

Given a sorted array, always picking the MIDDLE element as the root (recursively, for each half) guarantees a height-balanced BST in one pass - O(n) time, since each of the n elements is processed exactly once, and the recursive midpoint choice automatically keeps subtree sizes even.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why does inserting a SORTED sequence into a plain BST produce the worst-case shape?Every new value is either always the largest or always the smallest seen so far, so each insertion attaches only as a single right (or left) child - degenerating into a linked list with height n instead of log n
Why does picking the middle element guarantee balance when building from a sorted array?Splitting at the midpoint always creates two halves that differ in size by at most 1, so the resulting tree's height stays O(log n) - the same reasoning as a well-balanced binary search
What real-world problem is "sorted array to balanced BST" the solution for?Rebalancing an existing unbalanced BST: do an inorder traversal to get a sorted array, then rebuild it via this middle-picking technique - O(n) total to fully rebalance any BST

beginner.content:
The Range (Min/Max Bounds) Approach

An alternative to the inorder-sortedness check: pass down a valid (min, max) RANGE as you recurse. Each node must fall strictly within its inherited range; its left child inherits (min, node.val), its right child inherits (node.val, max) - correctly catching violations from ANY ancestor, not just the immediate parent.

expert.content:
Why Long (Not Integer) Bounds are Needed

Using Integer.MIN_VALUE/MAX_VALUE as initial sentinel bounds seems natural, but breaks if the tree legitimately CONTAINS a node with exactly that value - the comparison would incorrectly reject it. Using Long (or a nullable wrapper, as above) for bounds avoids colliding with the actual int range of node values entirely.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How does the range approach compare to the inorder-sortedness check?Both are O(n) and correct; range-based validates top-down in a single pass with explicit bounds, while inorder validates by checking strictly-increasing order during a left-root-right traversal - purely a style/preference difference
What's a classic WRONG approach to BST validation that this problem tests for?Checking only "node.left.val < node.val < node.right.val" locally at each node - this misses violations from grandchildren or deeper descendants that break the property relative to a higher ancestor
Does BST validation allow duplicate values?Depends on the exact BST definition used - strict BSTs (as in these examples, using <= and >=) disallow duplicates entirely; some variants allow duplicates only in one specific subtree by convention

beginner.content:
Using Inorder's Sorted Property

Since inorder traversal of a BST visits nodes in ascending order, the Kth SMALLEST element is simply the Kth value visited by inorder - stop as soon as a counter reaches K, no need to traverse the whole tree.

expert.content:
Kth Largest - Reverse Inorder, No Separate Logic Needed

The Kth largest is just the Kth smallest of a REVERSED order: traverse RIGHT before LEFT (a "reverse inorder"), and the Kth value visited is the Kth largest - same counting logic, one line swapped.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time complexity of finding the Kth smallest, and why does it beat sorting?O(h + k) - walk down to the leftmost node (O(h)) then visit k nodes; far better than O(n) or O(n log n) for a sort when k is small relative to n
How would you support REPEATED "find Kth smallest" queries efficiently as the BST changes?Augment each node with a "size of its left subtree" count, updated during insert/delete - this lets you jump directly toward the Kth element using the counts, in O(h) per query without a full inorder scan
Why does the early-return (count >= k) matter for efficiency?Without it, the traversal would continue visiting the ENTIRE tree even after finding the answer - the early exit keeps the cost proportional to k, not n

beginner.content:
Inorder Traversal with O(1) Space - No Stack, No Recursion

Every other traversal method needs O(h) extra space (call stack or explicit stack). Morris Traversal achieves O(1) EXTRA space by temporarily rewiring the tree itself: for each node with a left subtree, find its INORDER PREDECESSOR (the rightmost node in the left subtree) and make that predecessor's right pointer temporarily point back to the current node - a "thread" that lets traversal return upward without a stack.

expert.content:
Why the Tree Ends Up Exactly as It Started

Every thread created (predecessor.right = current) is EXPLICITLY removed the second time that predecessor is reached (predecessor.right = null) - the algorithm visits each thread exactly twice: once to create it (descending), once to detect and remove it (returning). This is what makes Morris Traversal safe to use on a tree you still need intact afterward, unlike naive "just add temporary pointers and leave them" approaches.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time and space complexity of Morris Traversal?O(n) time, O(1) EXTRA space - it does visit some nodes more than once (while threading/unthreading), but the total work across the whole traversal is still bounded by O(n)
Why is Morris Traversal rarely used in production code despite O(1) space?It temporarily mutates the tree structure, which is dangerous in concurrent/multi-threaded contexts (another thread could observe the temporary threaded state) and makes the code significantly harder to read/verify than recursive or stack-based versions
When would O(1) space actually matter enough to justify Morris Traversal's complexity?Extremely memory-constrained environments, or interview questions that EXPLICITLY forbid O(h) auxiliary space (a common "can you do better?" follow-up after a stack-based or recursive solution)

beginner.content:
The Min-Heap Property

A min-heap is a COMPLETE binary tree where every node is ≤ both its children - the SMALLEST element is always at the root, reachable in O(1). It's typically stored as a plain array using the 2i+1/2i+2/(i-1)/2 index formulas, no pointers needed.

expert.content:
Implementing a Min-Heap from Scratch with sink/swim

Insertion adds at the END, then "swims" up (swap with parent while smaller); extraction moves the LAST element to the root, then "sinks" down (swap with the smaller child while larger) - both O(log n), bounded by the tree's height.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why is peek() O(1) but poll() O(log n)?The minimum is always at the root (index 0), so reading it needs no traversal; removing it requires restoring the heap property afterward via sink(), which costs O(log n)
Why does "swim" only need to check the parent, while "sink" checks both children?Swimming up, each node has exactly ONE parent to compare against; sinking down, a node has up to TWO children, and must swap with whichever is smaller to maintain the min-heap property correctly
What's the time complexity of building a heap from n elements?O(n) via bottom-up heapify (not n inserts, which would be O(n log n)) - the same amortized analysis as Heap Sort's build phase

beginner.content:
The Mirror of Min-Heap

Every node is ≥ both its children - the LARGEST element sits at the root. Java's PriorityQueue is min-heap by default, so a max-heap needs a Comparator flipping the order.

expert.content:
Negation Trick - Simulating Max-Heap with a Min-Heap

Without a custom Comparator (e.g. in languages/libraries that only provide min-heaps), NEGATING values before inserting and negating again on extraction simulates a max-heap using pure min-heap logic - the smallest negative value corresponds to the largest original value.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why is Java's PriorityQueue min-heap by default, requiring a Comparator for max-heap?It's a design choice of natural ordering (ascending) matching Comparable's default contract - Collections.reverseOrder() or a custom lambda comparator inverts it for max-heap behavior
When would the negation trick be preferred over a custom Comparator?When working with primitive-only heap implementations that don't support custom comparators, or in performance-sensitive code avoiding the boxing/comparator-call overhead of object-based comparisons
What's a real use case that specifically needs a max-heap over a min-heap?Finding the K SMALLEST elements efficiently uses a max-heap of size K (evicting the current maximum when a smaller element arrives) - the mirror of using a min-heap to find the K largest

beginner.content:
What Does Heapify Do?

Heapify restores the heap property at ONE node, ASSUMING both its children are already valid heaps - it "sinks" the node down, swapping with its smaller (min-heap) or larger (max-heap) child, until the property holds locally. This single-node operation is the building block for both building a whole heap and for extraction.

expert.content:
Why Heapify's Precondition Matters - and What Happens If It's Violated

Heapify ONLY works correctly if both children subtrees are ALREADY valid heaps before it's called on the parent. Calling heapify TOP-DOWN (root first) on an arbitrary unsorted array does NOT correctly build a heap, because the precondition is violated - this is precisely why "build heap" processes nodes BOTTOM-UP (from the last non-leaf node backward), ensuring every heapify call's precondition is satisfied by the time it runs.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time complexity of a SINGLE heapify call?O(log n) - bounded by the height of the subtree it operates on, since it sinks at most that far
Why must "build heap" call heapify from the LAST non-leaf node BACKWARD to the root?Heapify's correctness depends on both children already being valid heaps - processing bottom-up guarantees that precondition is always satisfied by the time a given node's heapify call runs
What's the index of the last non-leaf node in a 0-indexed array of size n?n/2 - 1 (integer division) - every index beyond that has no children, since 2*(n/2) exceeds the array bounds

beginner.content:
Converting an Arbitrary Array into a Heap

Given any unsorted array, "build heap" rearranges it in place to satisfy the heap property everywhere - by calling heapify on every non-leaf node, starting from the LAST one and working backward to the root (index 0).

expert.content:
Build Heap is O(n), Not O(n log n) - the Full Proof

Naively, n/2 heapify calls each costing up to O(log n) suggests O(n log n). The tight bound is O(n): most nodes are near the bottom of the tree (height 0 or 1) and need very little sinking work, while only a FEW nodes near the root need the full O(log n). Summing (nodes at height h) × h across all heights forms a series that converges to O(n) total - this is a genuinely different (and better) result than n independent inserts, which WOULD cost O(n log n).

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why start heapify from n/2 - 1, not from 0?Indices n/2 through n-1 are all LEAVES (no children) - they're already trivially valid heaps of size 1, so heapify has nothing to do there; work only starts at the deepest non-leaf level
Why is build-heap O(n) but n individual inserts is O(n log n)?Build-heap exploits that most nodes are near the bottom (cheap to heapify); inserting one at a time always adds at the BOTTOM and swims UP, and on average across many inserts, that swimming cost sums to O(n log n)
What does Java's PriorityQueue(Collection) constructor use internally?The O(n) bottom-up heapify approach, not n sequential offer() calls - this is exactly why constructing a PriorityQueue from an existing collection is more efficient than building it up one offer() at a time

beginner.content:
Sorting by Repeated Extraction

The conceptual core of Heap Sort: put everything into a heap, then repeatedly extract the minimum (or maximum) - since each extraction always removes the current smallest remaining element, the extraction ORDER is automatically sorted. A PriorityQueue makes this trivial to express, though the in-place array version (covered under Sorting) avoids its O(n) extra space.

expert.content:
Why This PriorityQueue Version is O(n) Extra Space, Unlike In-Place Heap Sort

This version allocates a SEPARATE PriorityQueue plus a separate output array - O(n) extra space. The classic in-place array Heap Sort algorithm achieves the same O(n log n) time WITHOUT that extra space, by building the heap directly inside the original array and swapping the extracted max to the END of the shrinking heap region each time (see the "Heap Sort" topic under Sorting for the full in-place version).

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why does repeatedly extracting the min ALWAYS produce sorted order?A min-heap guarantees the root is the smallest remaining element at every point in time - removing it repeatedly is, by definition, removing elements in strictly non-decreasing order
Is this approach's time complexity the same as in-place heap sort?Yes - both are O(n log n): O(n) to build the heap plus O(n log n) for n extractions, each costing O(log n)
When might you actually use the PriorityQueue-based version in real code?When code clarity matters more than the O(n) space overhead, or when you're already using a PriorityQueue for another purpose (e.g. a Top-K structure) and sorting the remaining contents is a small side task

beginner.content:
Finding the Kth Largest Element with a Min-Heap

Keep a min-heap of size K as you scan the array; whenever it grows past K, evict the minimum. Whatever remains after the full scan has the root as the Kth largest - O(n log k), much better than sorting the whole array when k is small.

expert.content:
Quickselect - O(n) Average, the Faster Alternative

The heap approach is O(n log k). Quickselect (using Quick Sort's partition step, but recursing into only ONE side) finds the Kth largest in O(n) AVERAGE time - though O(n²) worst case, same risk profile as Quick Sort itself, mitigated with a random pivot.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why does Quickselect only recurse into ONE side, unlike full Quick Sort?It only needs to locate ONE specific position (the target index), so once the pivot lands there, the answer is found - there's no need to fully sort the other side, cutting the average work roughly in half each recursive step
When would you prefer the heap approach over Quickselect despite being asymptotically slower?When the data is a STREAM (elements arriving one at a time, unknown total count) - the heap approach naturally maintains a running "top K so far", while Quickselect needs the full array available upfront
What's Quickselect's worst-case time complexity, and how is it mitigated?O(n^2), from the same bad-pivot scenario as Quick Sort - a randomized pivot choice makes this vanishingly unlikely for any fixed adversarial input

beginner.content:
The General "Top K" Pattern

A huge family of interview problems reduces to the same shape: maintain a heap of size K, evicting the "weakest" candidate whenever a better one shows up. Beyond raw numbers, this works for ANY object with a defined priority - most frequent elements, closest points, cheapest flights.

expert.content:
K Closest Points to Origin - the Same Pattern, Different Priority

Same "heap of size K, evict the weakest" template, but the comparator is now DISTANCE from origin instead of frequency - demonstrating that the pattern generalizes to any custom priority, not just plain numbers.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why use a MAX-heap for "K closest" but a MIN-heap for "K largest"?The heap should always be able to evict the WORST candidate for the goal - for "K closest", the worst candidate is the FARTHEST (so a max-heap on distance lets you pop the farthest); for "K largest", the worst candidate is the SMALLEST (min-heap lets you pop the smallest)
What's the general time complexity of the Top-K-heap pattern?O(n log k) - each of the n elements does at most one O(log k) heap operation, since the heap never exceeds size k
When would bucket sort beat the heap approach for Top K Frequent?When frequencies are bounded by a small known range (at most n), bucket sort by frequency count achieves O(n) instead of O(n log k) - each bucket index IS a frequency value, and you read buckets from the top down

beginner.content:
Maintaining a Running Median with Two Heaps

Split the numbers seen so far into two halves: a MAX-heap holding the SMALLER half (its top is the largest of the small numbers), and a MIN-heap holding the LARGER half (its top is the smallest of the large numbers). The median is derivable from the two tops in O(1) - inserting a new number costs O(log n) to keep both heaps balanced.

expert.content:
Why the Balancing Logic Guarantees Correctness

The invariant maintained after every insertion: smallHalf.size() == largeHalf.size() or smallHalf.size() == largeHalf.size() + 1, AND every element in smallHalf is ≤ every element in largeHalf. Given that invariant, the median is trivially either smallHalf's top (odd total count) or the average of both tops (even total count) - no scanning or sorting ever needed.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time complexity of addNum() and findMedian()?addNum() is O(log n) (heap insertion plus rebalancing), findMedian() is O(1) (just reading the tops)
Why route every new number through smallHalf first, rather than deciding directly which heap it belongs in?It's a simplification trick: always insert into smallHalf, then immediately move its new max over to largeHalf - this single consistent rule automatically handles both "belongs in small half" and "belongs in large half" cases correctly without extra branching logic
How would you extend this to support REMOVING a number from the stream (a "sliding window median")?Heaps don't support efficient arbitrary removal - a common approach uses lazy deletion (mark removed, skip stale entries when they reach the top) combined with a hash map tracking pending removals per value

beginner.content:
The General Pattern Behind Median From Data Stream

"Two heap" is a named technique: split a dataset into two balanced halves using a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, maintaining the invariant that every lower-half element ≤ every upper-half element. It solves any problem needing fast access to a MIDDLE point in a dynamically changing dataset - not just plain medians.

expert.content:
Sliding Window Median - Two Heaps Plus Lazy Deletion

Extending two-heap to a SLIDING WINDOW (fixed-size window over a stream, median needed for each position) adds a real complication: heaps don't support efficient removal of an arbitrary element. The standard fix is LAZY DELETION - mark a value as "to be removed" in a hash map, and only actually discard it from a heap when it happens to reach the top, skipping over any stale entries encountered.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What other problems use the two-heap pattern besides finding the median?"IPO" (choose projects to maximize capital, splitting by affordability), and any "find the Kth-from-middle element dynamically" style problem
Why is lazy deletion necessary for a sliding window median, but not for the basic streaming median?The basic version only ever ADDS numbers, never removes them; a sliding window must also REMOVE the number leaving the window each step, and heaps have no O(log n) way to remove an arbitrary (non-top) element directly
Does lazy deletion change the overall time complexity?Amortized, no - each element is inserted once and removed (lazily or actually) once across the whole run, keeping total work O(n log n) for n operations, same order as the non-lazy version

beginner.content:
Why a Heap is the Standard Priority Queue Implementation

A priority queue needs fast insert AND fast extract-highest-priority. Comparing implementation choices makes clear why a heap wins:
Backing structureInsertExtract min/max
Unsorted arrayO(1)O(n) - must scan for the best
Sorted arrayO(n) - must shift to insert in orderO(1)
Binary heapO(log n)O(log n)
A heap is the balanced compromise - both operations logarithmic, neither one is a bottleneck.

expert.content:
Dijkstra's Algorithm - the Canonical Real-World Priority Queue Use

Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm needs to repeatedly grab the UNVISITED node with the smallest known distance - exactly a priority queue's job. Using a heap-backed PriorityQueue here is what brings Dijkstra's complexity down to O((V + E) log V), compared to O(V²) with a naive linear scan for the minimum each time.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why does Dijkstra's use a heap-based priority queue instead of scanning for the minimum?A linear scan for the smallest unvisited distance is O(V) per step, giving O(V^2) total; a heap gets that operation down to O(log V), bringing the total to O((V+E) log V)
What does "if (d > dist[node]) continue" handle in the Dijkstra code above?A STALE priority queue entry - since nodes can be added to the queue multiple times as shorter paths are discovered, this check skips outdated entries instead of reprocessing a node with worse information
Besides Dijkstra, what other algorithms fundamentally rely on a priority queue?Prim's Algorithm (Minimum Spanning Tree), Huffman Coding (always merging the two least-frequent nodes), and A* Search (priority by estimated total cost)

beginner.content:
The Prefix Tree Data Structure

A Trie stores strings character by character down a tree - every node represents one character, and words sharing a prefix share the same path from the root. This is what gives O(word length) insert/search, independent of how many total words are stored.
* marks the end of a complete word ("cat", "car")

expert.content:
Array-Based Children Instead of a HashMap

For a fixed, small alphabet (lowercase a-z), using a TrieNode[26] array instead of a HashMap<Character, TrieNode> avoids hashing overhead entirely - direct index access via c - 'a', matching the same optimization used for frequency counting.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time complexity of insert/search/startsWith?O(L) where L is the string's length - independent of how many other words are already stored
What's the space complexity of a Trie?O(total characters across all inserted words) in the worst case (no shared prefixes), but often much less in practice due to prefix sharing
Array-based children vs HashMap - what's the trade-off?Array is faster (no hashing) but wastes memory for a large/sparse alphabet (26 pointers per node even if only 1-2 are used); HashMap uses memory proportional to actual children, at the cost of hashing overhead per lookup

beginner.content:
Counting Words With a Given Prefix

Augment each Trie node with a counter tracking how many words pass through it - answering "how many words start with X" becomes an O(prefix length) lookup instead of scanning every stored word.

expert.content:
Finding the Longest Common Prefix of All Stored Words

Walk down from the root as long as each node has EXACTLY ONE child and isn't itself a complete word - the moment the path branches (or a word ends), the longest shared prefix has been found.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why does incrementing wordsWithThisPrefix on EVERY node along the insert path work correctly?Every node on a word's path is, by definition, a prefix of that word - incrementing all of them means each node's counter accurately reflects how many inserted words share that specific prefix
What's the time complexity of counting words with a prefix?O(prefix length) - a direct walk down the Trie, no scanning of the actual word list needed
Why must the longest-common-prefix walk stop at a node marking isEndOfWord?If a shorter word is ALSO a complete word stored in the Trie, extending the "common prefix" further would produce a prefix that isn't actually shared by that shorter word - the walk must respect word boundaries, not just branching

beginner.content:
Why Trie + DFS Beats Checking Each Word Separately

Searching a letter grid for MULTIPLE dictionary words at once is much faster with a Trie than running a separate DFS per word: the Trie lets DFS paths SHARE work across words with common prefixes, and prune a branch the instant no remaining word continues down that path.

expert.content:
Trie Pruning for Cleanup - Removing Found Words

A further optimization: once a word is found and its leaf node has NO children of its own, remove it from the Trie (and prune any now-empty ancestor nodes). This shrinks the search space for SUBSEQUENT DFS starts, avoiding wasted work re-discovering words already found.

beginner.content:
Suggesting All Words That Complete a Prefix

Given a prefix typed so far, find ALL stored words starting with it - walk the Trie down to the prefix's node in O(prefix length), then DFS from there collecting every complete word found below it.

expert.content:
Ranking Suggestions by Frequency - a Real Autocomplete Feature

Real autocomplete (search engines, IDEs) ranks suggestions by POPULARITY, not just alphabetically. Storing a frequency count at each word-ending node, then using a min-heap of size K during collection, gives the TOP-K most popular completions efficiently.

Why use a min-heap of size K instead of collecting all matches and sorting?Same Top-K pattern as elsewhere: bounding the heap to K keeps memory and per-insertion cost small (O(log k)), avoiding the need to hold and fully sort every matching word when only the top K are needed
What real systems use Trie-based autocomplete with frequency ranking?Search engine query suggestions, IDE code completion, and phone keyboard predictive text all use this exact pattern - a Trie for prefix lookup, frequency/recency data for ranking

beginner.content:
Search Supporting a Wildcard '.'

Design a dictionary supporting addWord and search, where search can include . as a wildcard matching ANY single character. A plain Trie traversal breaks on wildcards - the fix is to recursively try EVERY child when a . is encountered, instead of following one fixed path.

expert.content:
Worst-Case Complexity - When Wildcards Force Full Branching

A single . is cheap (branches into however many children exist at that position). But a pattern like "...." (ALL wildcards) forces the search to explore EVERY path in the Trie up to that length - worst case O(26ⁿ) for an n-character all-wildcard pattern, since every position branches into up to 26 possibilities.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why can't a plain iterative Trie traversal handle the '.' wildcard?Iterative traversal follows exactly ONE path per character; a wildcard needs to potentially follow MULTIPLE paths simultaneously, which naturally requires recursion (or an explicit stack/queue) to explore all branches
What's the best-case and worst-case time complexity of search()?Best case O(word length) with no wildcards (same as plain Trie search); worst case O(alphabet_size^wildcard_count) when wildcards force full branching at multiple positions
How would you extend this to support a '*' wildcard matching ZERO OR MORE characters?Significantly harder - it would need to try skipping the '*' entirely (zero match) AND consuming one more character while staying on the same '*' (one or more match) at each step, closer to full regex matching than simple Trie search

beginner.content:
A Trie Over Bits Instead of Characters

A Binary Trie stores integers bit by bit (usually from the MOST significant bit down), instead of characters. Each node has at most TWO children (0 or 1) - a fixed alphabet of size 2, which is what makes it so useful for numeric problems, especially involving XOR.

expert.content:
Why MSB-First Ordering is Essential for XOR-Related Queries

Inserting bits from the MOST significant bit down means that at EVERY point during a Trie search, the path taken so far represents the LARGEST-magnitude portion of the number already decided - which is exactly what makes greedy bit-by-bit decisions (like "maximize XOR") correct: getting the highest bit right matters more than any combination of lower bits ever could.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why is a Binary Trie's depth always fixed (e.g. 32 for a 32-bit int)?Every number is represented with the SAME fixed number of bits, so every insertion path has identical depth - unlike a character Trie where word lengths vary
What's the space complexity of a Binary Trie storing n numbers?O(n * BITS) in the worst case (no shared prefixes at the bit level), though shared high-order bits (common for numbers of similar magnitude) reduce this in practice
What class of problems is Binary Trie the standard tool for?Maximum/minimum XOR pair or triplet problems, and maximum XOR subarray (combined with prefix XOR) - anywhere the goal involves optimizing an XOR relationship between numbers

beginner.content:
Maximum XOR of Two Numbers in an Array

Naive approach checks every pair - O(n²). Insert every number into a Binary Trie, then for EACH number, greedily walk the Trie preferring the OPPOSITE bit at every level (maximizing XOR contribution) - O(n × BITS), dramatically faster.

expert.content:
Maximum XOR Subarray - Combining Binary Trie with Prefix XOR

XOR has a property just like sum: xor(l, r) = prefixXor[r] XOR prefixXor[l-1]. So maximizing a SUBARRAY's XOR reduces to: as you compute running prefix XORs left to right, insert each into a Binary Trie, and at each step find the maximum XOR against all PREVIOUSLY inserted prefixes - the same greedy Trie walk as the pair problem, applied to a running prefix XOR stream.

Interview Questions

What's the time complexity of Maximum XOR Pair with a Binary Trie?O(n * BITS) - n insertions plus n greedy walks, each O(BITS) - versus O(n^2) for the naive all-pairs comparison
Why must prefixXor(0) be seeded into the Trie before the main loop in Max XOR Subarray?It represents the "empty prefix" case, allowing a subarray starting from index 0 to be correctly considered (its XOR is simply prefixXor[r] XOR 0)
Why does node = node.children[bit] as a fallback (not returning early) matter when the wanted bit is unavailable?Even if the ideal (opposite) bit isn't available at this level, the search must still descend SOMEWHERE to continue evaluating lower bits correctly - falling back to the same-bit child is the only valid path forward in the Trie

beginner.content:
Representing a Graph as a 2D Grid

An adjacency matrix is a V × V array where matrix[i][j] = 1 (or a weight) means an edge exists from i to j. Checking "does an edge exist" is O(1); listing a vertex's neighbors is O(V) since the whole row must be scanned.

expert.content:
When O(V²) Space is Actually the Right Trade-off

An adjacency matrix wastes space on SPARSE graphs (few edges relative to V² possible ones), but for DENSE graphs (edges approaching V²), or algorithms that need frequent O(1) "does this edge exist" checks (like Floyd-Warshall, which inherently operates on a full V×V distance matrix), the matrix representation is the natural and efficient choice.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the space complexity of an adjacency matrix, and why is it wasteful for sparse graphs?O(V^2) always - for a sparse graph with only O(V) edges, most matrix cells are 0, wasting almost all the allocated space
Why is Floyd-Warshall naturally matrix-based rather than list-based?It needs O(1) access to the distance between ANY pair of vertices at every step of its triple-nested loop - a matrix provides this directly, while a list would require a lookup (or a separate distance array) for each pair
How do you represent a WEIGHTED graph with an adjacency matrix?Store the edge weight directly instead of 1 (matrix[i][j] = weight), and use a sentinel value like infinity (or -1) for "no edge exists" instead of 0, since 0 could be a legitimate weight

beginner.content:
Representing a Graph as a List of Neighbors Per Vertex

Each vertex maps to a LIST of its neighbors - space is O(V + E), proportional to what's actually in the graph, not V². This is the default choice for most graph algorithms (BFS, DFS, Dijkstra) since it directly hands you "iterate over this vertex's neighbors" in optimal time.

expert.content:
Weighted Adjacency List and Edge-Existence Trade-off

For weighted graphs, store int[]{neighbor, weight} pairs (or a small class) instead of plain integers. The one thing adjacency LIST is genuinely worse at: checking "does edge (u,v) exist" is O(degree of u) with a plain list - use a Set per vertex instead of a List if that specific query needs to be fast.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why is adjacency list the default representation for BFS/DFS?Both algorithms need to iterate over "all neighbors of the current vertex" repeatedly - adjacency list gives exactly that in O(degree), the minimum possible work, unlike a matrix's O(V) scan per vertex
What's the space complexity, and why is it better than a matrix for sparse graphs?O(V + E) - proportional to what actually exists in the graph, versus a matrix's fixed O(V^2) regardless of edge count; for sparse real-world graphs (E much less than V^2), this is a massive savings
How would you make edge-existence checks O(1) with an adjacency list?Use a HashSet (or Map for weighted) per vertex instead of a List - trades a bit of memory and iteration-order guarantees for O(1) average "does this edge exist" lookups

beginner.content:
Edges That Only Go One Way

In a directed graph (digraph), an edge from u to v does NOT imply an edge from v to u - "u follows v" on Twitter doesn't mean "v follows u". This asymmetry is why directed graphs support concepts undirected graphs don't: topological ordering (only meaningful with direction), and strongly vs weakly connected components.

expert.content:
In-Degree and Out-Degree - the Foundation of Topological Sort

Each vertex has an IN-DEGREE (edges pointing TO it) and OUT-DEGREE (edges pointing FROM it) - independent counts, unlike undirected graphs where degree is a single number. In-degree specifically is what Kahn's Algorithm for topological sort relies on: a vertex with in-degree 0 has no unprocessed prerequisites, so it's safe to process first.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why is topological sort only defined for DIRECTED acyclic graphs?Topological order requires a well-defined "comes before" relationship between vertices, which only makes sense when edges have direction - and it must be a DAG, since a cycle would create a contradictory ordering requirement
What's the difference between strongly and weakly connected in a directed graph?Strongly connected: a path exists in BOTH directions between every pair of vertices; weakly connected: a path exists between every pair when edge direction is IGNORED (treating the graph as undirected)
What real-world systems are naturally modeled as directed graphs?Task dependency graphs (build systems, course prerequisites), web page links, social media "follows", and version control commit history - all have inherently asymmetric relationships

beginner.content:
Edges That Go Both Ways

In an undirected graph, an edge between u and v means the relationship is SYMMETRIC - "u is friends with v" implies "v is friends with u". Implementing this just means adding BOTH directions when building an adjacency list, and each vertex has a single DEGREE (not separate in/out counts).

expert.content:
The Handshaking Lemma - Sum of Degrees is Always Even

Since every edge contributes exactly 1 to TWO vertices' degrees (one on each end), the sum of ALL vertex degrees in an undirected graph is always exactly 2 × (number of edges) - and therefore always EVEN. This isn't just a curiosity: it's a useful sanity check (and occasionally a direct proof tool) in graph theory problems.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why is the sum of degrees in an undirected graph always even?Each edge is counted exactly twice - once from each endpoint's perspective - so the total is always 2 times the edge count, an inherently even number
Which algorithms behave differently on undirected vs directed graphs?Cycle detection (undirected needs to track the parent to avoid falsely flagging the edge just traversed as a "back edge"), and connectivity concepts (undirected has one notion of "connected", directed splits into weakly/strongly connected)
Why does Union-Find (DSU) naturally fit undirected graph problems?DSU tracks which vertices belong to the same connected GROUP, a concept that's inherently symmetric - it doesn't need to distinguish direction, matching undirected graphs' structure directly

beginner.content:
Edges With a Cost, Not Just a Connection

A weighted graph attaches a NUMBER to each edge - distance, cost, time, capacity. This single addition changes which algorithms apply: plain BFS finds shortest paths only in UNWEIGHTED graphs (every edge "costs" 1); weighted graphs need Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, or Floyd-Warshall instead.

expert.content:
Why BFS Breaks on Weighted Graphs - and What Fixes It

BFS finds the shortest path by counting EDGES, implicitly assuming every edge costs exactly 1 - correct only for unweighted graphs. On a weighted graph, a path with MORE edges can have a SMALLER total weight than a path with fewer edges - BFS's level-by-level exploration has no way to account for that, which is exactly why Dijkstra replaces the queue with a PRIORITY QUEUE ordered by accumulated distance.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Which shortest-path algorithm is appropriate for a weighted graph with NEGATIVE edges?Bellman-Ford - Dijkstra's greedy "always expand the current smallest distance" assumption breaks with negative edges, since a longer initial path could still be improved later by a negative edge Dijkstra already dismissed
What's a "negative cycle", and why is it fundamentally problematic?A cycle whose total weight is negative - traversing it repeatedly decreases path cost without bound, making "shortest path" undefined (it approaches negative infinity); Bellman-Ford can DETECT such cycles but can't return a meaningful shortest path through them
How would you represent an UNWEIGHTED graph using weighted-graph code without modification?Assign every edge a weight of 1 - Dijkstra on a uniformly-weighted graph degenerates into behaving identically to BFS, confirming BFS is really just a special case of shortest-path search

beginner.content:
Traversing a Graph

  • BFS (Breadth-First Search) - explores level by level using a Queue; finds the SHORTEST path in an unweighted graph.
  • DFS (Depth-First Search) - explores as deep as possible along one branch before backtracking, using a Stack (or recursion).

Depth-First Search - Go Deep Before Backtracking

DFS explores as far as possible down one path before backtracking, using a STACK (or recursion, which uses the call stack implicitly) - the opposite exploration order from BFS's queue-based level-by-level approach. A visited set is essential to avoid infinite loops in graphs with cycles.

expert.content:
Iterative DFS with an Explicit Stack - and a Subtle Ordering Gotcha

Converting DFS to iterative form replaces the call stack with an explicit Deque. One common bug: pushing neighbors in NORMAL order makes them get visited in REVERSE order (since a stack pops the LAST pushed first) - if matching recursive DFS's exact visit order matters, neighbors must be pushed in reverse.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time and space complexity of DFS?O(V + E) time (every vertex and edge examined once), O(V) space for the visited set plus O(h) for the recursion/explicit stack, where h is the graph's exploration depth
Why does DFS need a visited set but a tree traversal usually doesn't?A tree has no cycles by definition, so a traversal naturally terminates; a general graph CAN have cycles, and without tracking visited nodes, DFS would loop forever revisiting the same cycle
When would you prefer DFS over BFS for graph traversal?When exploring ALL paths matters more than shortest path (e.g. finding connected components, detecting cycles, topological sort, or exhaustive search/backtracking problems) - BFS is specifically better when you need the SHORTEST path in an unweighted graph

beginner.content:
Finding Separate "Islands" in a Graph

A connected component is a maximal set of vertices all reachable from each other. Finding all components: run DFS (or BFS) from any UNVISITED vertex, marking everything it reaches as one component, and repeat from the next unvisited vertex until all vertices are covered.

expert.content:
Union-Find as an Alternative - Especially for Dynamic/Streaming Edges

DFS/BFS is ideal when the WHOLE graph is known upfront. When edges arrive ONE AT A TIME (a stream) and you need "how many components right now" after each addition, Union-Find is far more efficient - each new edge is a single near-O(1) union operation, versus re-running a full DFS/BFS scan.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time complexity of finding connected components via DFS/BFS?O(V + E) - the entire graph is visited exactly once, regardless of how many separate components exist
Why is Union-Find better than repeated DFS for a STREAM of incoming edges?Each new edge only requires one near-O(1) (amortized, with path compression + union by rank) union operation to update the component count, versus DFS which would need a full O(V+E) rescan of the ENTIRE graph after every single new edge
How does "connected components" generalize to "connected components in an IMAGE" (flood fill)?The exact same idea applied to a grid instead of an explicit graph - each pixel is a vertex, adjacency is defined by neighboring pixels sharing a property (e.g. same color), and DFS/BFS/Union-Find all work identically

beginner.content:
Detecting a Cycle in an UNDIRECTED Graph

DFS with a visited set - but a subtlety: encountering an already-visited neighbor is only a REAL cycle if that neighbor isn't the PARENT you just came from (in an undirected graph, the edge back to your immediate parent is expected, not a cycle).

expert.content:
Cycle Detection in a DIRECTED Graph - Needs a Different Trick

The "ignore the parent" trick doesn't work for directed graphs, since edges aren't symmetric. Instead, track nodes CURRENTLY on the active recursion path (inStack) - a cycle exists if DFS reaches a node that's ALREADY on the current path, not just previously visited at some point in the past.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why does the undirected "check parent" trick fail on directed graphs?In a directed graph, reaching a previously-visited node through a DIFFERENT unrelated path (not the current recursion path) is normal and NOT a cycle - the parent-check heuristic can't distinguish "safely revisited via a different branch" from "genuinely revisited via a back edge on the current path"
What does the inStack set represent conceptually?Exactly the set of ancestors of the current node in the DFS recursion tree - nodes still "in progress", not yet fully explored and backtracked from
How does cycle detection relate to Topological Sort?Topological sort is only defined for DAGs (Directed Acyclic Graphs) - detecting a cycle first (or discovering one DURING the topological sort attempt itself) is how you determine whether a valid topological order even exists

beginner.content:
Can the Graph Be 2-Colored?

A graph is bipartite if its vertices can be split into two groups such that every edge connects a vertex from ONE group to the OTHER - never within the same group. Checking: BFS/DFS coloring - assign alternating colors as you traverse; if a neighbor is already colored the SAME as the current vertex, the graph is NOT bipartite.

expert.content:
Why a Graph is Bipartite If and Only If It Has No Odd-Length Cycle

This is the key theorem behind bipartiteness: traveling around ANY cycle, colors must alternate (0,1,0,1,...) - for the cycle to close consistently (the last vertex's color must differ from the first, since they're connected by an edge), the cycle's LENGTH must be EVEN. An odd-length cycle makes this alternation impossible to close consistently - which is EXACTLY the situation the BFS coloring check detects as a conflict.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time complexity of the bipartite check?O(V + E) - a single BFS/DFS pass over the whole graph, same as standard traversal
Why does the algorithm loop over ALL vertices (for start = 0 to n-1), not just start from vertex 0?The graph might be DISCONNECTED - each connected component must be checked independently, since a coloring conflict could only be detected by actually visiting all reachable vertices from each unvisited component's starting point
What real-world problems reduce to bipartite checking?Job/worker matching feasibility checks, scheduling conflicts (two groups that can never overlap), and detecting whether a graph coloring with exactly 2 colors is possible for a resource-allocation constraint

beginner.content:
Ordering Tasks So Every Prerequisite Comes First

A topological order of a DAG lists vertices such that for EVERY directed edge u → v, u appears BEFORE v. It only exists for Directed Acyclic Graphs - a cycle would create an impossible "must come before itself" requirement. Two standard algorithms: Kahn's (BFS-based, using in-degrees) and DFS-based (using a finishing-order stack) - both covered in their own dedicated topics.

expert.content:
Why Topological Order is Generally NOT Unique

Multiple valid topological orders often exist - any two vertices with NO direct or indirect dependency relationship between them can appear in EITHER relative order. This non-uniqueness is exactly why "find the LEXICOGRAPHICALLY SMALLEST topological order" is itself a distinct, harder variant of the problem (solved by always picking the smallest available in-degree-0 vertex in Kahn's Algorithm, using a min-heap instead of a plain queue).

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why must the graph be a DAG for topological sort to exist?A cycle A -> B -> A would require A before B AND B before A simultaneously - a logical contradiction that makes a valid linear ordering impossible
What's the time complexity of topological sort (either algorithm)?O(V + E) - both Kahn's and DFS-based approaches visit every vertex and edge exactly once
What real-world systems compute topological orderings?Build systems (compiling files in dependency order), spreadsheet formula recalculation order, package manager dependency resolution, and course scheduling systems all rely on topological sort

beginner.content:
BFS-Based Topological Sort Using In-Degrees

Repeatedly process any vertex with IN-DEGREE 0 (no unprocessed prerequisites) - removing it "frees up" its outgoing edges, decrementing its neighbors' in-degrees. When a neighbor's in-degree hits 0, it becomes eligible too. A queue naturally manages this "process whatever's ready" order.

expert.content:
Why "order.size() != n" Reliably Detects a Cycle

Every vertex STUCK inside a cycle can never reach in-degree 0 - its in-degree only ever decreases when a PREDECESSOR is processed, but within a cycle, every vertex's predecessor is ALSO stuck waiting inside the same cycle. This deadlock means cycle vertices are NEVER added to the queue, so the final output list falls short of n vertices - a clean, direct way to both perform topological sort AND detect cycles in one pass.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time and space complexity of Kahn's Algorithm?O(V + E) time (every vertex and edge processed once), O(V) space for the in-degree array and queue
How would you find the LEXICOGRAPHICALLY SMALLEST valid topological order?Replace the plain Queue with a PriorityQueue (min-heap) - always picking the smallest available in-degree-0 vertex at each step produces the lexicographically smallest valid ordering
Why is Kahn's Algorithm considered more "explicit" about cycle detection than the DFS-based approach?The final processed count directly and unambiguously reveals a cycle (processed != n); the DFS-based approach needs a separate inStack tracking mechanism specifically added for cycle detection, since plain DFS traversal alone doesn't naturally surface this

beginner.content:
Topological Sort via DFS Finishing Order

Run DFS from every unvisited vertex; when a vertex FINISHES (all its descendants fully explored), push it onto a stack. Reversing the finish order (via the stack) gives a valid topological order - a vertex finishes AFTER everything reachable from it, so it naturally ends up appearing BEFORE those descendants once reversed.

expert.content:
Why "Finish Order Reversed" is Always a Valid Topological Order

For any edge u → v, DFS from u will always recurse into v (directly or transitively) BEFORE u itself finishes - v's DFS call completes (finishes) first, gets pushed to the stack first, and therefore ends up DEEPER in the stack. When the stack is later popped (or iterated as a list, as shown), u comes out BEFORE v - exactly satisfying the topological order requirement, for every edge in the graph.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time and space complexity of DFS-based topological sort?O(V + E) time (standard DFS traversal), O(V) space for the visited set, recursion stack, and result stack
Does this approach detect cycles on its own?Not without extra tracking - a separate inStack set (like the directed cycle detection technique) must be added if cycle detection is also required; plain DFS finish-order alone assumes the graph is already a valid DAG
How does DFS-based topological sort relate to Kosaraju's Algorithm for Strongly Connected Components?Kosaraju's first step is EXACTLY this DFS finish-order computation on the original graph - it then reuses that order to drive a second DFS pass on the graph's TRANSPOSE (all edges reversed) to discover SCCs

Shortest Paths from One Source, Non-Negative Weights

Dijkstra's Algorithm greedily expands the UNVISITED vertex with the smallest known distance, using a min-heap - once a vertex is finalized, its distance is guaranteed correct and never revisited. Works ONLY when all edge weights are non-negative.

expert.content:
Why Dijkstra Fails with Negative Edges - a Concrete Counterexample

Dijkstra permanently FINALIZES a vertex's distance the moment it's popped from the heap, assuming no future path could possibly improve it. A negative edge violates this assumption - a path through a LATER-explored, seemingly-worse vertex could use a negative edge to become cheaper than an already-finalized "shortest" path.

Growing a Minimum Spanning Tree One Vertex at a Time

A Minimum Spanning Tree connects ALL vertices with the MINIMUM total edge weight, using exactly V-1 edges and no cycles. Prim's grows the MST from a single starting vertex: repeatedly add the CHEAPEST edge that connects the current tree to a NEW vertex outside it - a min-heap tracks candidate edges efficiently.

expert.content:
Why Prim's is Essentially "Dijkstra With a Different Relaxation Rule"

Both algorithms use a min-heap to greedily expand the frontier - the ONLY structural difference: Dijkstra tracks TOTAL accumulated distance from the source, while Prim's tracks just the SINGLE cheapest EDGE weight connecting to the growing tree (ignoring how far that tree has traveled overall). This subtle change in what's compared is what turns "shortest path" into "minimum spanning tree".

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time complexity of Prim's with a binary heap?O((V + E) log V), identical complexity class to Dijkstra with a binary heap - the same greedy min-heap expansion pattern
Does Prim's work correctly with negative edge weights?Yes - unlike Dijkstra, Prim's correctness doesn't rely on "shorter accumulated path is always better" reasoning; it only ever compares single edge weights directly, so negative weights don't break its greedy guarantee
When would you prefer Prim's over Kruskal's for MST?Prim's is typically faster on DENSE graphs (adjacency matrix + simple array-based version can hit O(V^2), competitive with or better than Kruskal's sort-heavy approach); Kruskal's tends to be simpler and faster on SPARSE graphs

beginner.content:
Building an MST by Sorting Edges Globally

Unlike Prim's (which grows from one vertex), Kruskal's sorts ALL edges by weight ascending, then greedily adds each edge UNLESS it would create a cycle - checked in O(α(n)) using Union-Find. The result is always a valid MST once V-1 edges have been added.

expert.content:
Why Rejecting Cycle-Forming Edges Still Produces the GLOBALLY OPTIMAL MST

This is the "cycle property" of MSTs: for any cycle, the HEAVIEST edge in that cycle can never be part of ANY minimum spanning tree - removing it (keeping the rest) always gives an equal-or-better tree. Kruskal's, by processing edges lightest-first and rejecting anything that would close a cycle, is implicitly always rejecting exactly the WOULD-BE-heaviest edge of whatever cycle it would have formed - which is precisely what the cycle property guarantees is safe to discard.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time complexity of Kruskal's Algorithm?O(E log E) dominated by sorting edges (E log E is equivalent to E log V since E <= V^2), plus O(E * α(V)) for the Union-Find operations - the sort dominates
Why does Kruskal's need Union-Find specifically, rather than a simpler visited check?Unlike Prim's (which grows one connected tree), Kruskal's edges arrive in arbitrary graph order - determining "would this edge connect two ALREADY-connected components" requires efficiently tracking which arbitrary GROUP each vertex currently belongs to, exactly what Union-Find provides
Is the MST unique if all edge weights are distinct?Yes - with all distinct weights, both Prim's and Kruskal's are guaranteed to produce the SAME unique MST; with tied weights, multiple different valid MSTs (all with the same total weight) can exist

beginner.content:
Tracking Groups of Connected Elements

DSU (also called Union-Find) maintains a collection of disjoint (non-overlapping) sets, supporting two operations: find(x) - which set does x belong to (returns a representative "root"), and union(a, b) - merge a's and b's sets into one. Naive implementation without optimization: each element points to a parent, walking up to the root.

expert.content:
Path Compression + Union by Rank - Near O(1) Amortized

Two optimizations transform DSU from O(n) worst-case per operation to nearly O(1) amortized (technically O(α(n)), the inverse Ackermann function - effectively constant for any realistic n):
  • Path compression: during find, repoint every visited node DIRECTLY to the root, flattening future lookups.
  • Union by rank: always attach the SHORTER tree under the TALLER one's root, preventing chains from growing unnecessarily long.

What class of problems is DSU the standard tool for?Detecting cycles in an undirected graph, Kruskal's MST algorithm, counting/tracking connected components dynamically, and "redundant connection" style problems

beginner.content:
Redundant Connection - Finding the Edge That Creates a Cycle

Given a graph that was originally a tree (n vertices, n-1 edges) with ONE extra edge added, find that extra edge. Process edges in order, union-ing their endpoints - the FIRST edge whose endpoints are ALREADY in the same set is the redundant one (adding it would create a cycle).

expert.content:
Number of Provinces - Union-Find on a Connectivity Matrix

Given an n × n matrix where isConnected[i][j] = 1 means cities i and j are directly connected, find the number of PROVINCES (groups of indirectly connected cities). Union every direct connection, then count DISTINCT roots remaining - a clean application of tracking connected components dynamically.

Visualizing Recursive Calls as a Tree

Every recursive function's execution can be drawn as a TREE: the root is the initial call, and each node's children are the recursive calls IT makes. This "recursion tree" is exactly how to reason about time complexity - count the total number of nodes, or the work done at each node summed across the tree.

expert.content:
Using the Recursion Tree to Derive Time Complexity

Naive Fibonacci's recursion tree has TWO children per node, and the tree's height is n - a tree with branching factor 2 and height n has roughly 2ⁿ nodes, matching the well-known O(2ⁿ) complexity. This "draw the tree, count the nodes/work" method is the standard way to derive - or verify - a recursive algorithm's Big-O without needing the Master Theorem for simple cases.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How does a recursion tree explain why memoized Fibonacci is O(n)?Memoization prunes the tree drastically - once a subproblem's result is cached, its entire subtree of further recursive calls is skipped on subsequent encounters, collapsing the tree from exponential to linear size
What's the recursion tree's shape for a divide-and-conquer algorithm like Merge Sort?A tree with branching factor 2, height log n, but with the WORK done at each level (not just node count) being what matters - O(n) work summed at every one of the log n levels gives O(n log n) total
How does the recursion tree relate to the call stack's space usage?The call stack's maximum depth at any point corresponds to the recursion tree's HEIGHT along the current path being explored, not the tree's total node count - this is why space complexity is O(h), while time complexity relates to total nodes/work

beginner.content:
Generating All Subsets (the Power Set)

A set of n elements has 2ⁿ subsets - each element is either INCLUDED or EXCLUDED, independently. Backtracking generates them all by trying both choices at every element and recursing, with a base case that records the current partial subset once all elements have been decided.

expert.content:
Handling Duplicates - Subsets II

When the input array has DUPLICATE values, the naive approach produces duplicate subsets. The fix: SORT first, then at each recursion level, skip over a value if it equals the PREVIOUS value at the same level (meaning that "include/exclude" choice for this value was already explored from an earlier duplicate).

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why does a set of n elements have exactly 2^n subsets?Each element independently has 2 states (in or out); by the multiplication principle, n independent binary choices give 2^n total combinations
Why does "i > start" (not "i > 0") matter for the duplicate-skip condition?It only skips duplicates within the SAME recursive call's loop (the same "level" of choices being made), not duplicates that appear legitimately at DIFFERENT recursion depths - using i > 0 would incorrectly block valid subsets
How could you generate all subsets iteratively, without recursion?Start with just the empty set; for each new element, take every EXISTING subset and add a copy of it WITH the new element appended - doubling the subset count each iteration, matching the 2^n growth

beginner.content:
Generating Subsequences with a Condition

Subsequences generation uses the exact same include/exclude backtracking shape as subsets - the difference is usually a FILTER: only keep subsequences meeting some condition (a target sum, a specific length, alternating parity). This is where backtracking becomes genuinely useful over just enumerating everything.

expert.content:
Only the FIRST Matching Subsequence - Early Termination

When a problem needs just ANY one valid subsequence (not all of them), the recursion should RETURN a boolean/found-flag and stop exploring once found - avoiding wasted work exploring the rest of the search space after an answer is already in hand.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why does "find only ONE matching subsequence" run much faster than "find ALL"?It can stop exploring the moment a valid answer is found, pruning away the rest of the exponential search space that would otherwise still be checked when collecting every match
How does this problem relate to the 0/1 Knapsack / Subset Sum family?They share the identical include/exclude recursive structure - Subset Sum is exactly "does ANY subsequence sum to target", answerable with the same backtracking shown here (or solved faster with DP if only existence, not the actual subsequence, is needed)
What's the worst-case time complexity of exhaustively finding ALL matching subsequences?O(2^n) - every element still independently branches into include/exclude, regardless of the target-sum filter, since the filter only prunes AFTER a full path is built (unless additional pruning like "remaining sum can't reach target" is added)

beginner.content:
Generating All Orderings

A set of n distinct elements has n! permutations. Backtracking builds each one by choosing an UNUSED element at each position, recursing, then un-choosing it (backtrack) to try the next option - a used[] array tracks which elements are already placed in the current permutation.

expert.content:
Permutations with Duplicates - Avoiding Duplicate Output

With repeated values, the naive approach produces duplicate permutations. The fix: SORT first, then at each position, skip a value if it equals the PREVIOUS value AND that previous occurrence is currently unused - meaning both would produce an identical permutation from this position onward.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time complexity of generating all permutations?O(n! × n) - there are n! permutations, and copying each completed permutation into the result costs O(n)
Why is "!used[i-1]" specifically the correct duplicate-skip condition, not "used[i-1]"?It ensures duplicates are always placed in a FIXED relative order within any single permutation (the earlier occurrence must be used before the later one) - this canonical ordering eliminates duplicate permutations without accidentally skipping valid ones
How would you generate permutations WITHOUT extra space for a used[] array?Swap-based in-place generation: swap the current index with each later index in turn, recurse on the remainder, then swap back - avoids the boolean array at the cost of mutating (and restoring) the input array itself

beginner.content:
Choosing K Elements, Order Doesn't Matter

Combinations differ from permutations by ignoring ORDER - {1,2} and {2,1} count as the SAME combination. The backtracking trick: always choose elements in INCREASING index order (never look backward), which naturally avoids generating the same combination twice.

expert.content:
Pruning - Stop Early When Not Enough Elements Remain

A key optimization: if the remaining numbers (from i to n) can't possibly fill the remaining slots needed, stop trying immediately instead of recursing into a doomed branch - this pruning significantly reduces wasted exploration for larger n and k.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How many combinations of size k exist from n elements?C(n, k) = n! / (k! * (n-k)!), the binomial coefficient - unlike permutations, order doesn't multiply the count
Why does "start from i+1" prevent duplicate combinations, unlike permutations' used[] array?Combinations don't care about order, so restricting each choice to come AFTER the previous one guarantees each unique SET of elements is generated in exactly one canonical (sorted) order, never revisited from a different starting sequence
How does the "n - needed + 1" pruning bound get derived?If 'needed' more elements must be chosen from the remaining range [i, n], there must be at least 'needed' numbers available - meaning i can go no higher than n - needed + 1, or the branch can never complete a valid combination

beginner.content:
Combinations That Sum to a Target - REUSING Elements Allowed

Given candidates and a target, find all combinations summing to target, where each candidate can be used UNLIMITED times. The key difference from plain Combinations: when recursing after choosing candidates[i], the next call starts from i again (not i+1), allowing the same element to be picked repeatedly.

expert.content:
Combination Sum II - No Reuse, But Duplicates in the Input Array

A harder variant: each candidate usable at most ONCE, but the input array itself may contain duplicate values. Two changes from the basic version: recurse from i+1 (no reuse), and sort + skip same-level duplicates (same trick as Subsets II) to avoid duplicate combinations in the output.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why pass 'i' (not 'i+1') when reuse is allowed, but 'i+1' when it isn't?Passing i lets the NEXT recursive call still consider candidates[i] again (reuse); passing i+1 forces strictly forward progress, guaranteeing each candidate is used at most once
Why does sorting first enable the "break" optimization?Once candidates are sorted, any candidate exceeding the remaining target means EVERY later candidate (being even bigger) would too - so the loop can stop entirely instead of just skipping that one element
What's the worst-case time complexity of Combination Sum with unlimited reuse?Exponential in the target divided by the smallest candidate - roughly O(candidates^(target/min_candidate)), since the recursion depth can grow proportionally to how many times the smallest candidate could be reused

beginner.content:
Placing N Queens So None Attack Each Other

Place N queens on an N×N board with no two sharing a row, column, or diagonal. Since each ROW must have exactly one queen, the recursion places one queen per row, checking column and diagonal safety before committing - a textbook backtracking problem.

expert.content:
O(1) Diagonal/Column Checks with Bitmasks

Checking "is this column/diagonal already used" with a loop over previous rows is O(n) per check, O(n) per row, O(n²) per solution attempt.
