Using THREE bitmasks (columns, "/" diagonals, "\" diagonals) makes each safety check O(1) - a huge speedup for larger N, turning an already-exponential search into a much faster one.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why is placing one queen per ROW guaranteed to work, without checking rows for conflicts?The problem structure itself (one queen per row, row index used as the recursion depth) makes row conflicts impossible by construction - only column and diagonal conflicts need explicit checking
Why do the two diagonal bitmasks shift LEFT and RIGHT respectively as row increases?A "\" diagonal's column index increases by 1 each row down (shift left), while a "/" diagonal's column index decreases by 1 each row down (shift right) - the bitmask shift mirrors that column drift
What's N-Queens' time complexity, and can backtracking with pruning improve on brute force?Brute force checking all N^N placements is far worse than backtracking's effective search, which prunes invalid branches immediately - still exponential in the worst case (no known polynomial solution), but pruning makes it tractable for reasonably sized boards

beginner.content:
Filling a 9×9 Grid with Constraint-Checked Backtracking

For each empty cell, try digits 1-9; a digit is valid only if it doesn't already appear in the same ROW, COLUMN, or 3×3 BOX. Place a valid digit, recurse to the next empty cell, and backtrack (undo) if that path leads to a dead end.

expert.content:
Why This Design Is What Makes Backtracking Correct Here

The critical detail: after trying a digit and recursing, if the recursive call returns false (couldn't complete the board), the cell is RESET to '.' before trying the next digit. Skipping this reset would leave stale state polluting later attempts. Equally important: return false at the END of the digit loop (no valid digit worked) is what SIGNALS the failure back up to the CALLER, triggering that caller's own backtrack - this is the mechanism that lets failure propagate correctly through many levels of recursion.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why is isValid() checked O(9) times per digit attempt instead of maintained incrementally?The simple version re-scans row/column/box each time for clarity; a faster implementation maintains boolean[9][9] arrays for rows, columns, and boxes, updated incrementally, turning each check into O(1)
What makes Sudoku solving exponential in the worst case, despite the constraints?With few pre-filled cells, many digits remain individually "valid" at each step, so the search tree still branches significantly before constraints eliminate most paths - though in practice, constraint propagation prunes the search dramatically faster than a naive worst-case bound suggests
How could you speed up the search with a smarter cell-selection heuristic?Instead of always scanning row-by-row, choose the EMPTY cell with the FEWEST valid candidate digits first (minimum remaining values heuristic) - this fails faster on bad branches and succeeds faster on good ones

beginner.content:
Finding a Path Through a Grid

A rat starts at the top-left of a grid maze and must reach the bottom-right, moving only through open cells (marked 1, blocked cells marked 0). Backtracking tries each direction from the current cell, marking it visited, recursing, and UN-marking it if that direction leads to a dead end - the un-marking is essential so other paths can still use that cell.

expert.content:
Why the visited[] Reset is the Single Most Important Line

Forgetting visited[nr][nc] = false after backtracking is THE classic bug in maze/grid backtracking problems: without it, a cell that was part of one failed attempt stays permanently "blocked" for every OTHER path the search tries afterward - silently causing the algorithm to miss valid solutions, often with no error, just wrong (incomplete) output.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the worst-case time complexity of Rat in a Maze?O(4^(n*n)) in the worst case - at each cell, up to 4 directions can be tried, though the visited check and boundary checks prune most invalid branches in practice
How would you find just ONE valid path instead of ALL paths?Return a boolean from the recursive function, and stop exploring/return true immediately once a path is found - same early-termination principle as "find one matching subsequence"
How does this problem relate to DFS on a graph?It's literally DFS where each grid cell is a node and adjacent open cells are edges - the visited-and-backtrack pattern here is identical to how DFS avoids revisiting nodes, adapted to also UNDO the visited marking since multiple distinct paths need independent exploration

beginner.content:
Finding One Word in a Letter Grid

Given a grid of letters and a single target word, check if the word can be formed by a path of ADJACENT cells (no cell reused within one path). DFS from every starting cell, backtracking (temporarily marking cells visited, then un-marking) whenever a path doesn't pan out.

expert.content:
Why '#' Marking Beats a Separate visited[][] Array Here

Instead of allocating a whole extra boolean[][] array, temporarily overwriting the cell with a sentinel character (like '#', guaranteed not to match any real letter) achieves the same "don't revisit this cell" effect with ZERO extra space - the grid IS the visited-tracking structure, restored immediately after each failed attempt.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time complexity of Word Search for a single word?O(rows * cols * 4^L) where L is the word length - each of the rows*cols starting cells can trigger a DFS branching up to 4 ways at each of the L characters
Why must the sentinel character be restored even when a match IS found early in one branch?The || short-circuit means later DFS calls in the same expression never execute, but the calling code (the loop over all starting cells) still needs a clean, unmodified board if this search fails and moves to the next starting cell - though once a match returns true all the way up, the restore doesn't matter for THAT search's outcome
How does searching for MULTIPLE words (Word Search II) improve on running this once per word?Building a Trie of all target words first lets a single DFS pass share work across words with common prefixes and prune branches the moment no word continues down that path - see the dedicated Trie-based String Problems topic

beginner.content:
All Valid Combinations of N Pairs

Generate every well-formed combination of N pairs of parentheses. Track two counts as you build the string: open used so far, close used so far. Add '(' whenever open < n; add ')' only when close < open (never more closes than opens at any point - that's what makes a prefix valid).

expert.content:
Why "close < open" is the Entire Validity Guarantee

This single condition is doing ALL the work of validity checking: it guarantees that at every prefix of the string, the number of ) never exceeds the number of ( - which is EXACTLY the definition of a valid parenthesization prefix. Combined with the final length check (2n total characters means both counts reached exactly n), no separate "is this valid?" verification function is ever needed - correctness is built into the generation process itself.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How many valid combinations exist for N pairs, and what's the relevant sequence?The Nth Catalan number - C(2n, n) / (n+1) - which grows roughly as 4^n / n^1.5, so the algorithm's time complexity is bounded by that count times O(n) to build each string
Why is this considered "backtracking with built-in pruning" rather than "generate then filter"?Invalid branches (where close would exceed open) are never even attempted - the algorithm only ever explores paths that could still lead to a valid result, unlike generating ALL 2^(2n) bit-strings and checking each for validity afterward
How would you count JUST the number of valid combinations without generating them all?The Catalan number formula directly, or a DP recurrence: C(n) = sum over i of C(i) * C(n-1-i) - no need for backtracking at all if only the count is needed

beginner.content:
What is Pruning?

Pruning means detecting EARLY that a partial solution can never lead to a valid answer, and abandoning that branch immediately - instead of building it all the way out just to fail at the end. Every backtracking algorithm technically "works" without pruning, but pruning is what makes it FAST in practice, sometimes by orders of magnitude.

expert.content:
Three Common Pruning Strategies

  • Bound pruning: stop if the current partial result already exceeds/falls short of what's needed (as shown above with remaining < 0).
  • Constraint pruning: stop the moment a hard constraint is violated (N-Queens checking column/diagonal safety BEFORE recursing, not after).
  • Duplicate pruning: skip choices that would produce a result already generated by a different branch (the "skip same-level duplicates" trick in Subsets II / Permutations II / Combination Sum II).

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Does pruning change a backtracking algorithm's worst-case asymptotic complexity?Usually not in the theoretical worst case (the problem can still be inherently exponential), but it can dramatically reduce the PRACTICAL runtime by eliminating huge swaths of the search space early
Why check constraints BEFORE recursing rather than after building a complete candidate?Checking before avoids wasting time building out an entire invalid branch - a single early rejection can eliminate an entire exponential subtree of further invalid attempts in one comparison
What's the relationship between pruning and memoization?They're complementary but different: pruning eliminates branches that CAN'T lead to a valid/optimal answer; memoization avoids RECOMPUTING branches that have already been solved before - a backtracking + DP hybrid can use both together

beginner.content:
What is a Constraint Satisfaction Problem (CSP)?

A CSP asks: assign a value to each of several VARIABLES, from their respective DOMAINS, such that every CONSTRAINT between variables is satisfied. Sudoku, N-Queens, and graph coloring are all CSPs - backtracking is the general-purpose algorithm for solving them: assign a value, check constraints, recurse; undo and try another value if stuck.

expert.content:
Speeding Up CSPs - Variable and Value Ordering Heuristics

Real CSP solvers rarely process variables in a fixed order - two heuristics dramatically improve performance:
  • Minimum Remaining Values (MRV): assign the variable with the FEWEST legal values remaining first - it's the most constrained, and if it's going to fail, better to find out early.
  • Least Constraining Value: when choosing a value for a variable, prefer the one that rules out the FEWEST options for other variables - keeps the search space open longer.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How does Sudoku fit the CSP framework specifically?Variables = the 81 cells, domains = digits 1-9 for each, constraints = "no repeated digit in any row, column, or 3x3 box" - exactly the standard CSP structure
What's the difference between CSP backtracking and general backtracking?CSP backtracking specifically frames the problem as variables/domains/constraints and often applies domain-specific heuristics (MRV, constraint propagation like arc-consistency); general backtracking is the broader technique CSP-solving is built on top of
What is "constraint propagation" and how does it differ from backtracking itself?Propagation actively REDUCES other variables' domains based on a new assignment (e.g. removing a color from neighbors' options immediately after coloring a vertex), catching failures even before backtracking would discover them through further recursive attempts

beginner.content:
Selecting the Maximum Number of Non-Overlapping Activities

Given activities each with a start and end time, pick the MAXIMUM number that don't overlap. The greedy insight: always pick the activity that FINISHES EARLIEST among the remaining valid options - it leaves the most room for future activities. Sort by end time, then scan once.

expert.content:
Why "Earliest Finish Time" is Provably Optimal (Exchange Argument)

The proof that greedy works here uses an EXCHANGE ARGUMENT: suppose an optimal solution doesn't pick the earliest-finishing activity first. Swap it in instead of whatever the optimal solution DID pick first - since the earliest-finish activity ends no later, this swap can only free up MORE room for subsequent choices, never less. So an optimal solution using the greedy first choice always exists - by induction, the whole greedy strategy is optimal.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why sort by END time rather than start time or duration?End time directly measures how much room is left for FUTURE activities - sorting by start time or duration doesn't correlate with that, and can lead to suboptimal choices
What's the time complexity of Activity Selection?O(n log n), dominated by the sort; the greedy scan afterward is O(n)
Does a greedy approach work for the WEIGHTED version (each activity has a value, maximize total value)?No - weighted activity selection requires Dynamic Programming, since a locally "safe" greedy choice no longer guarantees the globally optimal total value once weights are unequal

beginner.content:
Filling a Knapsack When Items CAN Be Split

Given items with weight and value, and a knapsack capacity, maximize total value - items can be taken in FRACTIONS (unlike 0/1 Knapsack). The greedy strategy: always take as much as possible of the item with the HIGHEST value-per-weight ratio first.

expert.content:
Why Fractional Knapsack Allows Greedy, But 0/1 Knapsack Doesn't

Fractional Knapsack's greedy correctness relies ENTIRELY on being able to split items - taking the highest ratio item first is provably optimal because any "waste" of capacity can always be filled with a PARTIAL unit of the current best-ratio item. In 0/1 Knapsack, items are indivisible - the highest-ratio item might not fit at all, forcing a completely different combination to be better, which is exactly why 0/1 Knapsack needs Dynamic Programming instead.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time complexity of Fractional Knapsack?O(n log n), dominated by sorting items by value/weight ratio; the greedy fill itself is O(n)
Why does taking the highest ratio item first maximize value for the fractional version?Since fractions are allowed, filling capacity with the highest "value per unit weight" always yields at least as much value as any other allocation of that same capacity - an exchange argument identical in spirit to Activity Selection's
What real-world problems map to Fractional Knapsack rather than 0/1?Resource allocation problems where partial amounts genuinely make sense - blending commodities (like mixing ores by value/cost ratio), or allocating a divisible budget across investments

beginner.content:
Maximizing Profit with Deadlines

Each job has a DEADLINE and a PROFIT; each job takes exactly 1 unit of time, and only one job can run at a time. Schedule jobs to maximize total profit. Greedy strategy: sort jobs by profit DESCENDING, then for each job, schedule it as LATE as possible (closest to its deadline, but still before it) - leaving earlier slots open for other jobs.

expert.content:
Why "Schedule As Late As Possible" Beats "As Early As Possible"

Scheduling a job EARLY unnecessarily "wastes" an early time slot that a job with an EARLIER deadline might desperately need. Scheduling as LATE as possible (but still on time) preserves maximum flexibility for jobs that have tighter deadlines - a subtle but crucial greedy design choice that's easy to get backward.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time complexity of this Job Sequencing approach?O(n log n) for sorting plus O(n * maxDeadline) for the placement scan - can be improved to O(n log n) overall using a Disjoint Set Union to jump directly to the nearest free slot instead of scanning backward one by one
What does the boolean slotUsed[] array represent conceptually?Each time unit is a resource that can host at most one job - the array tracks which discrete time slots are already occupied
How would DSU speed up the "find the latest free slot" search?Each slot's DSU parent points to the next FREE slot at or before it; finding a slot is a find() call, and "using" a slot unions it with the slot before it - both become near O(1) amortized instead of a linear backward scan

beginner.content:
Minimum Removals to Make Intervals Non-Overlapping

The flip side of Activity Selection: instead of asking "how many can I KEEP", ask "how many must I REMOVE" so the rest don't overlap. Both questions share the same greedy foundation (sort by end time), and the answer to one directly gives the other: removals = total - maxKept.

expert.content:
Why the Overlapping Interval is Discarded, Not the Kept One

When two intervals overlap, the algorithm ALWAYS discards the one being examined and keeps the one with the EARLIER end time already recorded (never updating lastEnd to a later value on a conflict) - this is exactly the "always favor earliest finish" greedy principle, applied here as "never let the boundary get WORSE (later) than what's already been secured".

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How does "minimum removals" relate to "maximum non-overlapping intervals"?They're complementary: removals = total intervals - (maximum number that can be kept non-overlapping), which is exactly what Activity Selection computes directly
What's the time complexity of the minimum-removals approach?O(n log n) for the sort, O(n) for the single greedy scan - same complexity class as Activity Selection
Would sorting by START time work equally well here?No - sorting by end time is what guarantees the greedy "keep the earliest-ending" choice is always locally and globally correct; start-time sorting doesn't have that same optimality guarantee

beginner.content:
Employee Free Time - Merging Across Multiple Schedules

A harder variant of basic interval merging: given several employees' individual busy schedules (each already sorted and non-overlapping WITHIN a person), find the COMMON free time slots shared by everyone. The greedy approach: flatten ALL intervals together, sort by start, merge overlapping busy periods exactly like basic merge intervals - then the GAPS between merged intervals are the shared free time.

expert.content:
Why Flattening Everyone's Schedule Together is Correct

The key insight: "when is EVERYONE simultaneously free" is equivalent to "when is NO ONE busy" - which only requires knowing the UNION of all busy periods, not which specific person owns which interval. Once flattened and merged, the merged busy blocks represent all moments when at least one person is occupied; the gaps between them are, by elimination, when nobody is busy at all.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time complexity of Employee Free Time?O(n log n) where n is the total number of intervals across all employees - dominated by the sort, since merging and gap-finding are both O(n)
Could a heap-based K-way merge be used instead of flattening and sorting everything?Yes - since each employee's OWN schedule is already sorted, a min-heap tracking the earliest unprocessed interval per employee achieves the same result in O(n log k) where k is the number of employees, better when k is much smaller than n
Why must the greedy merge sort by START time specifically for THIS problem?The merge-adjacent-overlapping-intervals logic relies on processing intervals in start-time order so that "does the next interval overlap with what's currently merged" can be checked with a single comparison against the running merged block's end

beginner.content:
How Many Platforms Does a Railway Station Need?

Given trains' arrival and departure times, find the MINIMUM number of platforms needed so no two overlapping trains ever need the same platform. Greedy approach: sort arrivals and departures SEPARATELY, then sweep through in time order - a platform is needed whenever an arrival happens, freed whenever a departure happens (using two pointers).

expert.content:
Why This is Equivalent to "Maximum Overlapping Intervals"

The minimum platforms needed exactly equals the MAXIMUM number of trains simultaneously present at any single moment - the two-pointer sweep is a clever O(n log n) way to find that peak overlap without checking every possible time instant. This same technique (separately sorted "events" sweep) generalizes to any "max concurrent X" problem: meeting rooms needed, max simultaneous users online, peak concurrent downloads.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time complexity of the two-pointer sweep approach?O(n log n) - dominated by sorting arrivals and departures separately; the sweep itself is O(n)
How would you solve this with a min-heap instead of the two-pointer sweep?Sort trains by arrival time; for each new arrival, check if the heap's earliest departure is <= this arrival's time - if so, reuse that platform (pop and push); otherwise allocate a new platform (just push) - the heap's final size is the answer
What's the exact relationship to "Meeting Rooms II" (a common LeetCode framing)?They're the identical problem with different vocabulary - trains/platforms map directly to meetings/rooms, and both reduce to "find the maximum number of simultaneously active intervals"

beginner.content:
Optimal Prefix-Free Compression

Huffman Coding assigns SHORTER binary codes to MORE FREQUENT characters, minimizing total encoded size. It builds a binary tree greedily: repeatedly take the TWO least-frequent nodes (using a min-heap), merge them into a new node (frequency = sum), and repeat until one tree remains. A character's code is the path of 0s/1s from root to its leaf.

expert.content:
Why Merging the Two Least-Frequent Nodes is Optimal

The two rarest characters ending up DEEPEST in the tree (longest codes) minimizes their contribution to total size, since they occur least often - a classic greedy exchange argument: swapping any two leaves so a MORE frequent character got a LONGER code than a LESS frequent one would only increase the total encoded length, never decrease it. This guarantees Huffman's tree achieves the theoretical minimum total encoded size among all prefix-free codes.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time complexity of building a Huffman tree?O(n log n) - n-1 merge operations, each doing two O(log n) heap extractions and one O(log n) insertion
Why is the resulting code "prefix-free" (no code is a prefix of another)?Every character ends up at a LEAF of the tree, and no leaf can be an ancestor of another leaf in a binary tree - so no character's code path can be a prefix of another's
What real-world formats use Huffman Coding?DEFLATE (used in ZIP, gzip, PNG) uses Huffman Coding as one of its compression stages, typically combined with LZ77-style dictionary matching first

beginner.content:
Finding the Starting Point for a Complete Circular Trip

Given gas available and cost to travel between stations arranged in a circle, find the starting station that lets a car complete the full loop (if one exists). The greedy insight: if the TOTAL gas ≥ TOTAL cost, a valid starting point is GUARANTEED to exist - and it can be found in one pass by tracking where the running tank first goes negative.

expert.content:
Why Failing at Station i Rules Out EVERY Station Between startIndex and i

This is the subtle correctness argument: if starting at startIndex and the tank goes negative reaching station i, then starting from ANY station strictly between startIndex and i would ALSO fail - because that later start has LESS accumulated surplus gas than starting from startIndex did (it skips some of the positive contributions startIndex already banked). This is exactly why the algorithm safely jumps startIndex all the way to i+1 without needing to individually test every skipped station.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why does totalTank >= 0 guarantee a solution exists?If the total gas across the whole circuit is at least the total cost, some starting point must let the tank stay non-negative the whole way around - this is provable, and the algorithm's single pass happens to also FIND that point as a side effect
What's the time and space complexity?O(n) time, O(1) space - a single pass with running totals, no extra data structures
Is the answer guaranteed to be UNIQUE when a solution exists?Yes - it can be proven that if totalTank >= 0, exactly one valid starting index exists (given the circuit must be traversed once around without repeating), which is why the algorithm can confidently return a single index rather than a set of candidates

beginner.content:
Can You Reach the Last Index?

Each array element is the MAXIMUM jump length from that position. Determine if the last index is reachable from index 0. Greedy approach: track the FARTHEST reachable index seen so far as you scan left to right - if you ever reach a position beyond that farthest reach before updating it, you're stuck.

expert.content:
Jump Game II - Minimum Number of Jumps

A harder follow-up: find the MINIMUM jumps needed to reach the end (assuming it's always reachable). The greedy trick uses an implicit "BFS by levels" idea: track the current jump's reach and the NEXT jump's best possible reach; when the scan passes the current jump's boundary, that's when a jump is "used", moving the boundary forward.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why does "i > farthestReachable" correctly detect an impossible Jump Game?farthestReachable represents the BEST possible reach given everything seen so far - if the current index i already exceeds it, no sequence of jumps from earlier positions could have gotten here, so it's definitively unreachable
What's the intuition behind Jump Game II's "level by level" framing?currentEnd marks the boundary of everywhere reachable with the jumps used SO FAR (like a BFS level); farthest tracks the best possible NEXT boundary; crossing currentEnd forces incrementing the jump count, exactly like moving to the next BFS level
What's the time and space complexity of both versions?Both are O(n) time, O(1) space - single-pass greedy scans with running trackers, no extra data structures needed

beginner.content:
Minimizing Average Waiting Time - the General Ratio-Greedy Pattern

A whole family of problems is solved by sorting on the RIGHT ratio or simple key, not by anything complex. Classic example: given job durations, schedule them (one at a time, no preemption) to minimize AVERAGE waiting time across all jobs. Greedy answer: run the SHORTEST job first - "Shortest Job First" scheduling.

expert.content:
Why "Shortest Job First" Minimizes Total Waiting Time - Exchange Argument

Suppose an optimal schedule has a LONGER job immediately before a SHORTER one. Swapping their order: the shorter job now finishes earlier, reducing the waiting time of EVERY job after it by the difference in their durations, while the longer job's own start time doesn't get worse relative to jobs before it. Net effect: swapping always helps or ties, never hurts - so sorting shortest-first is optimal.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the general recipe for spotting a "sort by the right ratio/key" greedy problem?Look for an objective that's a SUM or AVERAGE over all items, where each item's contribution depends on WHEN it's processed relative to others - an adjacent-swap exchange argument usually reveals the correct sort key
How does this generalize Fractional Knapsack's value/weight ratio idea?Both are instances of "greedily order by a ratio that directly measures efficiency per unit of the constrained resource" - weight in Knapsack, time in scheduling; the underlying exchange-argument proof technique is the same
What's the time complexity of Shortest Job First scheduling?O(n log n), dominated by sorting - the waiting time computation afterward is a single O(n) pass

beginner.content:
Connect Ropes to Minimize Total Cost

Given ropes of different lengths, connecting two ropes costs the SUM of their lengths; find the minimum total cost to connect ALL ropes into one. Greedy insight: always connect the two SHORTEST ropes first - a min-heap makes finding "the two shortest, repeatedly, as the set changes" efficient.

expert.content:
Why This is Structurally Identical to Huffman Coding

Connect Ropes and Huffman Coding are the SAME algorithm in disguise: both repeatedly merge the two smallest values using a min-heap, and both are provably optimal by the identical exchange argument (any two ropes/frequencies connected/merged LATER than necessary only increases total cost, since their length/frequency gets counted as part of MORE subsequent merges the longer they wait unconnected).

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time complexity of Connect Ropes?O(n log n) - n-1 merges, each involving two O(log n) heap pops and one O(log n) push
Why is a heap needed here instead of just sorting once at the start?Every merge produces a NEW value that must be reinserted into consideration for future merges - a one-time sort can't accommodate a value that didn't exist yet when sorting happened; a heap supports this dynamic insert/extract pattern efficiently
What other classic problems use this exact "min-heap, merge two smallest, repeat" template?Huffman Coding (tree construction), and the general "merge K sorted lists efficiently" family, though that specific problem uses the heap slightly differently (tracking one element per list rather than merging pairs)

beginner.content:
Recursion

A recursive function calls itself with a smaller version of the problem until it reaches a base case that can be answered directly without further recursion. Every recursive function needs both a base case (to stop) and a recursive case (to progress toward it).

intermediate.content:
Dynamic Programming (Memoization)

Dynamic Programming speeds up recursive solutions that re-solve the same subproblems, by caching (memoizing) each subproblem's result the first time it's computed. This turns exponential-time recursion into linear or polynomial time.

beginner.content:
How Many Ways to Climb N Stairs, 1 or 2 Steps at a Time?

The number of ways to reach step n equals ways to reach n-1 (then take 1 step) PLUS ways to reach n-2 (then take 2 steps) - literally the Fibonacci recurrence in disguise. Bottom-up DP builds this from the base cases upward, O(n) time, O(1) space.

expert.content:
Generalizing to K Allowed Step Sizes

When steps of {1, 2, ..., k} are allowed instead of just {1, 2}, ways(n) = sum of ways(n - s) for each allowed step size s - a direct generalization, still O(n × k) time with a simple DP array.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why is Climbing Stairs literally the Fibonacci sequence?Its recurrence ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2) is identical in structure to fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2), just with different base case values
What's the space-optimized version's complexity, and why does it work?O(1) space - since each step only depends on the previous TWO values, only two variables need to be tracked instead of a full DP array
How would you solve this with matrix exponentiation for very large n?The Fibonacci-style recurrence can be expressed as a 2x2 matrix power, computable in O(log n) time via fast exponentiation - useful when n is astronomically large and O(n) is too slow

beginner.content:
Maximize Loot Without Robbing Two Adjacent Houses

At each house, choose: SKIP it (carry forward the best result without it), or ROB it (its value plus the best result from two houses back, since the adjacent one can't also be robbed). dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i]).

expert.content:
House Robber II - Houses Arranged in a CIRCLE

When the first and last houses are ADJACENT (circular arrangement), robbing both is forbidden. The trick: run the linear House Robber TWICE - once excluding the first house, once excluding the last house - and take the maximum. This correctly handles every valid configuration without needing new logic.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why does splitting into "exclude last" and "exclude first" correctly solve the circular version?Together the two cases cover EVERY valid selection: any valid robbery either skips the last house (covered by case 1) or skips the first house (covered by case 2) - it can never rob BOTH first and last, so one of the two cases always contains the true optimum
What's the time and space complexity of both versions?O(n) time; O(1) space with the rolling-variable optimization shown, though a naive dp[] array would be O(n) space
How would House Robber III (houses arranged in a TREE) differ?It needs Tree DP: each node returns two values - best loot if this node IS robbed, and best loot if it is NOT - combining children's results bottom-up, since "adjacent" now means parent-child rather than array-neighbor

beginner.content:
Kadane's as a Formal DP Recurrence

Kadane's Algorithm IS dynamic programming, just usually taught without the DP framing: define dp[i] = the maximum subarray sum ENDING exactly at index i. The recurrence dp[i] = max(arr[i], dp[i-1] + arr[i]) is the same "extend or restart" idea, just written as an explicit DP array instead of two rolling variables.

expert.content:
Maximum PRODUCT Subarray - Tracking Two DP States

Products behave differently from sums: a negative number can turn the SMALLEST product into the LARGEST. This means the DP state must track BOTH the max and min product ending at each index, since a future negative multiplier could flip the current minimum into the new maximum.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why does the standard "extend or restart" recurrence for SUM not directly work for PRODUCT?Sum is monotonic in a simple sense (adding more never flips a comparison's direction based on sign alone); multiplying by a negative number can turn the smallest value into the largest, so tracking only a "running maximum" misses cases where the running MINIMUM becomes relevant
Why swap maxSoFar and minSoFar when the current number is negative?Multiplying the previous minimum (likely a large negative product) by a new negative number produces a large POSITIVE product - by swapping first, the same max()/min() update lines correctly handle both cases without duplicated logic
What's the space complexity of both the sum and product versions?Both can be done in O(1) space using rolling variables instead of a full dp[] array, since each step only depends on the immediately preceding state

beginner.content:
The General 2D DP Grid Pattern

Many grid problems (unique paths, min path sum, max path sum, obstacle paths) share ONE shape: dp[r][c] depends only on dp[r-1][c] (from above) and dp[r][c-1] (from the left) - since movement is restricted to right/down. Fill the grid row by row, left to right, and each cell's answer is ready by the time you need it.

expert.content:
Grid Paths With Obstacles

A blocked cell simply has ZERO paths reaching it - it doesn't contribute to any cell that depends on it. This single change (checking for an obstacle and setting dp[r][c] = 0) adapts the same framework to a whole new variant without restructuring anything.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why can dp[r][c] be computed knowing only dp[r-1][c] and dp[r][c-1]?Movement is restricted to right/down only, so every path to (r,c) must arrive from EITHER directly above or directly to the left - no other cell can contribute
What's the time and space complexity, and how can space be reduced?O(rows*cols) time and space naively; space reduces to O(cols) since each row only needs the PREVIOUS row's values - a 1D rolling array suffices
How would you adapt this framework to MAXIMIZE collected value along the path instead of counting paths?Replace the sum (dp[r-1][c] + dp[r][c-1]) with a max (Math.max(dp[r-1][c], dp[r][c-1]) + grid[r][c]) - same framework, different combining operation, exactly the shift shown between Grid Paths and Minimum/Maximum Path Sum

beginner.content:
Space-Optimized Unique Paths - O(cols) Instead of O(rows × cols)

Since each row's DP values only depend on the PREVIOUS row (and the current row being built left to right), a single 1D array can be reused and updated in place - no need to store the whole 2D grid.

expert.content:
The Closed-Form Combinatorial Solution - O(1) (Ignoring Factorial Cost)

Unique Paths has a direct combinatorial answer: reaching the bottom-right requires exactly (rows-1) "down" moves and (cols-1) "right" moves, in ANY order - the count is the binomial coefficient C(rows+cols-2, rows-1). This avoids DP entirely for this specific (no-obstacle) variant.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why does the space-optimized version reuse the SAME array for every row?Before dp[c] is updated in the current row, it still holds the PREVIOUS row's value at that column - exactly "from above"; adding dp[c-1] (already updated for the current row) supplies "from left", so one array serves both roles correctly
Why doesn't the combinatorial formula work once obstacles are introduced?Obstacles break the clean "any arrangement of R downs and C rights" symmetry - specific paths become invalid in ways that don't reduce to a simple binomial coefficient, forcing a return to DP
What's the risk of computing C(n, k) via factorials directly (n! / (k! * (n-k)!))?Intermediate factorial values can overflow long very quickly for even moderately sized n - the iterative multiply-then-divide approach shown avoids this by keeping intermediate values smaller

beginner.content:
Minimizing the Sum Along a Path

Same grid-DP framework as Unique Paths, with the combine operation changed from SUM to MIN: dp[r][c] = grid[r][c] + min(dp[r-1][c], dp[r][c-1]) - each cell picks whichever of "from above" or "from left" gives the cheaper running total.

expert.content:
Reconstructing the Actual Minimum Path, Not Just Its Sum

To recover the actual PATH (not just its total cost), trace BACKWARD from the bottom-right: at each cell, check which neighbor (above or left) the DP value came from, and follow that trail back to the start.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the space-optimized time/space complexity for Minimum Path Sum?O(rows*cols) time, O(cols) space with a rolling 1D array - the same optimization applicable to Unique Paths transfers directly here
Why can path reconstruction only trace BACKWARD, not forward from the start?Each dp[r][c] value doesn't record WHICH neighbor it came from during the forward pass; re-deriving that choice requires comparing dp[r-1][c] vs dp[r][c-1] again during a backward trace - or maintaining an explicit "came from" pointer array during the forward pass instead
How would this problem change if diagonal movement were also allowed?The recurrence would need a third term: dp[r][c] = grid[r][c] + min(dp[r-1][c], dp[r][c-1], dp[r-1][c-1]) - same framework, one more neighbor to consider

beginner.content:
Each Item Taken At Most Once

Given items with weight and value, and a capacity, maximize value - each item is either taken WHOLE or not at all (unlike Fractional Knapsack). dp[i][w] = best value using the first i items with capacity w: either skip item i, or take it (if it fits) and add its value to the best result with the remaining capacity.

expert.content:
Space Optimization - Why the Weight Loop Must Go BACKWARD

Since dp[i][w] only depends on ROW i-1, a single 1D array can replace the 2D table - BUT the capacity loop must iterate BACKWARD (high to low). Forward iteration would let an item's own contribution leak into its OWN calculation within the same row, incorrectly allowing that item to be used more than once (turning 0/1 Knapsack into Unbounded Knapsack by accident).

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time and space complexity of 0/1 Knapsack?O(n * capacity) time; O(n * capacity) space for the 2D version, reducible to O(capacity) with the backward-iteration 1D optimization
Why must the space-optimized version iterate the capacity loop BACKWARD?Forward iteration would read dp[w - weight] AFTER it's already been updated for the CURRENT item in this same pass, effectively allowing the item to be counted twice - backward iteration guarantees dp[w - weight] still reflects the PREVIOUS item's state
Is 0/1 Knapsack NP-hard?The general (unbounded-weight, unbounded-capacity) version is NP-hard, but the DP solution shown is "pseudo-polynomial" - O(n*capacity) is polynomial in the VALUE of capacity, not in the number of BITS needed to represent it, which is why it's fast in practice for reasonable capacities but not truly polynomial-time

beginner.content:
Unlimited Copies of Each Item Allowed

Same setup as 0/1 Knapsack, but each item can be used ANY number of times. The only change to the space-optimized 0/1 solution: iterate the capacity loop FORWARD instead of backward - this lets an item's own just-updated value be reused within the same pass, exactly enabling repeated use.

expert.content:
Rod Cutting - Unbounded Knapsack in Disguise

Given a rod of length n and prices for each possible cut length, maximize revenue by cutting it into pieces (each length usable ANY number of times, in any combination) - exactly Unbounded Knapsack with "weight" = piece length and "value" = piece price.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the ONE-line difference between 0/1 and Unbounded Knapsack's space-optimized code?The capacity loop direction: backward (high to low) for 0/1 Knapsack, forward (low to high) for Unbounded Knapsack - everything else is identical
What other classic problems reduce to Unbounded Knapsack?Coin Change (minimum coins to make an amount, using unlimited coins of each denomination) and Rod Cutting both share the identical "unlimited reuse, maximize/minimize a value" structure
What's the time and space complexity of Unbounded Knapsack?O(n * capacity) time, O(capacity) space with the 1D optimization - same complexity class as 0/1 Knapsack, just a different reuse policy

beginner.content:
Each Item Has a Limited Quantity Available

A middle ground between 0/1 (quantity 1) and Unbounded (unlimited quantity): each item has a SPECIFIC count available. The naive approach treats each available copy as a separate 0/1 item - correct, but wasteful if counts are large.

expert.content:
Binary (Power-of-2) Grouping - O(n × log(count) × capacity)

Expanding into individual copies is O(sum of counts × capacity) - slow when counts are large. The optimization: group each item's available count into chunks of size 1, 2, 4, 8, ... (binary representation) - any quantity from 0 to count can be formed by SOME subset of these chunks, so treating each chunk as one 0/1 "super-item" covers all possibilities in far fewer iterations.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why does binary grouping into {1, 2, 4, 8, ...} chunks cover every possible quantity?Any integer can be represented as a sum of distinct powers of 2 (binary representation) - so choosing any subset of the power-of-2 chunks can reconstruct any count from 0 up to the total available
How does binary grouping improve the time complexity?Instead of O(count) separate 0/1 items per original item, it needs only O(log(count)) "super-items" - reducing overall complexity from O(sum(counts) * capacity) to O(n * log(maxCount) * capacity)
When does Bounded Knapsack reduce to 0/1 or Unbounded Knapsack as special cases?counts[i] = 1 for all items reduces to 0/1 Knapsack; counts[i] = infinity (or capacity/weights[i]) for all items reduces to Unbounded Knapsack

beginner.content:
Does ANY Subset Sum to a Target?

A yes/no version of 0/1 Knapsack: dp[i][s] = "can the first i elements form sum s?" - true if EITHER skipping element i already achieves s, OR including element i achieves the remaining s - arr[i].

expert.content:
Counting HOW MANY Subsets Sum to a Target

Change the boolean OR to an integer SUM: dp[s] now counts the NUMBER of subsets achieving sum s, not just whether one exists - same backward-iteration structure, different accumulation operation.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time and space complexity of Subset Sum?O(n * target) time, O(target) space with the 1D rolling-array optimization
Why is Subset Sum considered "pseudo-polynomial" rather than truly polynomial?Its complexity depends on the VALUE of target, not the number of bits needed to represent it - for a target with many digits, the algorithm becomes exponentially slower relative to the input's actual encoded size, which is why Subset Sum is technically NP-complete in general
How does Subset Sum relate to Equal Partition and Target Sum?Equal Partition is exactly "does a subset sum to totalSum/2"; Target Sum (with +/- signs) reduces to Subset Sum via algebraic manipulation - both are direct applications of this same core technique

beginner.content:
Can the Array Be Split into Two Equal-Sum Halves?

Directly reduces to Subset Sum: if the total sum is ODD, it's immediately impossible (two integer halves can't sum to an odd total). Otherwise, check if any subset sums to EXACTLY total / 2 - the remaining elements automatically form the other equal half.

expert.content:
Minimum Subset Sum Difference - a Direct Extension

Instead of checking for an EXACT half, find the subset sum CLOSEST to total / 2 - minimizing the difference between the two partition sums. Run the same Subset Sum DP to find ALL achievable sums up to total/2, then the best achievable sum s gives a minimum difference of total - 2*s.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why does an odd total sum immediately rule out an equal partition?Two equal integer parts must sum to an even total - an odd total has no possible split into two equal integers
Why does the minimum difference formula use "total - 2*closestSum"?If one partition sums to closestSum, the other sums to (total - closestSum); their difference is (total - closestSum) - closestSum = total - 2*closestSum
What's the time complexity of both problems?O(n * total/2), pseudo-polynomial in the sum's magnitude - same complexity class as plain Subset Sum, since both reduce directly to it

beginner.content:
Assigning + or - to Each Number to Hit a Target

Given numbers and a target, assign a + or - sign to EACH number so the total equals target; count how many ways this is possible. The algebraic trick: split numbers into a POSITIVE group P and NEGATIVE group N. Since sum(P) - sum(N) = target and sum(P) + sum(N) = total, solving gives sum(P) = (total + target) / 2 - turning this into counting Subset Sum ways for that specific value.

expert.content:
Why the Algebraic Reduction to Subset Sum is Valid

The derivation sum(P) = (total + target) / 2 comes directly from solving two simultaneous equations. This reduction is what turns an apparently "assign signs" combinatorics problem into a well-known "count subsets summing to X" problem - recognizing this kind of algebraic transformation is a common and valuable DP interview skill beyond just knowing the Subset Sum template itself.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why check "(total + target) % 2 != 0" before proceeding?sum(P) must be a whole number of actual array elements' worth - if (total + target) is odd, no valid integer split into P and N can satisfy both equations simultaneously
What's the time complexity of Target Sum?O(n * total), pseudo-polynomial - identical complexity class to the Subset Sum counting problem it reduces to
Could Target Sum be solved with plain backtracking instead?Yes, trying + and - at each number - O(2^n) without memoization; the DP reduction avoids that exponential blowup entirely by recognizing the underlying subset-counting structure

beginner.content:
The Classic Two-String DP

dp[i][j] = length of the LCS between the first i characters of A and first j characters of B. If the characters match, extend the diagonal; otherwise, take the best of dropping a character from either string.

expert.content:
Reconstructing the Actual LCS String

Trace BACKWARD from dp[n][m]: if characters match, that character is part of the LCS, move diagonally; otherwise, move toward whichever neighbor (up or left) has the larger value - the same DP table doubles as a path to reconstruct the answer, not just its length.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time and space complexity of LCS?O(n*m) time and space; space reduces to O(min(n,m)) with a rolling 2-row array, since each row only depends on the previous row
How does LCS differ from Longest Common Substring?LCS allows GAPS (non-contiguous matching, order preserved); substring requires CONTIGUOUS matching - the DP recurrence differs specifically in what happens on a mismatch (LCS takes max of two options, substring resets to 0)
What other well-known problems build directly on LCS?Shortest Common Supersequence (length = n + m - LCS length), and the "minimum deletions to make two strings equal" problem (deletions = n + m - 2*LCS length)

beginner.content:
The One Key Difference from LCS

Longest Common Substring requires CONTIGUOUS matching characters. The DP recurrence is almost identical to LCS, but on a mismatch, dp[i][j] RESETS to 0 (instead of taking the max of neighbors) - a broken match must start completely over, since a substring can't have gaps.

expert.content:
Suffix-Based O(n+m) Alternative - Generalized Suffix Trees/Arrays

The O(n·m) DP approach is fine for typical inputs, but for VERY large strings, building a generalized suffix tree (or suffix array with LCP array) over both strings combined finds the longest common substring in O(n+m) - the longest common prefix between any two suffixes from DIFFERENT source strings gives the answer directly.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why does the answer come from tracking a maxLength variable, not just dp[n][m]?Unlike LCS (where the final answer is always at the bottom-right corner), the longest common SUBSTRING can end anywhere in the middle of either string - the maximum dp[i][j] value across the ENTIRE table is the answer, not necessarily the last cell
Can the space be optimized to O(min(n,m))?Yes - each row only depends on the previous row (and the diagonal, which needs care), so a rolling 2-row array works, similar to LCS's space optimization
What's the relationship to Longest Palindromic Substring?Longest Palindromic Substring can be found by computing the Longest Common Substring between the string and its REVERSE - though extra care is needed to ensure the matched substring doesn't span across the "middle" in a way that isn't a true palindrome

beginner.content:
Minimum Insert/Delete/Replace Operations to Transform One String into Another

dp[i][j] = minimum edits to transform the first i characters of A into the first j characters of B. If characters match, no edit needed there; otherwise, take the best of insert, delete, or replace - each corresponding to a specific neighbor in the DP table.

expert.content:
Why Each Operation Maps to a Specific DP Neighbor

  • Insert a character into A (to match B's next char): comes from dp[i][j-1] - A's length stays effectively the same, B's "consumed" pointer advances.
  • Delete a character from A: comes from dp[i-1][j] - A's pointer advances without consuming any of B.
  • Replace a character in A: comes from dp[i-1][j-1] - both pointers advance together.
Understanding WHY each operation maps to that specific neighbor (not just memorizing the formula) is what lets you adapt Edit Distance to variants with different allowed operations or costs.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time and space complexity of Edit Distance?O(n*m) time and space; space reduces to O(min(n,m)) with a rolling 2-row array
What real-world systems use Edit Distance (or variants of it)?Spell checkers (suggesting corrections within a small edit distance), DNA sequence alignment in bioinformatics, and Git's diff algorithms all build on this core idea
How would you restrict Edit Distance to allow only DELETIONS (no insert/replace)?This becomes a direct application of LCS: minimum deletions to transform A into a subsequence of B (or vice versa) equals (length of A) - (LCS length) - a simpler, related problem

beginner.content:
LCS of a String and Its Own Reverse

The cleanest way to see this problem: the Longest Palindromic Subsequence of a string equals the Longest Common Subsequence between that string and its REVERSE. Any common subsequence between a string and its reverse reads the same forward and backward - by definition, a palindrome.

expert.content:
The Direct Interval DP Formulation

An alternative (equivalent) formulation defines dp[i][j] directly as the longest palindromic subsequence within the substring s[i..j] - useful because it generalizes more naturally to related "interval" palindrome problems (like Palindrome Partitioning) that don't reduce as cleanly to plain LCS.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why must the interval-DP version fill by increasing LENGTH, not row by row?dp[i][j] depends on dp[i+1][j-1], a SMALLER interval nested inside it - filling by increasing length guarantees that smaller interval is already computed by the time it's needed
Why does the LCS-with-reverse trick work here but NOT for Longest Palindromic Substring?A subsequence allows gaps, so matching characters between s and reverse(s) at ANY positions still forms a valid palindromic subsequence; a substring requires contiguity, and a naive LCS-with-reverse can accidentally match characters that don't correspond to a genuine contiguous palindrome
How does this relate to "minimum insertions to make a string palindrome"?Minimum insertions = string length - longest palindromic subsequence length - every character NOT part of the LPS needs a matching mirror character inserted

beginner.content:
Minimum Cuts to Split a String into All-Palindrome Pieces

Find the minimum number of cuts so every resulting piece is a palindrome. Two-phase DP: first precompute isPalin[i][j] for every substring (O(n²)), then minCuts[i] = fewest cuts for s[0..i], trying every possible LAST palindrome piece ending at i.

expert.content:
Why Precomputing isPalin[][] First is Essential for Efficiency

Without precomputing, checking whether s[j+1..i] is a palindrome inside the inner loop would cost O(n) per check, making the overall algorithm O(n³). Precomputing the whole isPalin[][] table ONCE (itself O(n²)) turns every subsequent lookup into O(1), reducing the total complexity to O(n²) - a textbook example of "precompute once, query many times" paying off.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the overall time and space complexity of minimum-cut palindrome partitioning?O(n^2) time (precompute table + fill minCuts array), O(n^2) space for the isPalin table
How does this differ from "return ALL possible palindrome partitionings" (a different classic problem)?That variant needs BACKTRACKING to enumerate every valid partition (potentially exponential output size), while this one only needs the MINIMUM cut count, solvable efficiently with pure DP without ever enumerating the actual partitions
Why does the isPalin[][] recurrence check "len <= 2 || isPalin[i+1][j-1]"?A substring of length 1 or 2 is a palindrome iff its endpoints match (no inner substring to check); for length 3+, it additionally requires the INNER substring (excluding both endpoints) to already be a palindrome

beginner.content:
The O(n²) DP Solution

dp[i] = length of the longest increasing subsequence ENDING exactly at index i. For each i, check every earlier j: if arr[j] < arr[i], this element could extend that subsequence.

expert.content:
O(n log n) with Binary Search - the Patience Sorting Trick

Maintain an array tails where tails[k] = the SMALLEST possible tail value of an increasing subsequence of length k+1. For each new number, binary search for where it belongs in tails - this array's LENGTH at the end is the LIS length, even though tails itself isn't necessarily a real subsequence of the input.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why does replacing a value in tails[] not corrupt the final LENGTH answer?tails[] only needs to track the SMALLEST tail achievable for each length - replacing a larger tail with a smaller one for the same length can only help FUTURE extensions, never hurts the count of how many distinct lengths have been achieved
Is tails[] itself a valid increasing subsequence of the input at the end?Not necessarily - its VALUES may not correspond to an actual single subsequence path through the original array; only its LENGTH is guaranteed to equal the true LIS length
Why is this technique called "patience sorting"?It mirrors the card game Patience/Solitaire, where cards are placed onto piles - each pile's top card corresponds to a tails[] entry, and the number of piles needed equals the LIS length

beginner.content:
Counting HOW MANY Longest Increasing Subsequences Exist

Track TWO arrays alongside each other: length[i] = LIS length ending at i (as before), and count[i] = how many distinct LIS of that length end at i. When extending from j to i, if the new length TIES the current best at i, ADD j's count; if it BEATS it, RESET to j's count.

expert.content:
Why "Reset on Strictly Better, Accumulate on Tie" is the Correct Rule

If a new path through j achieves a STRICTLY LONGER subsequence ending at i, all previously-counted (shorter) paths to i are irrelevant to the MAXIMUM length - count[i] must reset to reflect only paths achieving this new best length. If the new path TIES the current best length, it represents an ADDITIONAL distinct way to achieve that same best length, so its count contributes ADDITIONALLY, not by replacing.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time complexity of counting LIS this way?O(n^2), same as the basic O(n^2) LIS length algorithm - tracking two arrays instead of one doesn't change the asymptotic complexity
Can the O(n log n) patience-sorting technique be adapted to count LIS too?Yes, but it requires a more sophisticated data structure (like a Fenwick Tree indexed by value, tracking both max length and count at each position) - significantly more complex than the O(n^2) approach, usually not worth it unless n is very large
Why is the FINAL answer a SUM over all indices with length[i] == maxLength?The overall longest increasing subsequence could end at MULTIPLE different indices - the total count must combine the ways from every ending position that achieves the true maximum length

beginner.content:
Maximize SUM Instead of LENGTH

Same O(n²) LIS shape, but dp[i] tracks the maximum SUM of an increasing subsequence ending at i, not its length: dp[i] = arr[i] + max(dp[j]) for every valid j < i with arr[j] < arr[i].

expert.content:
Why the O(n log n) LIS Trick Doesn't Directly Transfer Here

Patience sorting's "smallest tail per length" invariant only optimizes for LENGTH. For maximum SUM, a subsequence with a smaller tail value isn't necessarily better - a larger tail value might belong to a HIGHER-sum path. This is why Maximum Sum Increasing Subsequence generally stays at O(n²) with plain DP, unless a more sophisticated structure (like a Fenwick Tree indexed by value, storing maximum sum instead of a simple boolean/count) is used to recover O(n log n).

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time complexity of the standard DP solution?O(n^2) - the same nested-loop shape as basic LIS, just tracking a different quantity per cell
Why can't the simple "smallest tail wins" patience-sorting invariant be reused directly?It optimizes purely for subsequence LENGTH; for maximum SUM, a subsequence with a larger tail could still have a much higher total sum, so "smallest tail" is no longer automatically "best" - the optimization criterion has fundamentally changed
What data structure would give a true O(n log n) solution?A Fenwick Tree (or Segment Tree) indexed by VALUE (coordinate-compressed if needed), supporting "query the maximum sum among all values less than X" and "update the maximum sum achievable ending at value X" - both O(log n) operations

beginner.content:
Finding the Cheapest Order to Multiply a Chain of Matrices

Matrix multiplication is associative but NOT commutative in cost - the number of scalar multiplications needed depends heavily on the PARENTHESIZATION order. dp[i][j] = minimum cost to multiply matrices i through j, trying every possible SPLIT point k as the "last" multiplication.

expert.content:
Why the Cost Formula is dims[i-1] * dims[k] * dims[j]

When splitting the chain at k, everything from i to k multiplies into ONE matrix of size dims[i-1] × dims[k], and everything from k+1 to j multiplies into ONE matrix of size dims[k] × dims[j]. Multiplying those two RESULTING matrices together costs exactly dims[i-1] × dims[k] × dims[j] scalar multiplications (standard matrix multiplication cost formula) - this FINAL combining step's cost is added on top of whatever it cost to build each half (dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j]).

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time and space complexity of Matrix Chain Multiplication?O(n^3) time (O(n^2) subproblems, each trying O(n) split points), O(n^2) space for the DP table
Why must the DP fill by increasing chain LENGTH rather than a simple nested row/column loop?dp[i][j] depends on dp[i][k] and dp[k+1][j] for various k - both are SHORTER sub-chains strictly contained within [i,j], so they must already be computed, which increasing-length filling guarantees
What's the relationship between Matrix Chain Multiplication and Optimal BST / Burst Balloons?All three share the "interval DP" template: dp[i][j] combines results from a split point k within the interval, trying every possible k - the specific cost function differs, but the fill-by-increasing-length structure is identical across all three

beginner.content:
Maximize Coins from Bursting Balloons in Order

Bursting a balloon at position k earns coins[left] * coins[k] * coins[right], where left/right are the CURRENTLY ADJACENT balloons (after previously burst ones are gone). The trick that makes this DP-friendly: think BACKWARD - instead of "which balloon do I burst first", ask "which balloon do I burst LAST within this range" - that balloon's neighbors at burst time are fixed as the range's boundaries, regardless of what happens inside.

expert.content:
Why "Burst Last" (Not "Burst First") is the Key Reframing

If you think about which balloon to burst FIRST, its neighbors change unpredictably depending on what gets burst around it later - a nightmare to model with clean subproblems. But if you decide which balloon burst LAST within a range, its neighbors at that final moment are GUARANTEED to be the range's own boundaries (nothing between them and the range edges is left, since everything else in the range was already burst) - this fixed boundary is exactly what makes clean, independent left/right subproblems possible.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why are virtual boundary balloons of value 1 added at both ends?They uniformly handle the edge case of bursting the actual leftmost/rightmost balloon in the original array, without needing special-case boundary logic - a balloon at the true edge simply multiplies by 1 on that side
What's the time and space complexity of Burst Balloons?O(n^3) time (O(n^2) intervals, each trying O(n) possible "last burst" choices), O(n^2) space for the DP table
What class of problems benefit from this "think about the LAST/OUTERMOST choice" reframing technique?Any interval DP problem where the natural "first choice" creates unpredictable dependencies - Matrix Chain Multiplication (last multiplication) and Optimal BST (root choice) use closely related reframing ideas

beginner.content:
Building a BST That Minimizes Expected Search Cost

Given keys with KNOWN search frequencies, arrange them into a BST minimizing total weighted search cost (frequency × depth, summed over all keys) - keys searched more often should sit CLOSER to the root. Interval DP: try every key as the ROOT of a range, recursively optimizing the left and right subtrees.

expert.content:
Why "+ freqSum" Correctly Accounts for the Depth Increase

Choosing ANY key r as the root of range [i, j] pushes EVERY OTHER key in that range one level DEEPER than it was within its own subtree's local optimum - adding the sum of ALL frequencies in the range (not just the root's) captures this uniform "+1 depth for everyone" effect in one term, without needing to individually track and re-add depth for every key separately.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time complexity of Optimal BST?O(n^3) naively (O(n^2) subproblems, each trying O(n) root choices, plus O(n) to sum frequencies each time) - improvable to O(n^2) by precomputing prefix sums of frequencies
How does Optimal BST relate to Huffman Coding?Both minimize a weighted-depth objective (frequency times depth), but Huffman builds the tree BOTTOM-UP greedily with no ordering constraint, while Optimal BST must respect the KEYS' SORTED ORDER (it's a valid search tree), which is exactly why Optimal BST needs DP instead of a simple greedy merge
What real system design problem resembles Optimal BST?Designing a decision tree or lookup structure where some keys are queried far more often than others - placing hot keys near the root minimizes average lookup cost, the same principle as caching frequently-accessed data closer to fast storage

beginner.content:
Diameter as a Tree DP Problem

Framing Diameter of a Tree formally as Tree DP: define dp[node] = height of the subtree rooted at node. The diameter THROUGH any node is dp[left] + dp[right] - computed as a side effect while the height itself is computed bottom-up (postorder), same technique covered under Trees, now explicitly named as a Tree DP pattern.

expert.content:
The General Tree DP Template This Problem Demonstrates

Tree DP always follows the same shape: define a value at each node that depends ONLY on its children's values (never its parent's), compute it POSTORDER (children before parent), and optionally track a GLOBAL best answer as a side effect while doing so. Diameter, Maximum Path Sum, and Tree Independent Set all follow this exact template with different per-node DP values.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why must Tree DP be computed POSTORDER, not preorder?A node's DP value depends on its CHILDREN's already-computed values - postorder guarantees children are fully processed before the parent needs their results
What's the time and space complexity of Diameter via Tree DP?O(n) time (single postorder pass, every node visited once), O(h) space for the recursion call stack
How does the "return value for parent" differ from the "global answer tracked as a side effect"?The return value is what the PARENT needs to compute ITS OWN local value (e.g. height, so the parent can compute height+1); the global side-effect variable tracks the best answer seen ANYWHERE in the tree, which the parent doesn't need and shouldn't propagate

beginner.content:
Maximum Sum Path Between ANY Two Nodes

Unlike a root-to-leaf path, this path can START and END anywhere, possibly "bending" at some peak node. Each node returns the best DOWNWARD-only extension it can offer its parent (since a parent can only chain ONE side, not both), while separately tracking the GLOBAL best full path (which CAN use both children at a peak).

expert.content:
Why the Return Value Differs from the Global Answer

This is the trickiest part of the problem: a path going UP through a node to its parent can only continue in ONE direction (a path can't branch), so the return value only offers the BETTER of left/right. But the GLOBAL best path, evaluated AT this node, CAN legitimately use both children simultaneously (forming a "peak" shape) - since that full path doesn't need to extend any further upward. Confusing these two different quantities is the single most common bug in this problem.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why clamp negative gains to 0 with Math.max(0, ...)?Extending a path through a negative-contribution subtree would only REDUCE the total sum - it's always at least as good to simply not include that side at all, treating its contribution as 0
What's the time and space complexity?O(n) time (one postorder pass), O(h) space for the recursion stack
What edge case does an all-negative tree test, and does this solution handle it?maxPathSum must be seeded at Integer.MIN_VALUE (not 0), since a valid path must include at least ONE node - even the single least-negative node should be reported correctly as the answer, which this seeding correctly allows

beginner.content:
House Robber III - Maximum Weight Independent Set on a Tree

Select a subset of nodes with MAXIMUM total value, such that no two selected nodes are directly connected (parent-child) - the tree version of House Robber. Each node returns TWO values to its parent: the best sum IF this node is included, and the best sum IF it's excluded.

expert.content:
Why "Excluded" Takes max(child.included, child.excluded) But "Included" Forces child.excluded

This asymmetry is the crux of the problem: including the CURRENT node FORCES both children to be excluded (they're directly adjacent - can't both be selected). But excluding the current node imposes NO constraint on the children relative to each other - each child is free to independently be included OR excluded, whichever gives IT the better local result.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time and space complexity?O(n) time (one postorder pass), O(h) space for recursion - each node does O(1) work combining its children's results
How does this generalize the array-based House Robber?Array House Robber's "adjacent" means consecutive INDEX; Tree Independent Set's "adjacent" means direct parent-child EDGE - the core include/exclude decision logic is conceptually identical, just applied to a tree structure instead of a linear array
Could this be solved with memoization on a HashMap instead of returning tuples?Yes - functionally equivalent, though returning a tuple directly (as shown) avoids the overhead of hashing tree node references and is generally the cleaner idiomatic solution for this specific problem

beginner.content:
Visit Every City Exactly Once, Minimize Total Distance

Brute force tries all n! orderings. Bitmask DP reduces this to O(2ⁿ × n²): the STATE is (mask, current city), where mask is a BITMASK recording which cities have been visited. Since only "which cities visited so far" and "where I am now" matter (not the exact visiting ORDER), this compresses the state space enormously.

expert.content:
Why the Bitmask Captures Everything Needed - and What It Deliberately Ignores

The key insight enabling this optimization: the FUTURE optimal path from state (mask, u) depends only on WHICH cities remain unvisited and WHERE we currently are - NOT on the specific ORDER those visited cities were reached in. This means many different visiting orders that happen to reach the same (mask, current city) pair can share ONE computed answer, collapsing what would be n! distinct paths down to just 2ⁿ × n distinct states.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time and space complexity of the bitmask DP TSP solution?O(2^n * n^2) time, O(2^n * n) space - exponential, but a massive improvement over the O(n!) brute force, making n up to roughly 20 feasible instead of only 10-11
Is TSP NP-hard, and does this DP solve it in polynomial time?TSP is NP-hard; this Held-Karp DP algorithm is still exponential (O(2^n * n^2)), just a much better exponential base than brute force - no known polynomial-time exact algorithm exists
What real-world problems reduce to (or approximate) TSP?Vehicle routing / delivery route optimization, circuit board drilling (minimizing tool travel distance), and DNA sequencing (fragment assembly ordering) - for large n, heuristics/approximations are used instead of exact DP

beginner.content:
Assigning N Workers to N Tasks, Minimizing Total Cost

Each worker has a different cost for each task; assign each worker to exactly one task (and vice versa) to minimize total cost. Same bitmask DP shape as TSP: state = (worker index, mask of tasks already assigned) - since workers are processed in a fixed order, only the current worker index and which tasks remain matter.

expert.content:
Why This is O(n × 2ⁿ) Instead of TSP's O(2ⁿ × n²)

Assignment Problem's state only needs "which WORKER we're on" (not which specific PATH of workers, since they're always processed 0, 1, 2, ... in order) - this is strictly simpler than TSP's state, which needs "current CITY" because the visiting order isn't fixed. This subtle structural difference is why Assignment Problem's bitmask DP is faster than TSP's despite looking superficially similar.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time and space complexity of the bitmask DP solution?O(n * 2^n) time, O(n * 2^n) space - exponential but far better than the O(n!) brute force of trying every permutation of worker-task pairings
What polynomial-time algorithm exists for Assignment Problem, and why doesn't TSP have an equivalent?The Hungarian Algorithm solves Assignment Problem in O(n^3) - genuinely polynomial. TSP has no known polynomial algorithm because it's NP-hard; Assignment Problem, despite looking similar, is actually a much "easier" problem (solvable via network flow / matching theory)
When would the bitmask DP approach still be preferred over the Hungarian Algorithm?When n is small enough that O(n * 2^n) is fast, and implementation simplicity matters more than optimality of complexity - the Hungarian Algorithm is considerably more intricate to implement correctly

beginner.content:
Counting Numbers in [0, N] With a Property, Digit by Digit

Digit DP answers questions like "how many numbers up to N contain no digit greater than 5" WITHOUT iterating every number individually (impossible for huge N). It builds the number ONE DIGIT AT A TIME, tracking whether the prefix built so far is still "tight" (equal to N's prefix, constraining future digit choices) or already "free" (strictly less, so any digit is allowed).

expert.content:
Why "tight" is the Whole Trick - and Why It Collapses to Just 2 States

Without the tight/free distinction, you'd need to track the ENTIRE prefix built so far to know what digits remain legal - infeasible for large N. The insight: only ONE bit of information matters - is the prefix built SO FAR still exactly equal to N's corresponding prefix (tight), or has it already gone strictly below (free)? Once free, EVERY remaining digit choice (0-9) is unrestricted, collapsing a seemingly huge state space down to just position × 2 states.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time complexity of Digit DP?O(digits * states * 10), where states is typically small (often just tight/free, sometimes with a few extra tracked properties) - astronomically better than O(N) brute force iteration for large N
Why is memoization keyed on (position, tight) enough, without needing the actual digits chosen?Given position and tight status, the FUTURE counting behavior is completely determined - it doesn't matter WHICH specific digits were chosen to arrive at this state, only where we are and whether we're still constrained
How would you count numbers in a RANGE [L, R] instead of just [0, N]?Compute count(R) - count(L-1), using the same digit DP twice (a common technique to convert a range query into two prefix queries, similar to how prefix sums handle range-sum queries)

beginner.content:
Adding More Tracked Properties to Digit DP

Beyond just "tight or free", Digit DP problems often need EXTRA state to track a running property - counting numbers with no two adjacent equal digits needs the PREVIOUS digit; counting numbers with digit sum divisible by k needs the running SUM MOD k. Each new constraint adds one more dimension to the memoization state.

expert.content:
Tracking Previous Digit - "No Two Adjacent Digits Equal"

Adding a "previous digit" dimension to the state lets the recursion FORBID choosing the same digit twice in a row. This demonstrates the general Digit DP recipe: identify what LOCAL information the constraint needs to check at each step, and add exactly that to the memoization key - nothing more, nothing less.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How do you decide what extra dimensions a Digit DP state needs?Ask: "what LOCAL information does the constraint need to check the NEXT digit choice?" - a digit-sum constraint needs the running sum (mod k, to bound the state space); an adjacency constraint needs the previous digit; the state should capture exactly and only what's needed to continue correctly
Why track sumMod (sum modulo k) rather than the raw running sum?The raw sum can grow unboundedly large for many digits, exploding the state space; since only DIVISIBILITY by k matters for the final answer, tracking just the remainder mod k bounds that dimension to exactly k possible values
What's the general time complexity pattern for Digit DP with extra state dimensions?O(digits * 2 * (extra state size) * 10) - each additional tracked property multiplies the state space, so problems requiring many independent constraints can become expensive; careful state minimization matters
