The Four Core Bitwise Operators

  • & (AND) - 1 only if BOTH bits are 1.
  • | (OR) - 1 if EITHER bit is 1.
  • ^ (XOR) - 1 if the bits are DIFFERENT.
  • ~ (NOT) - flips every bit.
These operate on EVERY bit of an int/long simultaneously, in a single CPU instruction - the reason bit tricks are often dramatically faster than equivalent arithmetic or conditional logic.
codeExplanations: a = 1100, b = 1010 in binary. & keeps a bit only where BOTH a and b have a 1, giving 1000 (8). | keeps a bit where EITHER has a 1, giving 1110 (14). ^ keeps a bit only where a and b DIFFER, giving 0110 (6). ~a flips every one of a's 32 bits, including the sign bit, which is why the result comes out negative (-13) instead of a small flipped number.

expert.content:
Why ~a Equals -(a+1) - Two's Complement Explained

Java integers use TWO'S COMPLEMENT representation: negating a number is done by flipping all bits and adding 1. So ~a (just the flip, no +1) equals -a - 1, or equivalently -(a+1) - which is why ~12 = -13, not -12. Understanding this is essential for correctly reasoning about bit tricks involving negative numbers or NOT.
codeExplanations: The loop prints ~a next to the value -(a+1) predicted by two's complement, for several inputs including 0 and a negative number. Every pair matches, confirming that Java's ~ operator is never a simple "flip the digits" operation on the number you see - it always lands on -(a+1), because flipping all bits of a two's-complement number is mathematically equivalent to negating it and subtracting one.

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the key self-inverse property of XOR, and why is it useful?a ^ a = 0, and a ^ 0 = a - XORing a value with itself cancels it out; this is the foundation of the "find the single non-duplicate" trick and swapping without a temp variable
How do you swap two variables without a temporary variable using XOR?a ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b; - each step uses XOR's self-inverse property to progressively exchange the values, though in practice a temp variable is usually clearer and just as fast
Why are bitwise operators generally faster than equivalent arithmetic operations?They map directly to single CPU instructions operating on all bits in parallel, while operations like division or modulo can require multiple clock cycles - though modern compilers often auto-optimize obvious arithmetic-to-bitwise conversions anyway (e.g. x/2 to x>>1 for unsigned values)

beginner.content:
Shifting Bits - Fast Multiplication/Division by Powers of 2

  • << (left shift) - shifts bits left, filling with 0s. x << n equals x × 2ⁿ.
  • >> (signed right shift) - shifts bits right, preserving the SIGN bit (fills with 1s for negative numbers). x >> n equals x / 2ⁿ (rounding toward negative infinity).
  • >>> (unsigned right shift) - shifts right, always filling with 0s, IGNORING sign - Java-specific, doesn't exist in C/C++.
codeExplanations: 5 << 2 shifts the bits of 5 left by two positions, which is the same as multiplying by 2 squared (4), giving 20. 20 >> 2 shifts right by two, dividing by 4, giving 5. -8 >> 1 shifts right but refills the vacated top bit with the ORIGINAL sign bit (1, since -8 is negative), so the result stays negative (-4). -8 >>> 28 instead refills with 0s regardless of sign, then shifts almost the entire 32-bit pattern out, leaving only the few leading bits of the original number's raw representation.

expert.content:
Why >> and >>> Differ ONLY for Negative Numbers

For positive numbers, both operators behave identically (the sign bit is already 0, so there's nothing different to preserve). The difference only manifests for NEGATIVE numbers: >> replicates the leading 1 (sign bit) as it shifts, keeping the number negative; >>> always fills with 0s, turning a negative number into a large POSITIVE one after shifting - a classic source of bugs when the distinction is forgotten.
codeExplanations: For -16 (negative), >> refills with the sign bit (1) so the number stays negative and shrinks toward zero correctly (-4), while >>> refills with 0s, turning the same bit pattern into a huge positive number because the sign bit is no longer treated specially. For 16 (positive) the sign bit is already 0, so both operators refill with 0s and produce identical results - proving the difference only ever matters for negative inputs.

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why doesn't C/C++ have Java's >>> operator?Java standardized signed integer representation (always two's complement) across all platforms; C/C++ historically left this implementation-defined, so an "unsigned right shift" on a signed type had ambiguous behavior - Java sidesteps this by defining >>> explicitly
Does left shift on a signed integer risk overflow the same way multiplication does?Yes - shifting bits off the left edge silently discards them, exactly like integer overflow from multiplication; x << n for large n can produce unexpected results if bits get shifted out of the 32/64-bit range
Why is x >> 1 sometimes preferred over x / 2 for performance-critical code?Shift is typically a single fast CPU instruction, while division can take multiple cycles - though for POSITIVE numbers specifically, since signed division rounds toward zero while >> rounds toward negative infinity, they only produce identical results for non-negative x

beginner.content:
Turning ON a Specific Bit

To SET bit i (force it to 1, regardless of its current value): OR the number with a mask that has ONLY bit i set - num | (1 << i). OR-ing with 0 leaves other bits unchanged; OR-ing with 1 forces that bit to 1.
codeExplanations: num starts as 0101. setBit(num, 1) builds the mask 1 << 1 = 0010 and ORs it in: any bit that's 1 in either operand becomes 1, so bit 1 flips from 0 to 1, giving 0111. Calling setBit(num, 1) again ORs the same mask into a number that already has bit 1 set - OR-ing a bit that's already 1 with another 1 just stays 1, so the value is unchanged, which is exactly the idempotent behavior "set" should have.

expert.content:
Setting a RANGE of Bits at Once

Setting bits [i, j] (inclusive) in one operation: build a mask with 1s in exactly that range, then OR it in - useful for problems that manipulate contiguous bit ranges (e.g. certain bitmask DP setups, or flag-register manipulation).
codeExplanations: (1 << (j-i+1)) - 1 first builds a block of (j-i+1) consecutive 1 bits at the LOW end of the number (a standard "k ones" trick), then << i slides that whole block left so it lines up exactly with positions i through j. OR-ing that shifted block into num turns on every bit in that range while leaving every other bit untouched, so setBitRange(0, 2, 4) lights up bits 2, 3 and 4 in one operation - shown as 11100 in the output.

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why does OR-ing with (1 << i) only affect bit i?Every other position of the mask is 0, and OR-ing with 0 always leaves the original bit UNCHANGED - only the single 1 bit at position i forces that specific position to 1
What's the time complexity of setting a single bit?O(1) - a single shift and OR operation, regardless of the number's magnitude
How does "((1 << (j-i+1)) - 1)" produce (j-i+1) consecutive 1 bits?1 << (j-i+1) produces a single 1 bit followed by (j-i+1) zeros; subtracting 1 "borrows" through all those zeros, turning them all into 1s - a standard trick for generating a block of k ones

beginner.content:
Turning OFF a Specific Bit

To CLEAR bit i (force it to 0): AND the number with a mask that has a 0 at position i and 1s everywhere else - num & ~(1 << i). AND-ing with 1 leaves a bit unchanged; AND-ing with 0 forces it to 0.
codeExplanations: num starts as 1111. ~(1 << 1) builds the mask 1101 (a single 0 at position 1, 1s everywhere else). ANDing num with that mask forces bit 1 to 0 while leaving every other bit as it was, giving 1101. Running clearBit again on the same number ANDs with the same mask again - bit 1 is already 0, and 0 AND anything stays 0, so the second call is a no-op, matching what "clear" should do to an already-clear bit.

expert.content:
Clearing All Bits FROM the Lowest Set Bit Downward, and Other Tricks

Two related tricks that come up frequently:
  • num & (num - 1) - clears the LOWEST set bit (used in the classic O(set bits) popcount algorithm).
  • num & (-num) - ISOLATES the lowest set bit (used in Fenwick Tree indexing).
Both rely on the same underlying behavior: subtracting 1 from a number flips its lowest set bit to 0 and everything below it to 1.
codeExplanations: num is 1100. num - 1 borrows through the lowest set bit, turning it into 1011 - the lowest 1 becomes 0 and every bit below it becomes 1. ANDing that with the original 1100 keeps only bits that were 1 in both, which excludes the now-zeroed lowest bit and the newly-flipped lower bits, leaving 1000 - the lowest set bit cleared. -num in two's complement equals ~num + 1; ANDing num with -num cancels out every bit except the lowest set one, isolating it as 0100 (decimal 4).

expert.content:

beginner.content:
Flipping a Specific Bit

To TOGGLE bit i (flip 0→1 or 1→0): XOR the number with a mask that has ONLY bit i set - num ^ (1 << i). XOR-ing with 0 leaves a bit unchanged; XOR-ing with 1 flips it - exactly the self-inverse property of XOR.
codeExplanations: num starts as 1010. toggleBit(num, 0) XORs it with 0001: bit 0 is currently 0, and 0 ^ 1 = 1, so it flips on, giving 1011. Calling toggleBit(num, 0) a second time XORs the SAME mask into the new value: bit 0 is now 1, and 1 ^ 1 = 0, so it flips back off, returning exactly to 1010 - demonstrating that XOR-toggling a bit twice is a no-op, since XOR is its own inverse.

expert.content:
Toggling ALL Bits (Bitwise Complement Within N Bits)

Java's ~num flips ALL 32 bits, including leading bits you might not care about, and produces a negative number for any positive input due to sign-bit flipping. To flip only the RELEVANT bits (e.g. within the actual bit-length of a small positive number), build a mask of exactly that many 1s and XOR with it instead of using raw NOT.
codeExplanations: bitLength computes how many bits are actually needed to represent num (e.g. 5 = 101 needs 3 bits). mask = (1 << bitLength) - 1 builds exactly that many 1 bits, matching num's own width - no more, no less. XORing num with that mask flips only those relevant bits (every 1 becomes 0 and every 0 becomes 1 within that width), which is why toggleAllBits(5) correctly gives 2 (010) instead of the huge negative number a raw ~5 would produce by also flipping the unused leading zero bits.

Why does the raw ~ operator misbehave for "toggle all bits of a small number"?~ operates on ALL 32 bits of the int, including unused leading zeros - flipping those turns them into 1s too, producing a large negative number instead of the intended small toggled value confined to the number's actual bit-length

beginner.content:
Testing Whether a Specific Bit is Set

To CHECK bit i: AND the number with a mask having only bit i set, then compare to 0 - (num & (1 << i)) != 0. Every OTHER bit gets ANDed to 0 regardless of its value, leaving only bit i's actual value to determine the result.
codeExplanations: num is 1010. For each i, (1 << i) builds a mask with only bit i set. ANDing num with that mask zeroes out every OTHER bit and leaves bit i's own value in place: for i=1 and i=3 (where num has 1s) the AND is nonzero, so isBitSet returns true; for i=0 and i=2 (where num has 0s) the AND is 0, so it returns false - exactly reproducing num's binary pattern 1010 read right to left.

expert.content:
Iterating Over All Set Bit POSITIONS Efficiently

A common pattern: process every SET bit's position (not just count them). Combine "isolate lowest set bit" with "find its position via a log or built-in bit-count method" - much faster than checking every possible position individually when the number is sparse (few bits set).
codeExplanations: num & (-num) isolates only the lowest set bit of num, and numberOfTrailingZeros converts that single-bit value directly into its position - no scanning loop needed. Each pass records that position, then num &= (num - 1) clears exactly that lowest set bit so the next iteration finds the next-lowest one. For 41 (binary 101001) this visits positions 0, 3, then 5 in three iterations total - one iteration per set bit, not per bit position.

beginner.content:
Counting the Number of 1 Bits (Popcount)

The simplest approach: check each of the 32 bits one at a time with (num >> i) & 1 and add up how many are 1. Correct, but does 32 iterations REGARDLESS of how many bits are actually set.
codeExplanations: The loop checks all 32 possible bit positions one by one with (num >> i) & 1, adding 1 to count every time that bit is 1. For 11 (binary 1011) three positions are 1, so count ends at 3; for 255 (binary 11111111) all eight low bits are 1, so count ends at 8. This always does 32 checks regardless of how many bits are actually set, which is what the Kernighan approach below improves on.

expert.content:
Brian Kernighan's Algorithm - O(Set Bits) Instead of O(32)

Repeatedly apply num & (num - 1), which clears the LOWEST set bit each time. Count how many times you can do this before num becomes 0 - that count IS the number of set bits. For SPARSE numbers (few 1s), this finishes far faster than checking all 32 positions. Java also exposes this natively via Integer.bitCount(), which is intrinsic-optimized by the JVM (often a single hardware POPCNT instruction).
codeExplanations: Each pass of the while loop applies num &= (num - 1), which clears exactly the lowest set bit, and increments count once per pass - so the loop runs exactly as many times as there are 1 bits, not 32 times regardless. Integer.bitCount() does the same job as a single built-in call, which the JVM can compile down to one hardware POPCNT instruction, confirmed here by both approaches agreeing on 3 for the number 11, and 31 for Integer.MAX_VALUE (which is all 1 bits except the sign bit).

beginner.content:
Checking if a Number is a Power of 2, in O(1)

A power of 2 has EXACTLY ONE set bit (e.g. 8 = 1000, 16 = 10000). Recall num & (num - 1) clears the lowest set bit - if num had only ONE set bit to begin with, clearing it leaves 0. So: num > 0 && (num & (num - 1)) == 0.
codeExplanations: num & (num - 1) clears the lowest set bit of num. If num had exactly ONE set bit to begin with (which is what "power of 2" means in binary), clearing it leaves 0, so the equality check passes. 16 (10000) has one set bit so it passes; 18 (10010) has two set bits so clearing the lowest one still leaves a nonzero value, correctly failing. 1 (2^0) also has exactly one bit set, so it passes; 0 is excluded by the num > 0 guard before the bit trick is even evaluated.

expert.content:
Why the num > 0 Guard is Essential

Without the num > 0 check, num = 0 would WRONGLY pass: 0 & (0 - 1) equals 0 & -1, and since -1 in two's complement is all 1 bits, ANDing with it leaves 0 unchanged - giving a false positive for zero, which is NOT a power of 2. Negative numbers are excluded for the same underlying reason: their two's complement representation always has the sign bit set alongside other bits, so this trick alone can't safely distinguish them without the explicit positivity check.
codeExplanations: For zero, 0 - 1 underflows to -1 (all 1 bits in two's complement), and 0 & -1 is still 0 - so the bit trick alone would wrongly call 0 a power of 2, which is why num > 0 is checked first and short-circuits before the trick runs. For -8, the guard also short-circuits immediately, since a negative number can never be a valid power of 2 regardless of what its bit pattern happens to look like.

beginner.content:
The Core XOR Identities

  • a ^ 0 = a - XOR with 0 is the identity operation.
  • a ^ a = 0 - a number XORed with itself cancels out to 0.
  • a ^ b = b ^ a - commutative.
  • (a ^ b) ^ c = a ^ (b ^ c) - associative, so order/grouping in a chain of XORs doesn't matter.
These four identities alone unlock the "find the unique/missing element" family of interview problems.
codeExplanations: a ^ 0 leaves 25 unchanged (identity), and a ^ a cancels to 0 (self-inverse). In the array loop, every value that appears exactly twice gets XORed into unique twice - and since XOR is associative and commutative, those two occurrences always end up cancelling each other out via a^a=0 regardless of what order they appear in, no matter what other values sit between them. The one value that appears only once has nothing to cancel it, so it survives as the final result: 4.

expert.content:
Swap Without a Temp Variable, and Find Two Unique Numbers

XOR's self-inverse property allows swapping two variables without a third: a ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b;. A harder classic: given an array where EXACTLY two numbers appear once and all others appear twice, XOR-ing everything gives x ^ y (the XOR of the two uniques). Find any SET bit in that result - it's a bit where x and y differ - then partition the array by that bit to separate x and y into two independent XOR-reduction groups.
codeExplanations: XORing the whole array cancels every paired value, leaving xorAll = x ^ y (the two uniques combined). xorAll & (-xorAll) isolates one bit where x and y must differ, since a shared bit would have cancelled to 0 in xorAll. Splitting the array by whether each number has that bit set guarantees x and y land in different groups, and within each group every OTHER value still appears in pairs and cancels via XOR - so each group's running XOR converges on exactly one of the two answers: 5 and 3.

beginner.content:
What an XOR Basis Represents

Numbers form a vector space over GF(2) under XOR. An XOR BASIS is a minimal set of numbers such that every XOR combination of ANY subset of the original array can be reproduced by XOR-ing some subset of the basis. Building it lets you answer questions like "what is the maximum possible XOR of any subset?" without checking all 2ⁿ subsets.
codeExplanations: 5, 1 and 2 are three independent "directions" in the bit-vector space, so XOR-ing all of them together (101 ^ 001 ^ 010) walks through each bit position: bit 0 has an odd number of 1s among the three (from 5 and 1), bit 1 has an odd count too (from 2), bit 2 has just one contributor (from 5) - giving 110, which is 6. This single combination is only one of eight possible subset-XOR results the full basis-building example below computes exhaustively.

expert.content:
Building the Basis with Gaussian Elimination over GF(2)

Maintain an array basis[] indexed by bit position (highest bit first). For each new number, reduce it by XOR-ing away any basis vector whose highest set bit matches one of the number's set bits; if the number becomes 0, it was already representable by the existing basis (discard it); otherwise, it contributes a NEW independent direction - insert it at its highest bit position. Once built, the MAXIMUM XOR achievable from the basis is found greedily: XOR the running result with any basis vector that INCREASES it.
codeExplanations: insert() walks a number from its highest bit downward: if a basis slot at that bit position is empty, the number becomes a new basis vector there; otherwise it gets XORed with the existing vector at that bit (eliminating that bit from the number, Gaussian-elimination style) and the walk continues to lower bits. After all four numbers are inserted, maxXor() greedily tries each basis vector from the highest bit down, keeping it only if XOR-ing it in makes the running result strictly bigger - which always sets the most significant available bit first, the same way comparing binary numbers works, arriving at 28.

beginner.content:
Representing a Set of Choices as a Single Integer

A BITMASK uses each bit of an integer to represent whether one item is INCLUDED (1) or EXCLUDED (0) from a set. For n items, an integer from 0 to 2ⁿ - 1 can represent EVERY possible subset - enumerating all 2ⁿ masks enumerates all subsets.
codeExplanations: mask counts from 0 up to 2^n - 1, where n is the number of items - every integer in that range has a unique pattern of 3 bits, and every possible pattern of 3 bits is visited exactly once. For each mask, the inner loop checks bit i with (mask & (1 << i)): a 1 there means item i is included in that mask's subset. Since every combination of "each item in or out" corresponds to exactly one integer, looping over all masks enumerates every one of the 8 possible subsets, from the empty set (mask 0) to all three items (mask 7).

expert.content:
Bitmask as DP/Backtracking State - Traveling Salesman Style

Beyond enumeration, a bitmask can represent "which subset of cities/tasks/items has been VISITED/USED so far", used as the STATE in DP or search. This compresses an otherwise unwieldy set-membership state into a single integer that's cheap to compare, hash, and transition (via OR to add an item, AND-NOT to remove one).
codeExplanations: visited |= (1 << 0) and visited |= (1 << 2) turn on bits 0 and 2, giving the pattern 101 - representing "cities 0 and 2 have been visited." Comparing visited against (1 << n) - 1 (all n bits set) checks whether every city has been visited; here it correctly reports false since city 1 and 3 aren't set. visited &= ~(1 << 0) then clears bit 0 specifically - a classic backtracking "undo" step - dropping the pattern back to 100 (only city 2 remains marked visited).

Why is bitmask enumeration limited to small n (typically n ≤ 20-25)?The number of masks is 2^n - it grows exponentially, so 20 items already means over a million masks; anything larger becomes computationally infeasible for exhaustive enumeration
How do you check if mask represents "all n items included"?Compare mask == (1 << n) - 1 - that expression produces exactly n consecutive 1 bits, the mask value representing full inclusion
Why use a bitmask instead of a boolean array or HashSet for "visited" state in DP?A bitmask is a single primitive int/long - cheap to copy, compare with ==, and use directly as a HashMap/array key, whereas a boolean array or HashSet needs deep comparison and more memory per state, which matters a lot when the DP has millions of states

beginner.content:
Using a Bitmask as a DP Dimension

BITMASK DP extends ordinary DP by adding "which subset of items has been used/visited" as part of the state, encoded as an integer mask. The state becomes dp[mask][...], and transitions move from one mask to another by setting a bit (mask | (1 << i)) when item i gets included.
codeExplanations: dp[mask][last] holds the cheapest cost to have visited exactly the cities in mask, ending at city last. Starting state dp[1][0] = 0 means "only city 0 visited, standing at city 0, cost 0." Each transition takes a reachable (mask, last) state and extends it to an unvisited next city, folding next's bit into mask and adding the travel cost - so by the time mask reaches (1<<n)-1 (all cities visited), the smallest dp[fullMask][last] across every possible last city is the answer to the full tour, which comes out to 17 for this cost matrix.

expert.content:
Complexity and When Bitmask DP is the Right Tool

Bitmask DP's state space is O(2⁽ × n), so it's only practical for small n (typically up to ~20). The classic signal that a problem wants bitmask DP: it involves "assigning/visiting/matching n items" where the OPTIMAL answer genuinely depends on WHICH SPECIFIC subset has been used so far (not just how many) - Traveling Salesman, Assignment Problem, and "count ways to partition into valid groups" problems are the canonical examples.
codeExplanations: dp[mask] is the minimum cost of assigning tasks in mask, one per worker, in worker order 0, 1, 2, .... bitCount(mask) counts how many tasks have already been assigned, which - since workers are filled strictly in order - tells you exactly which worker index is being assigned next, with no need to track it separately. For every unassigned task, the code tries assigning it to that next worker and updates dp[newMask] if the resulting cost is lower, so by the time mask covers all tasks, dp[(1<<n)-1] holds the cheapest full assignment - 12 for this cost matrix.

O(log n) Range Queries AND Point Updates

A Segment Tree is a binary tree where each node covers a RANGE of the array; leaves are single elements, and internal nodes combine their two children's ranges. Both range queries (sum, min, max over [l,r]) and point updates run in O(log n) - beating a plain array's O(n) range query or a prefix-sum array's O(n) update.

expert.content:
Why "No Overlap / Total Overlap / Partial Overlap" is the Whole Algorithm

Every query recursion boils down to exactly THREE cases at each node: the query range doesn't touch this node's range at all (return neutral value, e.g. 0 for sum), the query range FULLY contains this node's range (return the precomputed total directly, no need to go deeper), or PARTIAL overlap (recurse into both children and combine). This three-way split is what bounds the query to O(log n) - only O(log n) nodes ever have partial overlap at each level, and full/no-overlap nodes terminate immediately.

Interview Questions

Why allocate 4*n for the tree array instead of exactly 2n?4n is a safe, simple upper bound that guarantees enough space for a non-perfectly-balanced tree's node indices (based on 1-indexed heap-style numbering) regardless of n's exact value - the precise tight bound is more complex to derive
What's the time complexity of build, query, and update?build: O(n); query and update: O(log n) each - the tree's height bounds all per-operation work
When would you choose a Segment Tree over a Fenwick Tree?When the combine operation isn't simple addition (min, max, GCD - anything without an easy "inverse" for subtraction-based tricks), or when RANGE updates (not just point updates) are needed - Segment Tree with lazy propagation handles that cleanly, while Fenwick Tree needs more specialized tricks

beginner.content:
O(log n) RANGE Updates, Not Just Point Updates

Plain Segment Tree updates ONE element in O(log n). Updating an entire RANGE naively means updating each element individually - O(range size × log n), far too slow for large ranges. Lazy propagation fixes this: mark a node's update as PENDING instead of immediately pushing it to all descendants, only propagating it down when that subtree is actually visited later.

expert.content:
Why "Push Down Only When Visited" Preserves O(log n)

The key insight: a pending lazy update only needs to be PUSHED DOWN to children the moment that subtree is actually touched again by a LATER query or update - not immediately when the update is first applied. This defers potentially O(range size) work into small O(1) pushes that happen naturally, one level at a time, exactly when and where needed - keeping every single operation bounded at O(log n) instead of O(range size).

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the time complexity of range update and range query with lazy propagation?Both O(log n) - the same bound as plain Segment Tree's point operations, now extended to full ranges
Why must every query ALSO check and push down lazy[node], not just updates?A pending update might affect the value a query is about to read - if the query doesn't apply/push the pending update first, it could return a STALE (pre-update) value
What real-world problems need range updates efficiently?Range increment operations in competitive programming (add X to every element in [l,r]), interval-based scheduling/booking systems, and any scenario needing both efficient bulk updates AND efficient range queries simultaneously

beginner.content:
A Simpler O(log n) Structure for Prefix Sums

A Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree) supports point updates and PREFIX sum queries in O(log n), using a single array and clever bit manipulation - no explicit tree nodes or pointers needed, and far less code than a Segment Tree. The trick: index i's value covers a range determined by i's LOWEST SET BIT.

expert.content:
Why i & (-i) Isolates the Lowest Set Bit - and What It Means

In two's complement, -i is the bitwise NOT of i, plus 1. This flips every bit up to and including the lowest set bit, then adding 1 causes ALL those flipped bits to cancel except the original lowest set bit, which survives unchanged. The result: i & (-i) isolates JUST that one bit - which represents exactly how much RESPONSIBILITY index i has (how many array elements its stored value summarizes).

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why does update() move FORWARD (i += lowestBit) but prefixSum() moves BACKWARD (i -= lowestBit)?update() must touch every ancestor whose range INCLUDES index i - moving forward via the parent-in-the-tree relationship; prefixSum() must sum up disjoint ranges that TOGETHER cover [1, i] - moving backward decomposes i into those ranges
Why is Fenwick Tree usually preferred over Segment Tree for simple prefix/range SUM problems?Far less code (single array, no recursion needed), better constant factors (simpler bit operations vs tree traversal), and easier to implement correctly under interview time pressure - though it's less flexible for non-sum operations (min/max don't have the needed "inverse" for range subtraction)
Can a Fenwick Tree support RANGE updates with point queries, or range updates with range queries?Yes, with a trick: maintaining TWO Fenwick Trees together can support range updates and range sum queries simultaneously, using a mathematical transformation similar in spirit to how difference arrays extend plain prefix sums

cheatNotes: Big-O notation - Describes worst-case growth rate of time/space vs input size
O(1) - Constant time, e.g. array index access
O(log n) - Logarithmic time, e.g. binary search
O(n) - Linear time, e.g. a single pass over an array
O(n log n) - Linearithmic time, e.g. merge sort, quicksort (average case)
O(n^2) - Quadratic time, e.g. nested loops, bubble sort
O(2^n) - Exponential time, e.g. naive recursive Fibonacci
Two Pointers - Two indices moving through data, usually O(n)
Sliding Window - A moving subrange, avoids recomputing overlapping work
Prefix Sum - Precomputed running totals for O(1) range-sum queries
Fast & Slow Pointers - Floyd's cycle detection in a linked list
Monotonic Stack - A stack kept increasing/decreasing to answer next-greater/smaller in O(n)
BFS - Level-by-level graph traversal using a Queue, finds shortest path (unweighted)
DFS - Depth-first graph traversal using a Stack/recursion
Union-Find (DSU) - Tracks connected components with near-O(1) union/find
Dijkstra - Shortest path in a weighted graph with non-negative edges
Dynamic Programming - Caches subproblem results (memoization/tabulation) to avoid recomputation
0/1 Knapsack - Each item taken at most once, classic 2D DP
Backtracking - Try, recurse, undo - explores all valid combinations with pruning
Greedy - Makes the locally optimal choice at each step; correct only when the problem has the greedy-choice property
Trie - A tree of characters for O(word length) prefix search
Segment Tree / Fenwick Tree - O(log n) range query and point update
